Expression and Purification of Human-Glutamylcysteine Synthetase

γ-Glutamylcysteine synthetase (γ-GCS) catalyzes the ATP-dependent ligation ofl-glutamate andl-cysteine to forml-γ-glutamyl-l-cysteine; this is the first and rate-limiting step in glutathione biosynthesis. Inhibitors of γ-GCS such as buthionine sulfoximine are widely used as tools for elucidating glutathione metabolismin vivoand as pharmacological agents for reversing glutathione-based resistance to chemotherapy and radiation therapy in certain cancers. Although γ-GCS is readily isolated from rat kidneys, future drug design efforts are better based on structure–activity relationships established with the human enzyme. We report here the coexpression inEscherichia coliBL21(DE3) of the human γ-GCS catalytic (heavy) subunit and regulatory (light) subunit using pET-3d and pET-9d vectors, respectively. Intracellular assembly of the holoenzyme occurred without difficulty, and levels of expression were acceptable (∼32 mg holoenzyme/100 g cells). Recombinant human γ-GCS was purified to homogeneity in an overall yield of 45% by ammonium sulfate fractionation followed by sequential chromatography on Q-Sepharose ion-exchange, Superdex 200 gel filtration and ATP-affinity resins. Trace amounts ofE. coliγ-GCS were removed by immunoaffinity chromatography. The specific activity of the isolated enzyme was >1500 units/mg, comparable to the best preparations from rat kidney. TheKmvalues forl-glutamate,l-cysteine,l-γ-aminobutyrate (anl-cysteine surrogate), and ATP are 1.8, 0.1, 1.3, and 0.4 mM, respectively.

Recombinant human γ-GCS, like native rat γ-GCS, is feedback inhibited by glutathione and is potently inhibited by buthionine sulfoximine and cystamine.

INTRODUCTION
γ-Glutamylcysteine synthetase (-GCS)3 catalyzes the reaction L-Glutamate L-Cysteine ATP 3 L--Glutamyl-L-Cysteine ADP Pi[Reaction 1] the ®rst and rate-limiting step in glutathione (L-- glutamyl-L-cysteinylglycine, GSH) biosynthesis (1, 2). The mammalian enzyme is a heterodimer composed of a catalytic (heavy) subunit, Mr 73,000, and a regulatory (light) subunit, Mr 31,000. Association of the subunits is maintained by at least one disul®de bond in addition to noncovalent forces (3). Studies with both native and recombinant rat-GCS demonstrate that the isolated heavy subunit is competent to carry out Reaction 1 as well as all known partial reactions associated with the-GCS holoenzyme (2±4). However, when the light subunit is present, the Km for L-glutamate is reportedly reduced from 18 to 1.4 mM and the Ki for nonallosteric inhibition by GSH is increased from 1.8 to 8.2 mM (4, 5). Because intracellular levels of L-glutamate and GSH are 1± 3 and 1± 10 mM, respectively, it was concluded that presence of the light subunit is necessary for full activity of-GCS in vivo (4, 5).

Consistent with the central role played by GSH in cellular defenses against reactive oxygen species and electrophiles, GSH and the enzymes for its synthesis have been found in every mammalian cell line and tissue examined (2). Intracellular levels of GSH are regulated in part by the amount of-GCS present; feedback inhibition of-GCS by GSH, L-cysteine availability, and the rate at which GSH is transported out of the cell also contribute to GSH homeostasis (1, 2). In 1987 Vistica and colleagues (6) reported that a subpopulation of L1210 leukemia cells maintained a 1.5to 2-fold higher than normal GSH level as a result of-GCS overexpression and that the elevated GSH level accounted for the resistance of those cells to melphalan, a DNA cross-linking agent used in cancer chemotherapy. Similar observations were subsequently made with other tumor cell lines and with fresh tissue samples obtained from tumor-bearing animals and patients (7, 8). It is now clear that overexpression of-GCS can play an important role in the resistance of tumors to radiation therapy and to chemotherapy with redox cycling drugs (e.g., doxorubicin) and bifunctional alkylating agents (e.g., cis-platin, melphalan, or cyclophosphamide) (7, 8).

Animal studies and preliminary clinical trial results suggest further that administration of-GCS inhibitors such as buthionine sulfoximine (BSO) can in some systems reverse resistance to therapy based on overexpression of-GCS (1, 2, 7±9). Although BSO is currently in clinical trial for malignant melanoma and ovarian cancer as an adjuvant to melphalan (8, 10±12), it is not suf®ciently potent to allow complete-GCS inhibition to be easily maintained in vivo. In addition, BSO is rapidly excreted in the urine, necessitating administration of large amounts of drug (12±14). In order to develop and adequately test novel, improved-GCSinhibitors, we required a source of the relevant target enzyme, human-GCS. Because R. T. Mulcahy and co-workers had previously reported the cloning of the human liver heavy (15) and light (16)-GCS subunits and were willing to provide cDNA samples to us, we have undertaken the expression and puri®cation of human-GCS. We report here the results of those studies.

MATERIALS AND METHODS 
Materials E. coli BL21(DE3) and the expression vectors pET-3d and pET-9d were purchased from Novagen (Madison, WI). E. coli strain DH5 was obtained from Bethesda Research Laboratory (Gaithersburg, MD).

Restriction enzymes were purchased from New England Biolabs (Beverly, MA), and Pfu DNA polymerase and deoxynucleotides were purchased from Stratagene (La Jolla, CA). Deoxyoligonucleotides were synthesized by Operon Technologies, Inc. (Alameda, CA). Ampicillin, kanamycin, and isopropyl--D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) were obtained from United States Biochemical (Cleveland, OH). L-Buthionine-S,R-sulfoximine (BSO) was prepared as described previously (17). All other biochemical reagents were purchased from Sigma (St. Louis, MO). The cDNA for the heavy and the light subunits cloned in pSK-Bluescript vectors were a generous gift from R. T. Mulcahy (Department of Human Oncology, University of Wisconsin Medical School, Madison, WI). Rabbit antibodies to rat-GCS were prepared by Dr.Jihong Han of this laboratory using enzyme prepared essentially as described by Seelig and Meister (18). Methods Qiagen (Chatsworth, CA) plasmid mini kits were used to isolate plasmid DNA from bacterial cultures. Qiaex reagents and protocols, also from Qiagen, were used for the extraction of nucleic acid fragments from agarose gels. DNA sequencing was performed on an ALF automated sequencer using autoread kits and protocols provided by Pharmacia (Milwaukee, WI). Amino acid composition and N-terminal sequence analyses were performed by the Protein and Nucleic Acid Shared Facility of the Medical College of Wisconsin.

The ratio of light to heavy-GCS subunits in the ®nal preparation was calculated from quantitative amino acid data obtained following hydrolysis of subunits extracted from an SDS±PAGEgel. The amountof subunit was calculated from the most reliably determined amino acids ( 87% agreement with cDNAbased expectation); these were mainly the highly stable aliphatic amino acids and, for the heavy subunit, Tyr and Phe. The latter were too rare in the light subunit to accurately quantitate. Construction of the Expression Plasmids The pSK-GCS50 (15) and pSK-sGCS-7 (16) plasmids provided by Dr. Mulcahy were used to construct expression plasmids for the heavy and light subunits of human-GCS, respectively. Inserts for expression of nonfusion proteins using the pET-3d and pET-9dexpression vectors (19) were designed using a naturally occurring NcoI site at the 5 terminus of the coding sequence of each subunit and a BamHI restriction site engineered onto the 3 end of each cDNA. Since these restriction sites were not unique in either cDNA, a multiple fragment ligation strategy was devised (Fig. 1).

Although most of the necessary fragments could be directly obtained by appropriate restriction digestion of the original plasmids, the 3 portion of each cDNA had to be generated by PCR in order to include the BamHI site. Ampli®cation of the 3 fragment needed for the heavy subunit cDNAwasachieved using a complementary upstream primer (5-CTGATGAAATGAATTATAGCCTTA-3) and a downstream primer containing the two substitutions in the noncoding region, indicated in boldface type, necessary to create the BamHI site (5GAGAGGCATGGTACTGGATCCAGTTCGTCAATA3). Similarly, ampli®cation of the 3 fragment needed for the light subunit was achieved using a complementary 5 primer (5-AAACTTAGTTCAGAGCAAAAAGA3) and a downstream primer containing two substitutions in the noncoding region (5-ATTACAGGTAAGTTAGGATCCTAAGTCAGTTAAGA-3). Ampli®cation of the 3 fragments of each cDNA was carried out using Pfu DNApolymerase and 25 cycles of denaturation (94°C for 1 min), annealing (52°C for 50 s), and extension (72°C for 50 s), followed by a cycle of denaturation (94°C for 1 min), annealing (52°C for 50 s), and extension (72°C for 5 min). The fragments thus produced were separated by agarose gel electrophoresis, excised from the gel, and isolated.

ThePCR-ampli®ed192-bpfragmentcorrespondingtothe 3 portion of the heavy subunit was cleaved with BsmI and BamHI restriction endonucleases to generate the required 106-bp fragment; the 402-bp fragment corresponding to the light subunit was cleaved with BglI and BamHI restriction endonucleases to produce the necessary 99-bp fragment. Ligation of the gel-puri®ed fragments produced the required expression vectors. Thus, the 493-bp NcoI± BstXI, 1354-bp BstXI±BsmI, 106-bp BsmI±BamHI fragments were mixed with the 4601-bp BamHI±NcoI DNA fragment of pET-3d for a four-fragment ligation to construct the heavy subunit expression plasmid (pHGCSH-3d, Fig. 1A). Similarly, the light subunit expression plasmid (pHGCSL-9d, Fig. 1B) was constructed by ligation of the 736-bp NcoI±BglI and 99-bp BglI±BamHI coding fragments with the 4302-bp BamHI±NcoI fragment from pET-9d. Competent DH5 cells were transformed with the individual ligation mixtures, and ampicillin- or kanamycin-resistant cells were selected for the heavy or light subunit, respectively. Plasmids were puri®ed from single colonies. Correct fragment assembly was established by restriction mapping, and the sequence of the PCR-ampli®ed region of each plasmid was con®rmed by chain-termination sequencing (20). The validated plasmids for the heavy and light subunits were cotransformed into BL21(DE3), and cells resistant to both ampicillin and kanamycin were selected.

Expression of Human-GCS Single isolated colonies of transformed BL21(DE3) cells were inoculated into 2 YT medium (21) containing 200 g/ml ampicillin, 100 g/ml kanamycin and grown with shaking at 30°C. Expression of human-GCS was induced by addition of 2 mM IPTG when A600 was 1.5. At that time, additional ampicillin (200 g/ml) and kanamycin (100 g/ml) were added to ensure growth of only plasmid-containing cells, and glycerol (2% ®nal concentration) was added because it improved expression. The culture was allowed to grow until A600 was 3.2, and the cells were then harvested by centrifugation at 5000g for 15 min. Puri®cation of Human-GCS The entire procedure was carried out at 4°C. Bacterial pellets were suspended in 345 ml of homogenization buffer (50 mM Tris±HCl, pH 7.4, 5 mM L-glutamate, 5 mM MgCl2, 10% glycerol, 5 g/ml bovine pancreas ribonuclease, 5 g/ml bovine pancreas deoxyribonuclease, and a protease cocktail containing 1 g/ml each of leupeptin, pepstatin A, antipain, chymostatin, bestatin, and trypsin inhibitor). The cells were broken using a French Press at 16,000 psi, and a supernatant fraction was obtained by centrifugation of the crude homogenate at 30,000g for 45 min.

That solution was fractionated by adding solid ammonium sulfate to 40% saturation (226 g/liter solution), stirring for 30 min, and discarding the pellet obtained by centrifugation (30,000g for 40 min). The supernatant was brought to 60% saturation with ammonium sulfate by adding 120 g/liter, and after stirring 30 min, the pellet was collected by centrifugation and dissolved in 200 ml of isolation buffer (50 mM Tris±HCl buffer, pH 7.4, containing 5 mM L-glutamate, and 5 mM MgCl2). That solution was dialyzed overnight against 8 liters of isolation buffer and was then applied to a 2.5 40 cm column of Q-Sepharose anion-exchange resin (Pharmacia) equilibrated with the same buffer. After the resin was washed with isolation buffer until the A280 was 0.25,-GCS was eluted using a linear gradient established between 0 and 0.4 M NaClinisolation buffer. Activity-containing fractions from the Q-Sepharose chromatography were pooled and-GCS was precipitated by addition of ammonium sulfate (500 g/liter).

The pellet obtained by centrifugation was dissolved in 20 mM imidazole buffer, pH 7, containing 120 mM NaCl, 5 mM L-glutamate, and 5 mM MgCl2, and that solution was applied to a 1.6 85 cm Superdex 200 gel ®ltration column (Pharmacia) equilibrated and eluted with the same buffer. Fractions with the highest speci®c activities were pooled and dialyzed against 8 liters of 50 mM Na Mops buffer, pH 7.0, containing 5 mM L-glutamate. The dialyzed solution was made 1.25 mM in MnCl2 and immediately applied to a 1 8 cm column of ATP-agarose (C-8 attachment; Sigma) equilibrated with the same buffer. The column was washed in sequence with equilibration buffer ( 25 ml), equilibration buffer containing 0.25 M NaCl and 10% glycerol ( 20 ml), 50 mM Na Mops buffer, pH 7.0, containing 5 mM L-glutamate and 5 mM MgCl2 ( 15 ml), and the same buffer containing 1 mM ATP and 0.2 M NaCl ( 20 ml); the enzyme elutes in the last buffer. Fractions containing activity were immediately pooled and dialyzed against 50 mM Tris±HCl buffer, pH 7.4, containing 150 mM NaCl. Immunoaf®nity Chromatography Polyclonal antibody against E. coli-GCS was generated by immunizing a rabbit with E.

coli enzyme puri®ed to homogeneity essentially as described by Huang et al. (22). The immunoaf®nity column used to remove residual E. coli-GCS from the preparations of human-GCS was constructed using an immobilized protein A IgG puri®cation kit from Pierce (Rockford, IL). Brie¯y, 5 ml of immune serum was diluted with 5 ml of ``antibody-binding buffer'' provided in the kit and mixed with 1 ml of protein A±Sepharose preequilibrated with binding buffer. After being shaken gently for 1 h, the resin was collected by centrifugation and transferred to small column. The resin was next washed with binding buffer until A280 reached baseline, and it was then equilibrated with cross-linking buffer (0.2 M triethanolamine HCl, pH 8.2). The equilibrated resin was transferred to a tube, mixed with 2 ml of dimethyl pimelimidate solution (6.6 mg/ml in cross-linking buffer), and rocked gently to allow covalent cross-linking of bound IgG to the resin. After 1 h, the resin was washed extensively and sequentially with water, 0.1 M ethanolamine HCl, pH 8.2, water, and 1 M NaCl. The completed resin was equilibrated with 50 mM Tris±HCl, pH 7.4, containing 150 mM NaCl and stored at 4°C until used.

Human-GCS ( 12 mg) puri®ed through the ATP af®nity chromatography step was mixed with immunoaf®nity resin ( 1 ml) and allowed to stand for 30 min with occasional mixing. The resin was then returned to a column and washed with 50 mMTris±HClbuffer, pH 7.4, containing 150 mM NaCl. Activity-containing fractions were pooled, concentrated using a Centricon 30 microconcentrator (Amicon, Beverly, MA), and dialyzed against 20 mM imidazole HCl buffer, pH 7.4, containing 1 mM EDTA. If storage of the enzyme for more than a few days was contemplated, glycerol was added to a ®nal concentration of 25% to stabilize the activity. Enzyme Assays Human-GCS activity was determined spectrophotometrically on the basis of ADP formation using a pyruvate kinase±lactate dehydrogenase-based coupled assay system essentially as described previously (17, 18). The reaction mixtures contained, in a ®nal volume of 1.0 ml, 150 mM Tris±HCl buffer, pH 8.2, 100 mM KCl, 0.3 mM EDTA,40mMMgCl2,5mMATP,15mM L--aminobutyrate, 20 mM L-glutamate, 10 mM phosphoenolpyruvate, 0.3 mM NADH, 14 IU of pyruvate kinase, and 38 IU of lactate dehydrogenase. Reaction was initiated by addition of-GCS, and NADH oxidation, which is stoichiometrically equal to ADP formation, was monitored at 340 nm.

One unit of-GCS activity is the amount necessary to form 1 mol of ADP per hour under the conditions of the assay. Speci®c activity is expressed as units per milligram of protein. Protein was determined using the Bradford assay (23) with bovine serum albumin as standard. Initial velocity measurements for determination of Km values for L-glutamate, L-cysteine, L--aminobutyrate, and ATP were carried out in similar reaction mixtures except that concentrations of the nonvaried substrates were ®xed at 10-fold of their respective Km values as estimated in preliminary studies. Concentration ranges for the varied substrates were as follows: 0.9± 20mML-glutamate; 0.06± 1 mM L-cysteine; 0.8±20 mM L--aminobutyrate, 0.2±4 mM ATP. Inhibition by GSH was determined by adding ®xed amounts of GSH (0, 2, and 4 mM) to reaction mixtures in which L-glutamate was the varied substrate. Inhibition by BSO was determined by preincubating 10±50 units of-GCS with 100 mM Tris±HCl buffer, pH 8.2, containing 5 mM ATP, 20 mM MgCl2, and 100 MBSOat 37°C for 5 min and then measuring residual activity using the standard spectrophotometric assay.

Inhibition by cystamine was tested similarly by preincubating 10±50 units of human-GCS in 100mM Tris±HCl buffer, pH 8.2, with 100 M cystamine at 37°C for 10 min and measuring residual activity using the standard spectrophotometric assay. In both studies, control incubations lacked inhibitor.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Expression of Human-GCS In earlier studies by Huang et al. (4), rat-GCS was expressed in E. coli and puri®ed to homogeneity; those investigators were able to obtain expression of 38 mg of holoenzyme/100 g cells using a pT7-7 coexpression plasmid containing two T7 promoters in opposite directions, each immediately followed by either the heavy or the light subunit coding sequence. We initially attempted a somewhat similar coexpression strategy using a pET-3d vector in which a single T7 promoter was followed sequentially by the human light and heavy subunit coding sequences. This bicistronic vector resulted in expression with good stoichiometry between light and heavy subunits, but overall expression levels were poor. We next constructed individual, separately selectable expression vectors for each subunit as described under Materials and Methods (Fig. 1). Cotransformation of these into E.

coli BL21(DE3) gave acceptable levels of holoenzyme expression; in ®ve preparations wehaveconsistently obtained 32 mg holoenzyme/100 g cells calculated on basis of total activity and a speci®c activity of 1500 units/mg for pure-GCS. Critical factors in ensuring good results include the use of freshly transformed cells, attention to the cell density at which the culture is induced, the concentration of IPTG used to induce, the temperature of cell growth, and the inclusion of 2% glycerol in the growth medium; optimal values are given under Materials and Methods. We estimate that-GCS constitutes 1% of the soluble protein in the crude homogenate of the cells; solubilization of the cell debris pellet shows little-GCS by Western blotting, indicating that the enzyme does not form inclusion bodies. Importantly, under the conditions described, the expression of the light subunit exceeds that of the heavy subunit by 20%, minimizing the accumulation of catalytically active and dif®cult to separate free heavy subunit. Puri®cation of-GCS Human-GCS was puri®ed by ammonium sulfate fractionation followed sequentially by chromatography on Q-Sepharose, Superdex 200, ATP-af®nity resin, and an E. coli-GCSimmunoaf®nity column. Details of the individual steps are given under Materials and Methods, and the results are summarized in Table 1.

The protocol used was derived from that used routinely for isolation of the rat kidney enzyme (18), but included modi®cations intended to achieve separation of human and E. coli-GCS. Such separation proved dif®cult. In initial studies, the high-speed supernatant obtained from the crude homogenate was fractionated using ammoniumsulfate added in 5% increments from 35 through 65% saturation; precipitates containing-GCS activity were subjected to SDS±PAGE and probed with antibodies to E. coli and rat-GCS. Separation of the two enzymes was not obtained. Similarly, as shown in Fig. 2A, E. coli and human-GCS are not usefully separated by ion-exchange chromatography. This result was unexpected in view of an earlier report indicating that E. coli and rat-GCS are separated by chromatography on a DEAE±Sephacel (4). Because our preliminary studies using gel isoelectric focusing showed that the pI values of the E. coli and human-GCSareonlyslightly different ( 4.8 and ~5, respectively), we anticipated that E. coli-GCS would elute near mammalian-GCS. In fact, we ®nd that the E. coli monomer elutes slightly ahead of human-GCS (see shoulder on leading edge of the activity peak). Unfortunately, aggregates of E. coli-GCS trail through the peak of human-GCS. Nevertheless, a signi®cant amount of E.

coli activity is removed by not including the leading edge of the-GCS activity peak in the pooled fractions carried forward. As noted in Table 1, Q-Sepharose chromatography also removes most of the nonspeci®c ATPase activity present in the initial fractions; the fractions pooled from the Q-Sepharose column are thus the ®rst in which total-GCS activity can be accurately estimated by the ADP formation assay used. In the standard protocol for purifying rat-GCS the pool obtained from ion-exchange chromatography is dialyzed to remove salt prior to ATP af®nity chromatography (18, 24). Because E. coli and human-GCS differ signi®cantly in Mr, we chose instead to remove salt by gel ®ltration on Superdex 200, a resin that might also separate the bacterial and mammalian enzymes. As shown in Fig. 2B, E. coli and human-GCS are not cleanly separated. Western blotting of the Superdex 200 fractions displayed on SDS±PAGE without-mercaptoethanol again demonstrated that it is aggregates of E. coli-GCS that are present in fractions containing human-GCS; monomeric E. coli-GCS eluted just after human-GCS (fractions 68±88). Although chromatography on Superdex 200 does not remove all of the E. coli-GCS, we continue to include this step because it signi®cantly reduces the amount of the E.

coli enzyme and it fully removes other proteins (e.g., unidenti®ed proteins of 25 and 45 kDa) that are not eliminated by subsequent puri®cation steps. Where overall yield is of major concern, the gel ®ltration step can be omitted. Conditions for the ATP af®nity chromatography step are similar to those used for the rat kidney enzyme. It is important to use C8-linked ATP af®nity resin and to prepare the Mn2-containing buffer correctly and immediately before use (see Materials and Methods); in addition, the enzyme should be dialyzed into storage buffer as soon as possible after chromatography. Following the ATP af®nity chromatography step, the preparation of human-GCS typically contains 0.5 to 1% E. coli-GCS as judged by Western blotting or, more quantitatively, by cystamine inhibition (i.e., E. coli-GCS is not inhibited by cystamine, whereas rat or pure human-GCS is 100% inhibited). Where such levels of contamination are unimportant, no further puri®cation is necessary. We attempted to fully eliminate contaminating E. coli-GCS by altering the gradient used with QSepharose, by using other ion-exchange or gel ®ltration media (e.g.

Mono-Q, DEAE±Sephacel, Superdex 75, AcA 34), by using chromatofocusing or hydrophobic chromatography (e.g., phenyl-agarose), by pooling activity fractions more narrowly, and by repeating steps that offered partial resolution. None of these approaches were successful in reducing the level of contamination below 0.5%. We therefore constructed a column containing bound rabbit polyclonal antibodies to E. coli-GCS and passed the 99% pure human-GCS obtained following ATP af®nity chromatography through that column (see Materials and Methods). The eluent contained no detectable E. coli-GCS as judged by Western blotting or cystamine inhibition. In studies completed to date, immunoaf®nity columns have been washed and reused twice without loss of effectiveness. Puri®ed human-GCS is stable for at least 7 days when stored at 4°C in 20 mM imidazole HCl buffer, pH 7.4, containing 1 mM EDTA. Addition of 25% glycerol allows the enzyme to be stored at 20°C without freezing; under those conditions the activity is stable for at least 12 months. As has been observed with the rat kidney enzyme, freezing solutions of human-GCSresults in substantial, irreversible inactivation.

Characterization of Human-GCS After ATP af®nity chromatography or immunoaf®nity chromatography human-GCS exhibits a speci®c activity of 1500 units/mg; this value is comparable to the best values reported previously (18, 24) or obtained by us (Table 2) for rat kidney-GCS. Sriram and AliOsman have previously reported the isolation of 0.28 mg of-GCS with a speci®c activity of 1725 units/mg from a human malignant astrocytoma cell line (25); no other highly puri®ed preparation of the human enzyme has been reported. Figure 3 shows Coomassie bluestained SDS±PAGE gels for each of the key fractions obtained during the puri®cation of the enzyme. As shown, the ®nal preparation contains only bands corresponding to the light and heavy subunits of human-GCS. Identity of the bands was con®rmed by Nterminal amino acid sequencing. The observed heavy subunit sequence was GLLSQGSPLSWEETK and the light subunit sequence was GTDSRAAKALLARAR. As expected for proteins expressed in E. coli, both subunits are missing the N-terminally coded Met residue, but the sequences are otherwise identical to those predicted by the published cDNA sequences (15, 16).

Furthermore, quantitative amino acid analysis of the two SDS±PAGE bands indicates that the heavy and light subunits are present in essentially equal molar amounts(39.3 3.4pmolheavysubunitand38.7 3.2 pmol light subunit). This result establishes that holoenzyme rather than isolated heavy subunit has been isolated. Seelig et al. (3) report that the subunits of rat kidney-GCS can be linked by a disul®de bond; in their preparations the bond was largely intact in the isolated enzyme as estimated by SDS±PAGE carried out in the absence of-mercaptoethanol (3). Similar studies with our preparations of native rat kidney and recombinant human-GCS show that the subunits are 25±50% cross-linked by disul®de bonds. Although these values are lower than that reported by Seelig et al., the recombinant human-GCS appears very similar to native rat enzyme prepared and analyzed in this laboratory. Kinetic constants for the puri®ed recombinant human-GCS were determined as described under Materials and Methods (Table 2). As shown, Vmax and substrate Km values are essentially identical to those obtained with the native rat kidney enzymes assayed under the same conditions.

Literature values for the rat enzyme differ modestly, probably re¯ecting the fact that they were generally not determined under conditions in which the nonvaried substrates were truly saturating. The values shown in Table 2 differ signi®cantly from those reported for the human malignant astrocytoma enzyme (25). In that study, Km values for L-glutamate and L--aminobutyrate were reportedly 0.03 and 0.14 mM, respectively. An explanation for the difference between those results and ours is not evident. Tested as described under Materials and Methods, recombinant human-GCS was fully inhibited by BSO and by cystamine. Glutathione inhibits the enzyme competitively with respect to L-glutamate; the Ki value is 3.3 mM (data not shown). In summary, wehave developed an expression system that allows growth of cells and isolation of 10± 12 mgofhomogeneous recombinant human-GCSin 7 days at an overall yield of 45%. The isolated enzyme is stable, free of E. coli-GCS, and composed of equal amounts of heavy and light subunits. Human-GCS is shown to have substrate Km values essentially identical to those of native rat kidney-GCSandtobeinhibitable byL-SR-BSO, cystamine, and GSH.
In studies to be reported elsewhere, we have shown that the expression plasmids described can also be used to obtain the heavy and light human-GCS subunits separately.

Purification and characterization of 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase from human placenta

Abstract
5'-Methylthioadenosine phosphorylase has been purified to homogeneity (30,000-fold) from human full-term placenta by a procedure involving covalent chromatography on organomercurial-agarose as the major step. The specific activity of the homogeneous enzyme is 10.2 mumol of 5'-methylthioadenosine cleaved per min per mg of protein, and the overall yield is about 20%. The enzyme has a molecular weight of 98,000, as determined by gel filtration on Sephacryl S-200 and Superose 6B, and is composed by three apparently identical subunits with a molecular weight of 32,500. The isoelectric point is 5.5, and the optimal pH ranges from 7.2 to 7.6. The resistance of the enzyme to thermal inactivation is increased remarkably by the addition of 5'-methylthioadenosine or phosphate. The homogeneous enzyme shows an absolute requirement for -SH-reducing agents and is specifically and rapidly inactivated by thiol-blocking compounds. The reaction catalyzed by the enzyme is fully reversible with a Keq of 1.39 X 10(-2) (in the direction of phosphorolysis) at 37 degrees C and pH 7.4. The Km values for 5'-methylthioadenosine, phosphate, adenine, and 5-methylthioribose 1-phosphate are 5, 320, 23, and 8 microM, respectively.

5’-Methylthioadenosine phosphorylase(5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine:orthophosphate methylthioribosyltransferase, EC 2.4.2.28) catalyzes the phosphorolytic cleavage of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine, a sulfur adenosyl nucleoside formed from S-adenosylmethionine by several independent pathways(1, 2). The reaction products, adenine and 5-methylthioribose 1-phosphate, are recycled in turn to AMP(by adenine phosphoribosyltransferase, EC 2.4.2.7) and methionine, respectively(3, 4). It is worth mentioning, in this context, that the enzymatic breakdown of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine represents the only reaction leading to endogenous adenine(5), thus suggesting a critical role for 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase in a purine salvage pathway.

5’-Deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase was identified, for the first time, by Pegg and Williams-Ashman in rat ventral prostate (6), and it has been partially purified and characterized in a number of human(7, 8) and rat(9, 10) tissues, in human and murine cell lines(11-14), in Drosophila melanogaster(15), and in Caldariella acidophila(16). However, the lack of homogeneous preparations of the enzyme has hampered detailed studies concerning its physicochemical and kinetic properties. Moreover, only a few studies on the regulation and turnover of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase have been conducted(17,18).

The enzyme is found in all of the non-neoplastic tissues investigated, but it is absent in a number of transformed cells. In fact, several malignant cell lines lacking 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase activity(including human leukemia, malignant melanoma, and breast cancer cells) have been described(11, 12, 19, 20). A deficiency of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase has also been reported in two cases of human leukemia in vivo(21).

The molecular mechanism(s) responsible for the absence of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase activity are still obscure, although some hypotheses can be suggested. A genetic deletion, which might include loci critical to both 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase activity and malignant transformation, has been recently proposed on the basis of cytogenetic studies performed on malignant lymphoblasts from acute lymphoblastic leukemia(22). On the other hand, it is conceivable that some aberration either occurring at chromosomal level or involving the post-translational maturation of the protein can result in an inactive 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase.

In view of these considerations, an extensive purification of the enzyme is useful for elucidating its molecular and kinetic properties and for future studies on the molecular mechanism(s) leading to its deficiency. The present report describes for the first time the purification to homogeneity of a mammalian 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase. Several physicochemical and kinetic properties of the enzyme have also been elucidated. Particular attention has been paid to the reversibility of the reaction, as well as to the equilibrium constant, in view of a possible role of the enzyme in a purine salvage pathway. Preliminary results of this work have been presented elsewhere(23).

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES
Chemicals-S-Adenosylmethionine was prepared from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and isolated by ion-exchange chromatography(24). S-Adenosyl-L-[methyl-14C]methionine and [8-14C]adenine were supplied by the Radiocarbon Centre, Amersham, Bucks, United Kingdom. 5’-Deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine and [methyl-14C]5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine were prepared from labeled and unlabeled S-adenosylmethionine(25) and purified by HPLC(26). Adenine, p-chloromercuribenzoate, N-ethylmaleimide, 5,5’-dithiobis-(2-nitrobenzoate), iodoacetate, and iodoacetamide were supplied by Sigma.
The abbreviations used are: HPLC, high pressure liquid chromatography; SDS, sodium dodecyl sulfate.

5’-Methylthioadenosine Phosphorylase Assay-The activity of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase in the direction of phosphorolysis was determined by measuring the formation of [methyl-14C]5-methylthioribose-1-P from [methyl-14C]-methylthioadenosine (17). The standard reaction mixture, unless otherwise stated, contained (in a total volume of 200 μl) 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, 0.5 mM [methyl-14C]5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine (2 x 10^6 cpm/pmol), 1 mM dithiothreitol, and the indicated amounts of enzyme. After incubation at 37 °C for 20 min, the reaction was stopped by the addition of 50 μl of 3 M trichloroacetic acid, and 0.2-ml aliquots were applied to a 0.6 X 2-cm column of Dowex 50-H+ equilibrated with water. The [methyl-14C]5-methylthioribose-1-P was eluted directly into scintillation vials with 2 ml of 0.1 M HCl.

The enzyme activity in the direction of thioether synthesis was determined by following the formation of [8-14C]5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine from 5-methylthioribose-1-P and [S-14C]adenine. The reaction mixture, unless otherwise stated, contained (in a total volume of 200 μl) 50 mM Tris/HCl, pH 7.4, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 200 μM 5-methylthioribose-l-P, 100 μM [S-14C]adenine (1 x 10^6 cpm/μmol), and the enzyme. In these experiments, phosphate-free enzyme was employed.

The assay mixture was incubated at 37 °C for 20 min and then stopped by placing the test tube in boiling water. After the addition of 10 μl of 5 M NaOH, an aliquot (0.2 ml) was applied to a 0.6 x 2-cm column of boronate Bio-Gel 6P equilibrated with 0.25 M ammonium formate, pH 8.8. In order to remove unreacted adenine, the column was washed with 10 ml of equilibration buffer, and [8-14C]5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine was eluted directly into scintillation vials with 3 ml of 0.1 M acetic acid. The formation of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine from adenine and 5-methylthioribose-1-P was also checked by analyzing the assay mixture by HPLC (26). The latter results were superimposable upon those achieved by chromatography on boronate Bio-Gel 6P.

In these assays, the amount of protein was adjusted so that no more than 10% of the substrate was converted to product, and the reaction rate was linear as a function of time and protein concentration. One unit of the enzyme is defined as the amount which catalyzes the phosphorolytic cleavage of 1 pmol of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine at 37 °C.

Preparation of Tissue Extract-Unless otherwise stated, all procedures were carried out at O-4 °C. Full-term placentas were obtained within 1 h of delivery, and the umbilical cord, membranes, blood clots, and necrotic tissue were removed. The remaining material was cut into small pieces, washed with 0.9% NaCl, and homogenized in a Waring Blendor with 4 volumes of 10 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, containing 1 mM dithiothreitol (Buffer A). The homogenate was centrifuged (1 h at 15,000 x g), and the resulting supernatant was subjected to ammonium sulfate fractionation. The precipitate between 55 and 75% saturation was collected by centrifugation (15,000 x g for 20 min), dissolved in a minimal volume of Buffer A, and dialyzed overnight against 100 volumes of the same buffer. The dialyzed sample was then treated with cold acetone, and the precipitate between 40 and 60% saturation was dissolved in a minimal volume of Buffer A. The sample was then dialyzed overnight against three changes of 100 volumes of the same buffer.

Preparation of 5-Methylthioribose-I-P-5-Methylthioribose-1-P was prepared enzymatically from 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine and phosphate by employing a highly purified preparation of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (specific activity = 5 units/mg of protein). The reaction mixture contained 40 mg (130 μmol) of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine, 5 mM dithiothreitol, 10 mM potassium phosphate, pH 7.4, 4 mg of bovine serum albumin, and 0.5 unit of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase in a total volume of 20 ml. After incubation for 6 h at 37 °C, the reaction was stopped with 40 ml of 1-butanol. After centrifugation at 15,000 x g for 15 min, the organic phase and the protein at the interface were removed and the aqueous layer was treated twice with 40 ml of 1-butanol.

5’-Deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine and adenine were quantitatively extracted, as indicated by HPLC analysis of the organic phase, whereas 5-methylthioribose-1-P remained in the aqueous layer. In order to precipitate inorganic phosphate, the aqueous phase was then mixed with 1.2 ml of 5 M NH4OH and 14 ml of 0.5 M MgCl2, allowed to stand overnight at 4 °C. The mixture was then centrifuged (5000 x g for 15 min), and the supernatant was lyophilized. The solid was then resuspended in 80% ethanol, filtered to remove undissolved salts, and again lyophilized. The overall yield of 5-methylthioribose-1-P was about 35%, as determined by the orcinol method for ribose (27) after hydrolysis of the sample in 0.2 M HCl at 40 °C for 30 min. 5-Methylthioribose (produced by acid hydrolysis of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine (28)) was used as a standard. The product was free of inorganic phosphate (29) and did not contain adenine, 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine, or 5-methylthioribose as determined by HPLC (26) or TLC (30) analyses. The latter method was also employed to confirm the identity of the material.

Molecular Weight Determination-The molecular weight of the native protein was determined by Sephacryl S-200 and Superose 6B gel filtration techniques. Sephacryl S-200 (1.5 X 95 cm) and Superose 6B (1.5 x 60 cm) columns were calibrated with blue dextran, bovine liver aldolase (Mr 158,000), bovine serum albumin (68,000), equine myoglobin (17,800), and cytochrome c (12,500). In both cases, elution was carried out at a flow rate of 2 ml/h with 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, 1 mM dithiothreitol, and 0.2 M NaCl. Fractions (1.5 ml) were collected and assayed for 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase activity and for protein content. The data were plotted in terms of log of molecular weight against Kav (31).

Polyacrylamide Gel Electrophoresis-Sodium dodecyl sulfate slab gel electrophoresis was carried out at room temperature by using a 7.5, 10, or 12.5% acrylamide resolving gel and a 5% acrylamide stacking gel(32). Samples containing about 5-15 μg of protein were incubated for 5 min at 100 °C in 0.125 M Tris/HCl, pH 6.8, containing 1% SDS, 1% 2-mercaptoethanol, 8 M urea, and 0.001% bromphenol blue. After being cooled, the samples were layered directly on the stacking gel, and electrophoresis was carried out at 120 V for about 5 h. The gels were then fixed in 40% methanol, 10% acetic acid overnight and stained with 0.02% Coomassie Brilliant Blue in the same solution. The gels were destained at room temperature with 10% acetic acid, 10% methanol. Nondenaturing disc gel electrophoresis was carried out at various pH values (7.4, 8, and 8.5) by using 7.5% acrylamide as a resolving gel and 3% acrylamide as a stacking gel. The buffer was 50 mM potassium phosphate plus 5 mM dithiothreitol, and the electrophoresis was carried out overnight at 5 mA/gel at 4 °C. The gels were then stained as described above. In some cases, the gels were not stained but were sliced into 2-mm sections, and each of the latter was incubated overnight at 4 °C with 150 μl of a solution containing 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, 5 mM dithiothreitol, and 150 μg of bovine serum albumin. 5’-Deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase activity, in the direction of phosphorolysis, was determined in each sample as described above.

Protein Determination-Protein concentration was estimated according to Bradford (33) using human y-globulin as standard. The absorbance of column eluates was monitored at 280 nm.

RESULTS
Purification Procedure-Unless otherwise stated, all steps were conducted at O-4 °C. The sample obtained from acetone fractionation (see “Experimental Procedures”) was clarified by centrifugation at 15,000 x g for 30 min and then applied to a DEAE-Sephacel column (5 X 25 cm) previously equilibrated with Buffer A at a flow rate of 60 ml/h. The column was washed with 500 ml of the equilibration buffer, and a linear gradient (1.2 liters) of 0-0.1 M NaCl in Buffer A was applied. 5’-Deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase activity was eluted between 0.03 and 0.05 M NaCl, and fractions containing at least 0.06 units/mg of protein were concentrated 20-fold by ultrafiltration (Amicon PM-10 Diaflow membranes) and dialyzed extensively against 25 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, containing 1 mM dithiothreitol (Buffer B).

The sample was then applied, at a flow rate of 10 ml/h, to a hydroxylapatite column (2 X 15 cm). After the elution of non-absorbed proteins with Buffer B, the column was washed with about 100 ml of 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, containing 1 mM dithiothreitol. 5’-Deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase was then eluted using a linear gradient (300 ml) of 50-250 mM potassium phosphate, pH 7.4. Fractions containing 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase activity were concentrated 30-fold by ultrafiltration and freed from dithiothreitol by repeated concentration and dilution with 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4. The partially purified enzyme was then applied, at a flow rate of 5 ml/h, to a column (1 X 6 cm) of organomercurial-agarose equilibrated with 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.4.

The elution was carried out stepwise with 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4; 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, 2 M KCl; and 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, 2 M KCl, 2 mM 2-mercaptoethanol (Met); and 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, 2 M KCl, 40 mM 2-mercaptoethanol (Fig. 1). Fractions containing at least 3 units/mg of protein were pooled, concentrated to 1 ml by ultrafiltration, and dialyzed overnight against 1000 volumes of 10 mM Tris/HCl, pH 7.4, 1 mM dithiothreitol. At this purification stage, the sample gave two to three major bands on SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis.

Final purification was achieved by anion-exchange chromatography. A fast protein liquid chromatograph (Pharmacia) equipped with a Mono Q column pre-equilibrated with 10 mM Tris/HCl, pH 7.4, containing 1 mM dithiothreitol was employed at room temperature. Aliquots of the sample (250-500 μl) were injected at a flow rate of 1 ml/min, and 0.5-ml fractions were collected. As shown in Fig. 2, a gradient of 0-0.5 M NaCl was applied after the elution of non-retained proteins (Fig. 2). Fractions containing enzyme activity were pooled, concentrated to 0.5 ml by ultrafiltration, and dialyzed against 1000 volumes of Buffer B.

A summary of the purification procedure is given in Table I. Approximately 200 μg of purified enzyme was obtained from two placentas in about 23% yield. The final specific activity (three different preparations) ranged between 9 and 11 pmol of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine cleaved per min per mg of protein. This represents more than 29,000-fold purification from the 15,000 x g supernatant.

The homogeneity of the purified enzyme was evaluated by polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis under native conditions at various pH values (7.4, 8, and 8.5). As shown in Fig. 3, 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase activity co-migrated with the single protein band. Moreover, the purified enzyme gave a single protein band when analyzed by polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis in the presence of SDS at various percentages of acrylamide (7.5, 10, and 12.5%).

Stability of the Enzyme-The purified enzyme was found to be quite stable. Less than 10% of activity was lost after 1 month of storage at -20 °C in the presence of 5 mM dithiothreitol and 50 mM potassium phosphate, pH 7.4. In the absence of reducing agents, however, the enzyme was rapidly inactivated (50% inactivation within 24 h at both 4 and -20 °C).

Molecular Weight Determination-The molecular weight of native 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase was determined by gel filtration on Sephacryl S-200 as well as on Superose 6B (data not shown). The homogeneous enzyme was eluted from both columns as a single symmetrical peak corresponding to an apparent Mr of 98,000. When the 15,000 x g supernatant was chromatographed under the same conditions, a comparable Mr value was obtained, indicating that no artifacts had occurred during the purification procedure.

The Stokes radius of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase was estimated by exclusion chromatography using standards of bovine liver aldolase (Stokes radius = 5.12 nm), bovine serum albumin (3.5 nm), equine myoglobin (2.07 nm), and cytochrome c (1.64 nm). From plots of -(log Kaav) versus the Stokes radius, a value of 4.3 nm was calculated for 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (data not shown).

Polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis under denaturing conditions showed a single protein band with an estimated Mr of 32,500 which suggests that 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase is a trimer whose subunits have identical masses. The purified enzyme (5 μg) was also subjected to thin-layer isoelectric focusing over a pH range of 4.5-7. The protein focused as a single band at about pH 5.5.

Properties of Purified 5’-Deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine Phosphorylase-As reported in Fig. 4, the rate of the reaction was markedly increased with increasing temperature. Up to 67 °C, the reaction rate was linear throughout a 30-min incubation period, and even at 77 °C the rate was still linear for 15 min.

The purified enzyme was quite stable when preincubated for 15 min at 40-55 °C, but preincubation for the same time at 70 °C resulted in a complete loss of activity (Fig. 5). A significant protection against thermal inactivation was observed when the phosphate-free enzyme was preincubated for 15 min with 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine (Fig. 5) or phosphate (data not shown). More than 80% of activity was retained in the presence of 1 mM 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine at 70 °C. Comparable results were obtained in the presence of 300 mM potassium phosphate, pH 7.4.

The effect of pH on the enzyme activity was investigated over a pH range of 5.5-9. The optimum pH of the reaction ranged from 7.1 to 7.6, with one-half of the maximal activity at pH 6.2 and 8.6.

When dithiothreitol was removed from the enzyme preparation by dialysis, 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase activity decreased to about 50%. The addition of reducing agents (dithiothreitol, 2-mercaptoethanol, reduced glutathione) fully restored the activity. Moreover, as indicated in Table II, the phosphorolytic cleavage of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine was inhibited remarkably by preincubation of the enzyme with micromolar concentrations of several thiol-blocking agents (p-chloromercuribenzoate, N-ethylmaleimide, and 5,5’-dithiobis-(2-nitrobenzoate)).

In order to investigate the effect of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine on the reactivity of the sulfhydryl groups of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase, the phosphate-free enzyme was incubated for 10 min with different amounts of the thioether before the addition of N-ethylmaleimide (Table II). The results indicate that binding of the substrate exerts a "masking" effect on rapidly reacting -SH groups.

Reversibility of the Reaction and Equilibrium Constant-The reversibility of the reaction was investigated by monitoring 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine synthesis after incubation of 5-methylthioribose-1-P and adenine with phosphate-free enzyme. Fig. 6 shows HPLC analyses of assay mixtures containing increasing amounts of enzyme: a peak with the retention time of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine was detected only in the presence of enzyme, and the area under this peak was strictly dependent upon enzyme concentration.

To calculate the equilibrium constant of the reaction, different concentrations of 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine and phosphate were incubated at pH 7.4 and 37 °C in the presence of an excess of phosphate-free enzyme. The reaction was monitored in the direction of phosphorolysis until no further production of 5-methylthioribose-1-P and adenine was detected (about 150-180 min). From the concentration of substrates and products at equilibrium, a constant of 1.39 x 10^-7 was calculated. Such a Keq value is similar to those reported for other nucleoside phosphorylases, including purine nucleoside phosphorylase from calf and rat liver (34, 35) and uridine phosphorylase and thymidine phosphorylase from rat liver (36).

Kinetic Constants-The Km for 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine, estimated by an Eisenthal and Cornish-Bowden plot (37) at a saturating concentration of phosphate (50 mM), is 5 μM. This value is in good agreement with those reported for the 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase from several other sources (7-10).

The Km value for phosphate, calculated by the same procedure, is 320 μM and does not differ from that reported for the enzyme from rat liver (10).

The Km values for adenine and 5-methylthioribose-1-P are calculated by employing a new assay method (see “Experimental Procedures”) based on the separation of [8-14C]adenine and [8-14C]5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine by boronate gel chromatography. The Km of 5-methylthioribose-1-P, calculated at a saturating level of adenine (200 μM), is 8 μM, whereas that of adenine (at a saturating 5-methylthioribose-1-P level of 100 μM) is 23 μM.

DISCUSSION
Previous attempts to purify mammalian 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase from several sources resulted in preparations with specific activities of 0.25 unit/mg (7), 0.025 unit/mg (38), and 0.023 unit/mg of protein (10). This paper describes the purification to homogeneity of human placenta 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase; the preparation has a specific activity of more than 10 units/mg of protein. The native enzyme has a molecular weight of 98,000, which is in excellent agreement with data obtained in our (7) and other (10) laboratories on partially purified 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase from human and rodent tissues. On the other hand, the reported molecular weight of the rat lung enzyme (45,000) (9) is significantly different, thus suggesting structural differences between the human and the rat enzyme. Human placenta 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase is composed of three apparently identical subunits and shares the same trimeric molecular structure of the analogous mammalian enzyme, purine-nucleoside phosphorylase (39). Moreover, the Mr of the subunit of purine-nucleoside phosphorylase (30,000) (39) is comparable to that of 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (32,500), thus suggesting the occurrence of a common ancestral gene. Studies on the homology of the amino acid sequences of the two proteins are required, however, to substantiate this view. The high efficacy of organomercurial-agarose in binding the enzyme suggests that 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase contains several -SH groups. The low amounts of homogeneous protein available to date have prevented the direct titration of cysteine residues. In this context, it is worth noting that mammalian purine nucleoside phosphorylase contains numerous -SH groups, i.e., 12 mol/mol of enzyme (40) and, more interestingly, that 1 cysteine residue is directly involved in the catalytic mechanism of several purine and pyrimidine-nucleoside phosphorylases (36, 41). The calculated Km value for 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine (5 μM) is in excellent agreement with the values reported for the enzyme from other sources (7,8,13). Since the cellular levels of the thioether are less than 2 μM (26), a strict regulation of enzyme activity by 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine level should be operative in vivo. Alternatively, the affinity of the enzyme for phosphate is somewhat lower (Km = 320 μM), and the cellular concentration of this ion (generally higher than 1 mM) indicates that the enzyme is saturated in vivo by phosphate. The phosphorolytic cleavage of 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine is completely reversible, as shown by the formation of the nucleoside after incubation of 5-methylthioribose-1-P and adenine with phosphate-free enzyme. This is in agreement with previous preliminary results of Shugart et al. (15) on a 13-fold purified enzyme from D. melanogaster. However, in spite of the Keq greatly favoring the synthesis of 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine and the high affinity of the enzyme for 5-methylthioribose-1-P (Km = 8 μM) and adenine (Km = 23 μM), it is unlikely that the synthetic reaction is operative in vivo due to the rapid enzymatic removal of adenine (42) and 5-methylthioribose-1-P (3). On the other hand, it is possible that the exposure of cells to adenine analogs or antimetabolites capable of interfering with adenine recycling may result in the reversal of the phosphorolytic reaction and an accumulation of 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine and/or synthesis of 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine analogs. In this light, further studies are needed to evaluate a possible role of 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase in the mechanism of action of some purine analogs or antimetabolites endowed with pharmacological effects.

The homogeneous enzyme shows an absolute requirement for -SH-reducing agents and is specifically and rapidly inactivated by thiol-blocking compounds.
