Puriﬁcation of lamb brain ketimine reductase and identiﬁca-tion as CRYM by MS/MS.
Lamb forebrain ketimine reductase was puriﬁed  470fold to apparent homogeneity with a yield of 0.2% byutilizing four different chromatographic steps (Fig. 3). Thepuriﬁed enzyme was found to have a speciﬁc activity of15 U/mg. There was a low recovery of protein after the ﬁnalstep (24 lg), but a marked gain in speciﬁc activity (Fig. 3).
The enzyme was found to be highly unstable and prone tooxidation as was found by earlier researchers (Nardini et al.1988a,b). A single protein band at  35 kDa on SDS–PAGEwas observed (Fig. 3). The puriﬁed protein was trypsin-digested and identiﬁed by MS/MS. The highest rankingprotein identiﬁcation was bovine l-crystallin (CRYM) with alog (e) score of )869, 1429 total peptides, 68 unique peptidesidentiﬁed, and 75% coverage. Identiﬁed peptides covered allexons (Fig. 4) corresponding to the full-length 314 aminoacid bovine CRYM isoform, GenBank AccessionNP_001039379, and the bovine CRYM has 91% identityto the human CRYM, Accession number NP_001879.1 (Fig. 4). A minor contaminant was identiﬁed as pyridoxalphosphate phosphatase with a log (e) score of )22 with onlyfour total peptides and three unique peptides identiﬁed, and10% coverage.
Identiﬁcation of recombinant human CRYM as ketiminereductaseThe recombinant human CRYM orthologue of the full-length314 amino acid bovine CRYM isoform was heterologouslyexpressed in E. coli to conclusively conﬁrm the identity ofthe ketimine reductase. HisTrap-puriﬁed recombinant humanCRYM was subjected to SDS–PAGE, and displayed a singleband at  35 kDa (Fig. 3). The puriﬁed human enzymeeluted from a Superdex 200 HR column with an apparent Mrof  70 000, conﬁrming its native form as a homodimer. Ithad a maximum speciﬁc activity as a ketimine reductase of9.6 U/mg using AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor.The pH optimum was found to be identical to that of porcineketimine reductase (Nardini et al. 1988a) at pH 4.5 under thesame reaction conditions, and similar to that found for bovinecerebellum ketimine reductase (pH 5) (Nardini et al. 1988b).The reaction rate exhibited with NADPH is 40% thatexhibited with NADH when AECK is the co-substrate.For comparison purposes with previous research, variouspotential substrates for lamb ketimine reductase were tested(Table 1). Similar assay conditions and substrate concentra-tions were used as in previous studies (Nardini et al.1988a,b). Assays using 0.2 mM NADH or NADPH insodium acetate buffer (100 mM, pH 5) were performed.Maximal activity with lamb ketimine reductase was foundusing AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor. Thissubstrate speciﬁcity is similar to that found previously forporcine kidney ketimine reductase (Nardini et al. 1988a). Incomparison, the best substrate for bovine cerebellumketimine reductase was found to be P2C with NADPH ascofactor (Nardini et al. 1988b).
Michaelis-Menten kineticsA double reciprocal plot of kinetic data indicated that humanrecombinant CRYM catalyses a sequential mechanism(Fig. 5). Thus, kinetic data were globally ﬁtted to theequation for a bi-bi sequential mechanism using non-linearregression:v ¼ vmax½A½B½A½B þ Ka½B þ Kb½A þ KiaKbwhere [A] represents AECK substrate concentration and [B]represents NADH concentration. In the presence of 0.053 lgof enzyme, a Km of 47 ± 10 lM and Vmax of 9.6 ± 0.3 lmol/min/mg was determined using varying NADH concentrationsand AECK as substrate (Fig. 5). A Km of 3.6 ± 1.4 lM wasdetermined for NADH under the same conditions. Theseresults compare favourably to those documented previously for porcine kidney ketimine reductase, where the Km valuesobtained under similar conditions for AECK and NADHwere found to be 77 lM and 27 lM, respectively (Nardiniet al. 1988a).
Inhibition studiesPrevious reports indicated that 3,5,3¢- L-triodothyronine (T3)strongly binds to CRYM in the presence of NADPH (Vieet al. 1997), with the strength of binding in the order:D-T3  L-T3 > L-thyroxine (T4) > reverse T3 (Beslin et al.1995). Assays were therefore conducted to investigatewhether T3 inhibits the ketimine reductase activity of humanrecombinant CRYM. Inhibitory data were recorded using0.13 lg enzyme in each assay mixture. Assays wereconducted at varying concentrations of T3, AECK, andNADH. Global non-linear regression analysis of all datarevealed that the equation for competitive inhibition was thebest ﬁt:v ¼ ðVmax½SÞ½S þ Kmð1 þ ½IKI Þ :At a pH of 5, using a 100 mM acetate buffer, T3 was foundto be a strong competitive inhibitor with regard to AECKwith a Ki of 278 ± 12 nM (Fig. 6).At neutral pH the inhibition was far stronger, but it wasnot possible to accurately determine a Ki value using AECKas substrate, as the inhibition no longer ﬁtted any of theclassical equations (Fig. 7). This is because of the reportedvery low KD for T3 at neutral pH of 0.31 nM (Beslin et al.1995). The assays in Fig. 7 were done at an enzymeconcentration of 44.5 nM as at neutral pH enzyme activitywith AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor is 25% thatat pH 5. The curves at different T3 concentrations have acalculated V max that would be expected if the concentrationof enzyme were equal to (44.5-[T3]). This inhibitory effectis consistent with inhibition of enzyme activity by T3 andthe 0.31 nM K D for T3 binding (Beslin et al. 1995) toCRYM. This type of inhibition by T3 is almost equivalent to an irreversible inhibitor in enzyme kinetic terms and iteffectively means that ketimine reductase activity would benegligible when T3 is in excess of CRYM in vivo.

DiscussionLamb forebrain ketimine reductase was puriﬁed to apparenthomogeneity using a rapid puriﬁcation protocol, identiﬁed asCRYM by MS/MS, and the identiﬁcation conﬁrmed byassaying recombinantly expressed human CRYM. Theenzymatic function of CRYM has remained elusive in spiteof research efforts spanning more than 20 years. It is ahomologue of a number of prokaryote enzymes involved inamino acid metabolism, including ornithine cyclodeaminase(Goodman et al. 2004) and lysine cyclodeaminase (Tsotsouand Barbirato 2007), although CRYM has previously beenshown to have no cyclodeaminase activity (Goodman et al.2004). CRYM has been shown to be a major cytosolic T3binding protein and a key redox-dependent regulator ofintracellular T3 bioavailability and transactivation to thenucleus (Mori et al. 2002). CRYM mRNA expression is alsodown-regulated by follicle stimulating hormone in mam-malian ovary and it may play an important regulatory rolein steroidogenesis (Ko et al. 2003). A direct role ofCRYM/ketimine reductase enzyme substrates as regulators of steroidogenesis cannot be ruled out. CRYM has also beenshown to be the most abundantly expressed protein in thelens of diurnal marsupials (Segovia et al. 1997). Our dataclearly identify CRYM as a ketimine reductase in lamb brainand show that human CRYM has similar reductase activity(Fig. 4). This research is the ﬁrst to conclusively demonstratean enzyme function for CRYM. The strong inhibition ofenzyme activity by T3 is a unique ﬁnding deﬁning it as a keyregulator of amino acid metabolism, especially as it would bea key regulator of the pipecolic acid pathway, which is thepredominant lysine catabolic pathway in adult mammalianbrain. The ketimine reductase activity of CRYM and thepotent inhibition of activity by T3 suggest that in vivoconcentrations of T3 and CRYM, as well as activities ofassociated enzymes supplying ketimine substrates to CRYM,can be expected to have a profound effect on the intracellularconcentrations of ketimines. In addition, our ﬁndings suggesta reciprocal role of ketimine reductase enzyme activity inregulation of T3 transactivation to the nucleus.The X-ray crystal structure of human CRYM was solvedin 2007, but with no bound ligand apart from the cofactorNADPH, as its enzyme role was not known prior to thepresent research (Cheng et al. 2007). The X-ray crystalstructure of P. syringae P2C/Pyr2C reductase was solved in2005 (Goto et al. 2005). The enzyme was shown to belongto a new family of oxidoreductases and is not a structuralhomologue of CRYM, even though it catalyses similarreactions. Thus, bacterial P2C reductase and mammalianCRYM represent good examples of convergent evolution.Ketimine reductase previously puriﬁed from porcine kid-ney was reported to have an apparent Mr of 73 000 using gelﬁltration, but no data on the subunit composition werepresented (Nardini et al. 1988a). Nevertheless, this ﬁndingcompares favourably with the Mr of the recombinant homod-imeric lamb forebrain ketimine reductase determined in thepresent work to be  70 000. Moreover, the reaction rate dataare similar in the two studies. Taken together the evidencesuggests that the porcine kidney ketimine reductase and lambforebrain ketimine reductase are orthologues. However, thepartially puriﬁed bovine cerebellar enzyme was reported to bea homodimer with a Mr of  100 000 (Nardini et al. 1988b).Thus, it is possible that the lamb forebrain ketimine reductaseand the bovine cerebellar reductase are not orthologues, butrather different enzymes. Of note was our inability to purifyketimine reductase from lamb cerebellum using the reportedpuriﬁcation protocols, which would be consistent withﬁndings that CRYM concentrations in cerebellum are mark-edly reduced in comparison with cerebral levels (Suzuki et al.1991). The presence of the reported bovine cerebellumketimine reductase suggests the possibility that more than oneketimine reductase is present in the brain.l-Crystallin expression has been found to be signiﬁcantlyaltered in a number of neurological and psychiatric disordersincluding familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Fukada et al. 2007), facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (Reedet al. 2007), multiple sclerosis (Avasarala et al. 2008),schizophrenia (Middleton et al. 2002), and Alzheimerdisease (George et al. 2009). In addition, there are twoknown point mutations of human CRYM, both of which areassociated with non-syndromal deafness (Abe et al. 2003).The effects of these mutations on enzyme activity must nowbe evaluated. The inference is that levels of CRYM/ketiminereductase substrates are important determinants in hearing asCRYM mRNA is highly expressed in human inner ear (Aokiet al. 2000). Altered CRYM expression has also beenreported in various cancers such as non-small-cell lungcancer (Chong et al. 2006), glioblastoma (Khalil 2007), andprostate cancer (Malinowska et al. 2009). CRYM is alsosuspected of playing a role in diabetes as hyperglycaemia hasbeen shown to elevate expression of this protein in vivo andin vitro (Al-Kafaji and Malik 2009). These ﬁndings related toCRYM should be re-evaluated in the context of its ketiminereductase activity and the role that CRYM substrates mayplay in these pathologies.As there is likely more than one ketimine reductase in thebrain we are currently intensively concentrating our researchefforts to purify other ketimine reductases from mammalianbrain. Enzyme assays of the known CRYM/ketimine reduc-tase mutants would also be beneﬁcial in clarifying their rolein enzyme activity in relation to disease phenotypes. Ourﬁndings of T3 regulation of CRYM/ketimine reductaseenzyme activity deﬁne a new direct role in metabolicregulation for T3. Thyroid hormones are known to haveprofound effects on neurotransmission (Vara et al. 2002),brain development (Bernal 2005), and neural plasticity(Vallortigara et al. 2008). The ketimine reductase inhibitionby T3, thus raises an interesting question as to what role theaccumulation of CRYM enzyme substrates have in theseprocesses. T3 control of levels of ketimines, which areconsidered putative neurotransmitters/neuromodulators, addsa new layer to the complexity of neurochemistry, suggestingsubtle interactions among the endocrine system, amino acidmetabolism and neurotransmission.

paper result.text:
Mammalian forebrain ketimine reductase identified as μ-crystallin; potential regulation by thyroid hormones

Abstract
Ketimine reductase (E.C. 1.5.1.25) was puriﬁed to apparenthomogeneity from lamb forebrain by means of a rapid multi-step chromatography protocol. The puriﬁed enzyme wasidentiﬁed by MS/MS (mass spectrometry) as l-crystallin. Theidentity was conﬁrmed by heterologously expressing humanl-crystallin in Escherichia coli and subsequent chromato-graphic puriﬁcation of the protein. The puriﬁed humanl-crystallin was conﬁrmed to have ketimine reductase activitywith a maximum speciﬁc activity similar to that of native ovineketimine reductase, and was found to catalyse a sequentialreaction. The enzyme substrates are putative neuromodulator/transmitters. The thyroid hormone 3,5,3¢-L -triiodothyronine(T3) was found to be a strong reversible competitive inhibitor,and may have a novel role in regulating their concentrations.l-Crystallin is also involved in intracellular T3 storage andtransport. This research is the ﬁrst to demonstrate an enzymefunction for l-crystallin. This newly demonstrated enzymaticactivity identiﬁes a new role for thyroid hormones in regulatingmammalian amino acid metabolism, and a possible reciprocalrole of enzyme activity regulating bioavailability of intracellularT3.

Keywords: l-crystallin, ketimine, triiodothyronine, CRYM.

Ketimine reductases speciﬁcally catalyse the reduction ofimine bonds using either NADH or NADPH as cofactor. Theyinclude the previously partially characterised D1-piperideine-2-carboxylate (P2C)/D1 -pyrroline-2-carboxylate (Pyr2C)reductase (E.C.

1.5.1.21) isolated from porcine kidney (Petra-kis and Greenberg 1965) and Pseudomonas putida (Payton andChang 1982), and ketimine reductase (E.C. 1.5.1.25) isolatedfrom bovine cerebellum (Nardini et al. 1988b) and porcinekidney (Nardini et al. 1988a). Two different ketimine reduc-tases have previously been partially puriﬁed from bovinecerebellum (Nardini et al. 1988b) and porcine kidney cortex(Nardini et al. 1988a), and partly characterised. No sequencedata were obtained, and as a result no gene assignments arecurrently available for these reductases.
Ketimine reductase substrates include the sulphur-contain-ing cyclic ketimines S-(2-aminoethyl)- L-cysteine ketimine(AECK), lanthionine ketimine (LK) and cystathionine keti-mine (CysK) (Fig. 1). These originate from sulphur-contain-ing amino acids such as cysteine and homocysteine, whichare converted to the cyclic sulphur-containing amino acidprecursors by cystathionine b-synthase (Cavallini et al.1991). These precursors are then transaminated by glutamine transaminase K [GTK; also known as kynurenine amino-transferase isozyme I (KAT1)] (Cooper 2004), or possiblyoxidised by L -amino acid oxidase, to form the correspondinga-keto acids, which non-enzymatically cyclise to form thecyclic ketimines (Cavallini et al. 1991) (Fig. 2).
D1 -Piperideine-2-carboxylate and D1 -pyrroline-2-carbox-ylate (Fig. 1) are also ketimine reductase substrates. P2C isderived from lysine catabolism from the pipecolic acidpathway.

In mammals, lysine is metabolised by two mainpathways – the saccharopine pathway and the pipecolic acid pathway. The saccharopine pathway predominates in extra-cerebral tissues, whereas the pipecolic acid pathway is themain route for lysine catabolism in the adult brain (Garweget al. 1980). In the pipecolic acid pathway, oxidation ofL-lysine at the a-carbon results in the formation of an a-ketoacid that cyclises to P2C (Garweg et al. 1980). Pyr2C arisesfrom the oxidation of D-proline by D-amino acid oxidase.Ketimine reductases catalyse its reduction to L-proline(Petrakis and Greenberg 1965).
Cystathionine ketimine and LK have been reported to bepresent in human cerebral cortex, AECK and CysK in bovinebrain, and CysK and LK in human urine (Cavallini et al.1991). The reduced enzyme products of AECK, LK andCysK, namely 1,4-thiomorpholine-3-carboxylic acid (TMA),1,4-thiomorpholine-3,5-dicarboxylic acid and cyclothionine, respectively, have been reported to be present in bovine brainand in human urine (Cavallini et al. 1991).
Biological activity that could affect neurological functionhas been demonstrated for the sulphur-containing cyclicketimines. LK is known to bind strongly to isolated brainmembranes, resulting in signiﬁcant increases of cAMP.

Thisbinding was found to be saturable, reversible and speciﬁc.Speciﬁc binding was shown by the fact that LK could only bedisplaced by other ketimines, AECK and CysK, and catechol-amines (Dupre et al. 1993). AECK is a strong competitiveinhibitor of D-amino acid oxidase (Ricci et al. 1983), and mayact as an endogenous regulator of glutamate NMDA receptoractivity through modulation of D-serine levels. This implies aspeciﬁc neuromodulator/transmitter role for the ketimines withparticular importance in the brain. In contrast, little is knownregarding the biological functions of P2C or Pyr2C. L-Pipecolic acid, derived from the reduction of P2C by ketiminereductase, has been shown to be a weak inhibitory neurotrans-mitter (Charles 1986). No other biological functions have beenreported for P2C or Pyr2C and their reduced products.
Cyclic ketimines are present in solution as an equilibriummixture of cyclic enaminic, cyclic ketiminic, and open-chainforms, with cyclic forms predominating under physiologicalconditions (Cavallini et al. 1991). However, ketimine reduc-tases appear to only catalyse the reduction of the ketiminicform as: when assayed at pH 5 some substrates, such asCysK, do not exist as enamines (Nardini et al. 1988a); theketimine reductase product using AECK as substrate is the cyclic amino acid TMA (Nardini et al.

1988a), which cannotarise from reduction of the open chain form.
Here, we report the puriﬁcation of a ketimine reductasefrom lamb cerebral cortex and the identiﬁcation of the lamband human enzyme as the protein l-crystallin (CRYM), forwhich an enzymatic function had not previously beendetermined. We also report the strong competitive enzymeinhibition by the thyroid hormone 3,5,3¢- L-triiodothyronine(T3). This new role for T3 in regulation of cyclic ketiminelevels represents an important new mechanism in ourunderstanding of the biochemical actions of T3, and is animportant addition to our understanding of the neurochemicalrole of thyroid hormones.

Materials and methods
Materials and assaysAll chemicals and reagents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich(Sydney, Australia) unless stated otherwise. AECK and CysK weresynthesized as per the protocols of Cavallini et al. (1983), and P2Cby the protocol of Meister (1954). The full length human CRYMORF bacterial expression clone (product # I0311) was purchasedfrom GeneCopoeia (Rockville, MD, USA). All chromatographicmedia and columns were purchased from GE Healthcare (Sydney,Australia) and Bio-Rad (Sydney, Australia).Ketimine reductase assays were performed in a similar manner tothose previously reported (Nardini et al. 1988a,b), using a standardmixture in 100 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5) at 37°C.

One unitof enzyme activity is deﬁned as the amount of enzyme that catalysesthe oxidation of 1 lmol of NADH per minute at 37°C in a standardreaction mixture.For enzyme kinetic measurements, assays were adapted tomicrotiter plates using a BMG Fluostar Galaxy (Offenburg,Germany) and were performed in a total volume of 200 lL ofbuffer containing 20% w/v glycerol, 100 mM sodium acetate (pH 5)with variable concentrations of substrates at 37°C. The reaction wasinitiated by the addition of enzyme which had been diluted in assaybuffer. Fluorescence detection, excitation wavelength of 360 nm andemission wavelength of 460 nm, was used instead of UV absorbancefor monitoring the conversion of NADH or NADPH to NAD orNADP, respectively. Standard curves were generated with varyingconcentrations of NADH and NADPH. The non-enzymatic decreasein ﬂuorescence of NADH or NADPH, because of the acidic assayconditions, was compensated for by running a blank simultaneouslycontaining all assay components except for the ketimine substrate.The reduction product of AECK was identiﬁed as the cyclic aminoacid TMA (Fig. 1) by the procedure of Nardini et al. (1988a).Inhibition studies involving T3 were carried out at pH 5 and alsoat pH 7 (100 mM potassium phosphate buffer).

A stock solution ofT3 was made up in dimethylsulfoxide and varying amounts added tothe reaction mixture. In a separate experiment, it was determinedthat the amount of dimethylsulfoxide in the reaction mixtureresulting from addition of T3 stock solutions did not inhibit theenzyme activity.Enzyme kinetic data were globally ﬁtted and analysed usingGraphPad Prism 5 software (GraphPad software Inc., San Diego,CA, USA) using non-linear regression. Puriﬁcation protocolPotassium phosphate buffer [10 mM, pH 7, 10% (v/v) glycerol,1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT)] was used in all protocols unlessotherwise speciﬁed. All puriﬁcation protocols were performed at4°C. Brain ketimine reductase was puriﬁed from lamb frontalcortical sections using multiple chromatography columns, andpuriﬁed to apparent homogeneity by tracking enzyme activity usingAECK (1 mM) and NADH (0.2 mM) as substrates. A Bio-RadBiologic HR chromatography worksystem was used for puriﬁcationsteps. Sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis(SDS–PAGE) was used to monitor the puriﬁcation. Pall, Inc.concentrating membranes (Port Washington, NY, USA) with a cut-off of 30 kDa were used, except in the case of the ﬁnal puriﬁcationstep where a 10 kDa membrane was used.Preparation of lamb brainsLamb brains were purchased from a local abattoir, chilled on icewithin 30 min of slaughter, and stored within 2 h at )80°C.

Enzymeactivity was found to be stable for prolonged periods in the frozenbrain at this temperature. Thawed frontal cortex sections (250 g wetweight in total) were added to 700 mL of ice-cold potassiumphosphate buffer, and homogenised in a Waring blender (Torrington,CT, USA) at high speed for 2 min. The homogenate was centrifugedfor 60 min in a Beckman centrifuge (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA,USA), at 30 000 g using a JA-20 rotor.Anion exchange chromatographyAs per the protocol of Nardini et al. (1988a), the supernatant(650 mL) was immediately applied to a 100 mL XK50/20 columncontaining DEAE fast Sepharose weak anion exchanger (GEHealthcare) equilibrated with potassium phosphate buffer. Thesupernatant was pumped onto the column at 8 mL/min. The DEAEcolumn was washed with 95 mM KCl in phosphate buffer until theabsorbance at 280 nm was less than 0.1, and protein was then elutedat 6 mL/min with 165 mM KCl in phosphate buffer. Activefractions were pooled and solid ammonium sulphate (AS) wasimmediately added to a ﬁnal concentration of 700 mM.Hydrophobic interaction chromatographyThe pooled active fractions were then pumped onto an XK16/20column containing 12 mL of phenyl sepharose HP (GE Healthcare)at 6 mL/min. The column was previously equilibrated withphosphate buffer containing 700 mM AS.

The column was thenwashed with the same concentration of AS in phosphate buffer, untilthe UV absorbance at 280 nm was less than 0.02, then protein waseluted at 6 mL/min with a 100-0%. AS gradient of 12 columnvolumes followed by 5 column volumes of phosphate buffer. Activefractions eluted in a single peak and were collected, concentrated to12 mL, and buffer exchanged to 20 mM phosphate buffer a usingSephadex G-25 column.Flow-through protocolIn preliminary experiments, ketimine reductase was found not tobind to either hydroxylapatite or heparin sulphate in the presenceof phosphate buffer at 20 mM. Thus, a ﬂow-through protocol usingthese two matrices, together with a HiTrap Blue column, was usedto quickly remove many protein contaminants. The ﬂow-throughprotocol made use of a ceramic 10-mL hydroxylapatite column (80 lm ceramic beads), 10-mL heparin sulphate fast ﬂow, and 1-mLHiTrap Blue connected in series. The columns were equilibratedwith 20 mM phosphate buffer. After the sample from the previouspuriﬁcation step was injected onto the columns and washed with35 mL of buffer at 1 mL/min, the hydroxylapatite column andheparin columns were disconnected.

The HiTrap Blue column waswashed with 10 column volumes of 20 mM phosphate buffer, andthe protein samples eluted using 1 lM NADPH directly onto a pre-equilibrated 1-mL Resource Q strong anion exchange column. Thecolumn was washed with 10 column volumes of 20 mM phosphatebuffer containing 20% (v/v) glycerol and eluted with a 0–500 mMKCl gradient, in 20 mM phosphate buffer, over 12 column volumesat 1 mL/min. A single peak was collected and the pooled samplesconcentrated to 110 lL. Protein samples in 5-lL aliquots were ﬂash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at )80°C.Sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresisBio-Rad 5· loading dye, containing bromophenol blue dye andb-mercaptoethanol (200 mM) were added to protein samples in1.5-mL Eppendorf tubes, which were then heated for 2 min in aboiling water bath. SDS–PAGE was performed using NuSep(Sydney, Australia) 10-well Tris–Gly 4–20% LongLife gels. Bio-Rad Broad Range molecular mass markers were added to the ﬁrstlane (200, 116, 97, 66, 45, 31, 21.5, 14.4, 6.5 kDa). SDS–PAGEconditions: 55 min at 155 V using a Bio-Rad power source until thebromophenol blue dye front had reached the base of the gel. Thegels were stained with colloidal Coomassie Blue stain/methanol(4 : 1) overnight.

The gels were then destained with 20% methanol,after which they were washed and analysed.Protein identiﬁcation by MS/MSGel bands were excised after their positions were revealed bystaining. The protein in each band was reduced with DTT, alkylatedwith iodoacetamide, and digested in-gel with trypsin (Haynes et al.1998). Extracted peptides were subjected to nanoLC-MS/MS (massspectrometry) (Lee et al. 2009). Brieﬂy, peptides were separated byreversed-phase chromatography and eluted directly into a ThermoLTQ-XL ion trap mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientiﬁc, Waltham,MA, USA). The six most abundant peptides detected in a surveyscan of 400–1500 amu were subjected to collision induceddissociation. Raw ﬁles were converted to mzxml format and spectrawere searched against the bovine sequence database (release date 13April 2010) using the XTandem algorithm running under TheGlobal Proteome Machine interface (Craig et al. 2004). The peptidemass tolerance was set at 2 Da, fragment ion mass tolerance at0.2 Da, cysteine was considered to be modiﬁed with iodoacetamideand methionine was considered to be variably modiﬁed by Soxidation. Spectra were also searched against a reversed database toestimate false discovery rates, and using minimum criteria of threepeptides identiﬁed and a log (e) score of <)10.

With these searchcriteria no proteins were identiﬁed in the reversed database searches.Expression and puriﬁcation of recombinant proteins inEscherichiacoliThe full length human CRYM ORF bacterial expression clone(Entrez gene ID: 1428 transcript variant 1, longer isoform)contained an N-His6 tag and T7 promoter in a pReceiver-B01vector, and ampicillin selectivity. It was transformed into E. coli (Fusion Blue cells) and E. coli BL21 (DE3)STAR (Inoue et al.1990). For production of the CRYM the transformed E. coli BL21(DE3)STAR was streaked onto Luria-Bertani agar plates containingampicillin (100 lg/mL). The plates were incubated overnight at37°C and a single colony was picked and cultured in 1 L of Luria-Bertani medium with 1 mM ampicillin at 37°C and with constantshaking on an orbital shaker until the OD 600 reached 0.5.Recombinant protein expression was induced with 1 mM isopro-pyl-b-D -1-thiogalactopyranoside, followed by incubation overnightat 18°C with constant shaking. The culture was then centrifuged at6000 g for 20 min at 4°C, and the pellet resuspended in 20 mL ofbinding buffer [Tris buffer (20 mM, pH 7.9) containing NaCl(500 mM) and imidazole (5 mM)]. The cell suspension was lysedusing three passes of a French press at 10 000 psi. Furthercentrifuging at 20 000 g resulted in the isolation of a solubleprotein-containing supernatant.

The supernatant was applied to anickel-charged His-Trap afﬁnity column (1 mL). The column waspre-equilibrated with cold binding buffer. After binding of theprotein to the column, the column was successively washed with (i)5 column volumes of binding buffer, (ii) 5 volumes of Tris buffer(20 mM, pH 7.9) containing NaCl (500 mM) and imidazole(60 mM). The CRYM protein was then eluted with Tris buffer(20 mM, pH 7.9) containing NaCl (500 mM) and imidazole(500 mM), and collected in 0.5 mL fractions. Most of the proteinand ketimine reductase activity was found to be in three consecutivefractions totalling 1.5 mL. These were combined and desalted usinga 5-mL desalting column equilibrated with 10 mM potassiumphosphate buffer (pH 7) containing 20% (v/v) glycerol and 1 mMDTT. Aliquots (15 lL) were ﬂash-frozen in 500 lL Eppendorftubes and stored at )80°C. Protein concentration was determinedusing a Bio-Rad Bradford assay with bovine serum albumin as astandard and was determined to be 8 mg/mL. Protein purity wasdetermined by SDS–PAGE and MS/MS protein identiﬁcation, withonly one major band on SDS–PAGE and only one major proteindetected by MS/MS.Gel ﬁltrationA Superdex 200HR gel ﬁltration column (GE Healthcare) was usedto check the apparent Mr.

The column was eluted at 0.5 mL/minusing 150 mM NaCl in 10 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7).The column was calibrated with GE Healthcare Protein standards(ferritin, 440 kDa; aldolase, 158 kDa; ovalbumin, 43 kDa; andribonuclease, 13.7 kDa).Data presentationAll data are presented as the mean ± SE.

Results
Puriﬁcation of lamb brain ketimine reductase and identiﬁca-tion as CRYM by MS/MS.
Lamb forebrain ketimine reductase was puriﬁed  470fold to apparent homogeneity with a yield of 0.2% byutilizing four different chromatographic steps (Fig. 3). Thepuriﬁed enzyme was found to have a speciﬁc activity of15 U/mg. There was a low recovery of protein after the ﬁnalstep (24 lg), but a marked gain in speciﬁc activity (Fig. 3).
The enzyme was found to be highly unstable and prone tooxidation as was found by earlier researchers (Nardini et al.1988a,b). A single protein band at  35 kDa on SDS–PAGEwas observed (Fig. 3). The puriﬁed protein was trypsin-digested and identiﬁed by MS/MS. The highest rankingprotein identiﬁcation was bovine l-crystallin (CRYM) with alog (e) score of )869, 1429 total peptides, 68 unique peptidesidentiﬁed, and 75% coverage. Identiﬁed peptides covered allexons (Fig.

4) corresponding to the full-length 314 aminoacid bovine CRYM isoform, GenBank AccessionNP_001039379, and the bovine CRYM has 91% identityto the human CRYM, Accession number NP_001879.1 (Fig. 4). A minor contaminant was identiﬁed as pyridoxalphosphate phosphatase with a log (e) score of )22 with onlyfour total peptides and three unique peptides identiﬁed, and10% coverage.
Identiﬁcation of recombinant human CRYM as ketiminereductaseThe recombinant human CRYM orthologue of the full-length314 amino acid bovine CRYM isoform was heterologouslyexpressed in E. coli to conclusively conﬁrm the identity ofthe ketimine reductase. HisTrap-puriﬁed recombinant humanCRYM was subjected to SDS–PAGE, and displayed a singleband at  35 kDa (Fig. 3). The puriﬁed human enzymeeluted from a Superdex 200 HR column with an apparent Mrof  70 000, conﬁrming its native form as a homodimer. Ithad a maximum speciﬁc activity as a ketimine reductase of9.6 U/mg using AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor.The pH optimum was found to be identical to that of porcineketimine reductase (Nardini et al. 1988a) at pH 4.5 under thesame reaction conditions, and similar to that found for bovinecerebellum ketimine reductase (pH 5) (Nardini et al.

1988b).The reaction rate exhibited with NADPH is 40% thatexhibited with NADH when AECK is the co-substrate.For comparison purposes with previous research, variouspotential substrates for lamb ketimine reductase were tested(Table 1). Similar assay conditions and substrate concentra-tions were used as in previous studies (Nardini et al.1988a,b). Assays using 0.2 mM NADH or NADPH insodium acetate buffer (100 mM, pH 5) were performed.Maximal activity with lamb ketimine reductase was foundusing AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor. Thissubstrate speciﬁcity is similar to that found previously forporcine kidney ketimine reductase (Nardini et al. 1988a). Incomparison, the best substrate for bovine cerebellumketimine reductase was found to be P2C with NADPH ascofactor (Nardini et al. 1988b).
Michaelis-Menten kineticsA double reciprocal plot of kinetic data indicated that humanrecombinant CRYM catalyses a sequential mechanism(Fig. 5). Thus, kinetic data were globally ﬁtted to theequation for a bi-bi sequential mechanism using non-linearregression:v ¼ vmax½A½B½A½B þ Ka½B þ Kb½A þ KiaKbwhere [A] represents AECK substrate concentration and [B]represents NADH concentration. In the presence of 0.053 lgof enzyme, a Km of 47 ± 10 lM and Vmax of 9.6 ± 0.3 lmol/min/mg was determined using varying NADH concentrationsand AECK as substrate (Fig. 5).

A Km of 3.6 ± 1.4 lM wasdetermined for NADH under the same conditions. Theseresults compare favourably to those documented previously for porcine kidney ketimine reductase, where the Km valuesobtained under similar conditions for AECK and NADHwere found to be 77 lM and 27 lM, respectively (Nardiniet al. 1988a).
Inhibition studiesPrevious reports indicated that 3,5,3¢- L-triodothyronine (T3)strongly binds to CRYM in the presence of NADPH (Vieet al. 1997), with the strength of binding in the order:D-T3  L-T3 > L-thyroxine (T4) > reverse T3 (Beslin et al.1995). Assays were therefore conducted to investigatewhether T3 inhibits the ketimine reductase activity of humanrecombinant CRYM. Inhibitory data were recorded using0.13 lg enzyme in each assay mixture. Assays wereconducted at varying concentrations of T3, AECK, andNADH. Global non-linear regression analysis of all datarevealed that the equation for competitive inhibition was thebest ﬁt:v ¼ ðVmax½SÞ½S þ Kmð1 þ ½IKI Þ :At a pH of 5, using a 100 mM acetate buffer, T3 was foundto be a strong competitive inhibitor with regard to AECKwith a Ki of 278 ± 12 nM (Fig.

6).At neutral pH the inhibition was far stronger, but it wasnot possible to accurately determine a Ki value using AECKas substrate, as the inhibition no longer ﬁtted any of theclassical equations (Fig. 7). This is because of the reportedvery low KD for T3 at neutral pH of 0.31 nM (Beslin et al.1995). The assays in Fig. 7 were done at an enzymeconcentration of 44.5 nM as at neutral pH enzyme activitywith AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor is 25% thatat pH 5. The curves at different T3 concentrations have acalculated V max that would be expected if the concentrationof enzyme were equal to (44.5-[T3]). This inhibitory effectis consistent with inhibition of enzyme activity by T3 andthe 0.31 nM K D for T3 binding (Beslin et al. 1995) toCRYM. This type of inhibition by T3 is almost equivalent to an irreversible inhibitor in enzyme kinetic terms and iteffectively means that ketimine reductase activity would benegligible when T3 is in excess of CRYM in vivo.

DiscussionLamb forebrain ketimine reductase was puriﬁed to apparenthomogeneity using a rapid puriﬁcation protocol, identiﬁed asCRYM by MS/MS, and the identiﬁcation conﬁrmed byassaying recombinantly expressed human CRYM.

Theenzymatic function of CRYM has remained elusive in spiteof research efforts spanning more than 20 years. It is ahomologue of a number of prokaryote enzymes involved inamino acid metabolism, including ornithine cyclodeaminase(Goodman et al. 2004) and lysine cyclodeaminase (Tsotsouand Barbirato 2007), although CRYM has previously beenshown to have no cyclodeaminase activity (Goodman et al.2004). CRYM has been shown to be a major cytosolic T3binding protein and a key redox-dependent regulator ofintracellular T3 bioavailability and transactivation to thenucleus (Mori et al. 2002). CRYM mRNA expression is alsodown-regulated by follicle stimulating hormone in mam-malian ovary and it may play an important regulatory rolein steroidogenesis (Ko et al. 2003). A direct role ofCRYM/ketimine reductase enzyme substrates as regulators of steroidogenesis cannot be ruled out. CRYM has also beenshown to be the most abundantly expressed protein in thelens of diurnal marsupials (Segovia et al. 1997). Our dataclearly identify CRYM as a ketimine reductase in lamb brainand show that human CRYM has similar reductase activity(Fig. 4). This research is the ﬁrst to conclusively demonstratean enzyme function for CRYM.

The strong inhibition ofenzyme activity by T3 is a unique ﬁnding deﬁning it as a keyregulator of amino acid metabolism, especially as it would bea key regulator of the pipecolic acid pathway, which is thepredominant lysine catabolic pathway in adult mammalianbrain. The ketimine reductase activity of CRYM and thepotent inhibition of activity by T3 suggest that in vivoconcentrations of T3 and CRYM, as well as activities ofassociated enzymes supplying ketimine substrates to CRYM,can be expected to have a profound effect on the intracellularconcentrations of ketimines. In addition, our ﬁndings suggesta reciprocal role of ketimine reductase enzyme activity inregulation of T3 transactivation to the nucleus.The X-ray crystal structure of human CRYM was solvedin 2007, but with no bound ligand apart from the cofactorNADPH, as its enzyme role was not known prior to thepresent research (Cheng et al. 2007). The X-ray crystalstructure of P. syringae P2C/Pyr2C reductase was solved in2005 (Goto et al. 2005). The enzyme was shown to belongto a new family of oxidoreductases and is not a structuralhomologue of CRYM, even though it catalyses similarreactions.

Thus, bacterial P2C reductase and mammalianCRYM represent good examples of convergent evolution.Ketimine reductase previously puriﬁed from porcine kid-ney was reported to have an apparent Mr of 73 000 using gelﬁltration, but no data on the subunit composition werepresented (Nardini et al. 1988a). Nevertheless, this ﬁndingcompares favourably with the Mr of the recombinant homod-imeric lamb forebrain ketimine reductase determined in thepresent work to be  70 000. Moreover, the reaction rate dataare similar in the two studies. Taken together the evidencesuggests that the porcine kidney ketimine reductase and lambforebrain ketimine reductase are orthologues. However, thepartially puriﬁed bovine cerebellar enzyme was reported to bea homodimer with a Mr of  100 000 (Nardini et al. 1988b).Thus, it is possible that the lamb forebrain ketimine reductaseand the bovine cerebellar reductase are not orthologues, butrather different enzymes. Of note was our inability to purifyketimine reductase from lamb cerebellum using the reportedpuriﬁcation protocols, which would be consistent withﬁndings that CRYM concentrations in cerebellum are mark-edly reduced in comparison with cerebral levels (Suzuki et al.1991).

The presence of the reported bovine cerebellumketimine reductase suggests the possibility that more than oneketimine reductase is present in the brain.l-Crystallin expression has been found to be signiﬁcantlyaltered in a number of neurological and psychiatric disordersincluding familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Fukada et al. 2007), facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (Reedet al. 2007), multiple sclerosis (Avasarala et al. 2008),schizophrenia (Middleton et al. 2002), and Alzheimerdisease (George et al. 2009). In addition, there are twoknown point mutations of human CRYM, both of which areassociated with non-syndromal deafness (Abe et al. 2003).The effects of these mutations on enzyme activity must nowbe evaluated. The inference is that levels of CRYM/ketiminereductase substrates are important determinants in hearing asCRYM mRNA is highly expressed in human inner ear (Aokiet al. 2000). Altered CRYM expression has also beenreported in various cancers such as non-small-cell lungcancer (Chong et al. 2006), glioblastoma (Khalil 2007), andprostate cancer (Malinowska et al. 2009). CRYM is alsosuspected of playing a role in diabetes as hyperglycaemia hasbeen shown to elevate expression of this protein in vivo andin vitro (Al-Kafaji and Malik 2009).

These ﬁndings related toCRYM should be re-evaluated in the context of its ketiminereductase activity and the role that CRYM substrates mayplay in these pathologies.As there is likely more than one ketimine reductase in thebrain we are currently intensively concentrating our researchefforts to purify other ketimine reductases from mammalianbrain. Enzyme assays of the known CRYM/ketimine reduc-tase mutants would also be beneﬁcial in clarifying their rolein enzyme activity in relation to disease phenotypes. Ourﬁndings of T3 regulation of CRYM/ketimine reductaseenzyme activity deﬁne a new direct role in metabolicregulation for T3. Thyroid hormones are known to haveprofound effects on neurotransmission (Vara et al. 2002),brain development (Bernal 2005), and neural plasticity(Vallortigara et al. 2008). The ketimine reductase inhibitionby T3, thus raises an interesting question as to what role theaccumulation of CRYM enzyme substrates have in theseprocesses. T3 control of levels of ketimines, which areconsidered putative neurotransmitters/neuromodulators, addsa new layer to the complexity of neurochemistry, suggestingsubtle interactions among the endocrine system, amino acidmetabolism and neurotransmission.

content:
Cloning, expression, and characterization of the human mitochondrial beta-ketoacyl synthase. Complementation of the yeast CEM1 knock-out strain

Abstract
A human beta-ketoacyl synthase implicated in a mitochondrial pathway for fatty acid synthesis has been identified, cloned, expressed, and characterized. Sequence analysis indicates that the protein is more closely related to freestanding counterparts found in prokaryotes and chloroplasts than it is to the beta-ketoacyl synthase domain of the human cytosolic fatty acid synthase. The full-length nuclear-encoded 459-residue protein includes an N-terminal sequence element of approximately 38 residues that functions as a mitochondrial targeting sequence. The enzyme can elongate acyl-chains containing 2-14 carbon atoms with malonyl moieties attached in thioester linkage to the human mitochondrial acyl carrier protein and is able to restore growth to the respiratory-deficient yeast mutant cem1 that lacks the endogenous mitochondrial beta-ketoacyl synthase and exhibits lowered lipoic acid levels. To date, four components of a putative type II mitochondrial fatty acid synthase pathway have been identified in humans: acyl carrier protein, malonyl transferase, beta-ketoacyl synthase, and enoyl reductase. The substrate specificity and complementation data for the beta-ketoacyl synthase suggest that, as in plants and fungi, in humans this pathway may play an important role in the generation of octanoyl-acyl carrier protein, the lipoic acid precursor, as well as longer chain fatty acids that are required for optimal mitochondrial function.

Over the last decade, it has become clear that fungal and plant mitochondria are capable of synthesizing fatty acids de novo (1–6). The enzymes involved in the pathway are freestanding, monofunctional proteins of the type II variety and are distinct from the multifunctional polypeptide type I FASs1 present in the cytosol of fungi and animals. Thus far, the preponderance of evidence suggests that these mitochondrial FAS pathways function to produce octanoyl-ACP, the precursor of lipoic acid (4) and longer chain-length fatty acids that may be utilized for the remodeling of mitochondrial membrane phospholipids (7). The presence of a similar mitochondrial FAS system in animals has been suspected for some time, based initially on the discovery of an ACP-like protein in animal mitochondria (8, 9). However, only recently have other components of a putative mitochondrial FAS been identified, cloned, and characterized; they include the human ACP and malonyl transferase (10) and enoyl reductase (11). In continuation of the search for other components, we have now identified and characterized a single candidate for a type II human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase, the critical enzyme required for catalysis of the chain-elongating condensation reaction.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES
Cloning of the Human Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase—Using the sequences of several authentic type I and type II β-ketoacyl synthases as probes to BLAST search the human genome sequence data base, we identified a sequence (accession NP_060367) that also was represented in a human EST clone (IMAGE clone 3446492, ATCC MGC-4956) and appeared likely to encode a full-length human β-ketoacyl synthase, together with an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence. A cDNA from this EST clone was used as template to generate a construct for expression in Escherichia coli. Specific primers (KSmitqeT/B, Table I) with appropriate restriction sites for cloning were designed, and the cDNA encoding the putative β-ketoacyl synthase was amplified using PCR, essentially as described earlier (12). The E. coli expression construct carried a 37-residue N-terminal deletion that we deduced, by analysis of multiple sequence alignments, might represent a mitochondrial targeting sequence. The amplified fragment was purified using a QIAquick PCR purification kit (Qiagen), cleaved with appropriate restriction enzymes and cloned into the pQE80 L (QE) E. coli expression vector (Qiagen). To facilitate purification of the recombinant protein by affinity chromatography, a His6-tag was encoded at the N terminus of the construct. The authenticity of the cloned, amplified fragments was confirmed by DNA sequencing.

Verification That the Putative N-terminal Mitochondrial Recognition Elements Direct the β-Ketoacyl Synthase into Mitochondria—A PCR-amplified fragment (primer set KSmit1–38gfpT/B, Table I) encoding the first 38 amino acid residues (putative targeting sequence) of the human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase was directionally cloned into the EcoRI and KpnI sites of the pEGFP-N3 vector (Clontech) to facilitate expression as the N-terminal partner of a KSmit1–38-EGFP fusion protein. Authenticity of the cloned fragment was confirmed by DNA sequencing. HeLa cells, grown in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium supplemented with 10% bovine fetal calf serum, were cotransfected with two plasmids using FuGENE 6 reagent; one plasmid encoded the KSmit1–38-EGFP fusion protein (or as a control the pEGFP-N3 parental vector), the other encoded pDsRed2-Mito (Clontech), which served as a mitochondrial marker. Cells were cultured for 60 h, fixed with paraformaldehyde, and analyzed for green and red fluorescence using a Sony confocal microscope.
Complementation of the Yeast Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase Mutant, cem1, by the Human Mitochondrial Enzyme—The human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase cDNA sequence was amplified by the PCR from plasmid pCMV-SPORT6 using the primers KSmitcem1.T and KSmitcem1.B. The resulting SpeI/ClaI fragment was incorporated into pUG35 (13) giving the multicopy yeast expression plasmid pKSmit-GFP. The plasmid was transformed into the Saccharomyces cerevisiae mutant BY4743 (Euroscarf, Frankfurt/Main, Germany; MATa/α, his3Δ/1his3Δ1, leu2Δ0/leu2Δ0, lys2Δ0/LYS2, MET15/met15Δ0, ura3Δ0/ura3Δ0, Δcem1::kanMX4/CEM1). In this diploid, one of the two CEM1 alleles (condensing enzyme mitochondrial) is disrupted by the kanMX4 marker, providing resistance against the antibiotic geneticin (G418). The transformed diploid was sporulated, and subsequently the spore tetrads were dissected by micromanipulation. Individual spores were analyzed for respiratory competence on YEPL (yeast extract/peptone/lactose) medium containing lactate as a carbon source. CEM1 disruption was indicated by G418 resistance and the presence of pKSmit-GFP by uracil prototrophy of the cells. Dextrose-containing complex (YEPD (yeast extract/peptone/dextrose)) medium and uracil-free synthetic complete (SCD-Ura) medium were prepared according to Ausubel et al. (14). YEPL media contained 2% lactate, pH 6.5, instead of glucose, and YEPD + G418 contained 200 mg/l of geneticin (Sigma).
Tissue Specificity of Expression of Human Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase—A 32P-labeled probe was synthesized by the random priming method using [α-32P]dCTP (3000Ci/mmol), a PCR-amplified mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase template cDNA and NEBlot kit (New England Biolabs). A human multiple tissue Northern blot (Clontech) was exposed to the purified radiolabeled probe (∼1 × 107 dpm/blot), using ExpressHyb hybridization solution (Clontech), and was processed according to the manufacturer's recommendations. The blot was analyzed using a phosphoimager (Strom 840, Molecular Dynamics).
Expression and Purification of Human Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase—The recombinant pQE 80L vector was expressed in E. coli DH5α cells. Cells were grown at 37 °C in LB medium to a density equivalent to A600 of 0.5 and induced with 0.4 mm isopropyl-β-d-thiogalactopyranoside at room temperature overnight. Cells were harvested and using a microfluidizer (Microfluidics, Newton MA) were lysed in buffer (25 mm Tris-HCl, pH 7.8, 300 mm NaCl) containing protease inhibitors (leupeptin 5 μg/ml, trans-epoxysuccinyl-LGB 10 μm, pepstatin 1 μg/ml, and antitrypsin 5 μg/ml). The cell debris was pelleted by centrifugation at 30,000 × g for 40 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatant was passed through a 0.45-μm filter and loaded at 20 °C onto a HiTrap Chelating HP column (5 ml bed volume, Amersham Biosciences). The column was washed with 50 mm imidazole in buffer A (25 mm Tris-HCl, pH 7.8, 300 mm NaCl, 10% glycerol) then the tightly bound proteins were eluted with 250 mm imidazole in buffer A. The latter protein fraction was rechromatographed on the same column, essentially in the same manner, except that an additional wash with 100 mm imidazole in buffer A was included prior to elution of the tightly bound proteins. The purified protein was subjected to ultrafiltration, both to remove imidazole and to effect transfer to the storage buffer (25 mm Tris-HCl, pH 7.8, 300 mm NaCl, 2 mm EDTA, 2 mm dithiothreitol, and 10% glycerol). The enzyme was stable for at least 6 months when stored at –80 °C.
β-Ketoacyl Synthase Activity Using Acetyl-CoA as Primer—Recombinant mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase was assayed for condensing activity using [1-14C]acetyl-CoA as the primer and malonyl-ACPmit as the chain extender. The malonyl-ACPmit was first generated in situ from malonyl-CoA and holoACPmit using human mitochondrial malonyl transferase (10). The reaction mixture contained 83 mm potassium phosphate buffer, pH 6.8, 0.3 mm dithiothreitol, 1 mm EDTA, 200 μm malonyl-CoA, 60 μm holoACPmit, and 100 ng of human mitochondrial malonyl transferase in a final volume of 30 μl and was incubated at 37 °C for 15 min. Then [1-14C]acetyl-CoA (54 Ci/mol, 50 μm final concentration) was added. The mixture was aliquotted into two tubes and incubated for 20 min at 37 °C without or with 1 μg (725 nm) of mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase. The reaction was terminated by trichloroacetic acid precipitation.
Synthesis of Acyl-ACPmit Substrates—The C2:0–C16:0 acyl-ACPmit thioesters were synthesized enzymatically using recombinant human phosphopantetheinyl transferase (15) and C-terminally His6-tagged apoACPmit. A typical reaction mixture, 5 ml in volume, containing 20 mm BisTris-HCl, pH 6.5, 10 mm MgCl2, 15 μm apoACPmit and 75 μm acyl-CoA, was incubated with 250 nm phosphopantetheinyl transferase at 37 °C overnight. The reaction mixture was then desalted into buffer B (20 mm BisTris-HCl, pH 6.5, 10% glycerol) using a Vivaspin concentrator (5,000-Da cutoff, Vivascience) and repurified at 20 °C on a Hi-Trap Q HP anion exchange column. The bound proteins were eluted with a 20-ml gradient of 0–250 mm NaCl in buffer B, followed by a 5-ml gradient of 250–500 mm NaCl in buffer B. The anion exchange chromatography procedure effected a partial separation between residual unmodified apoACPmit and the various acyl-ACPmit species, which eluted later. Fractions were analyzed by SDS-PAGE to assess protein purity and by mass spectrometry to identify those fractions that contained authentic acyl-ACPmit thioesters, essentially free of residual apoACPmit. Starting with ∼1 mg of apoACPmit, the overall yields of acyl-ACPmit thioesters were typically ∼ 60%, with the exception of C-16-ACPmit for which the yield was 30%.
Isolation of Apo and Holo Forms of Human Mitochondrial ACP—The C-terminally His6-tagged apoACP was expressed in an Sf9/baculoviral host/vector system and purified as described earlier, and the holo-form was derived from it using human phosphopantetheinyl transferase (10, 15).
Mass Spectrometry—Samples were desalted using a C4 ZipTip (Millipore, Bedford, MS), mixed with the matrix (sinapinic acid, 10 mg/ml in 30% acetonitrile, 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid) in a 10:1 ratio (v/v), and 1 μl of the resulting mixture was spotted onto a stainless steel matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization plate. Analysis was performed on an Autoflex® matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of-flight biospectrometry work station (Bruker Daltonics, Billerica, MA) in a positive linear mode. The mass scale was externally calibrated utilizing cytochrome c. Both singly and doubly charged ions were used for a molecular mass determination.
β-Ketoacyl-ACP Synthase Assay—The β-ketoacyl synthase activities were assayed according to Garwin et al. (16). The incubation mixture (total volume 20 μl) contained 0.2 m potassium phosphate buffer, pH 6.8, 1 mm EDTA, 0.3 mm dithiothreitol, 660 nm malonyl/acetyl transferase (a recombinant form of the single domain derived from the rat cytosolic type I FAS (17)), 10 μm ACPmit, 20 μm [2-14C]malonyl-CoA (52 Ci/mol), 1–50 μm acyl-ACPmit, and 25 ng (27 nm) of mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase. The malonyl-ACPmit was first generated from malonyl-CoA and ACPmit, using malonyl/acetyl transferase, by incubation for 15 min at room temperature. Then the reaction was started by addition of acyl-ACPmit and mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase, continued for 2 min at 37 °C, and finally terminated by the addition of 0.4 ml of reducing reagent (0.1 m K2HPO4, 0.4 m KCl, 30% tetrahydrofuran, and 5 mg/ml NaBH4). The contents of the assay tubes were mixed vigorously and incubated at 37 °C for 45 min. Toluene (0.4 ml) was added, the contents of the tubes were vortexed for 2 min, and a portion (0.4 ml) of the upper phase was taken for liquid scintillation spectrometry. Blank reactions were performed without acyl-ACPmit. Kinetic parameters were determined using EnzymeKinetics (Trinity Software); values represent the means ± S.D. for calculations using Lineweaver-Burk and non-linear regression methods.
Effects of Cerulenin on Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase Activity— Mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase (0.25 μg) was preincubated for 15 min at room temperature with 0–1 mm cerulenin in a final volume of 20 μl. Portions of the reaction mixture were then assayed for residual activity in 0.2 m potassium phosphate buffer, pH 6.8, 1 mm EDTA, 0.3 mm dithiothreitol, 660 nm malonyl/acetyl transferase, 10 μm ACPmit, 20 μm [2-14C]malonyl-CoA (52 Ci/mol), 10 μm C6:0-ACPmit, and 25 ng of β-ketoacyl synthase (final volume of 20 μl).
RESULTS
Identification of the Putative Human Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase—A single candidate sequence for a freestanding, type II β-ketoacyl synthase was identified in both the human and mouse genomic sequence data bases (sequences 85% identical). Compared with β-ketoacyl synthase sequences from prokaryotes, the putative 459-residue mammalian mitochondrial counterparts have extensions of ∼40 residues at the N termini that are rich in basic amino acids and lack acidic residues (Fig. 1). These features are characteristic of mitochondrial targeting sequence elements. The sequence of a recently discovered β-ketoacyl synthase from Arabidopsis thaliana also includes an N-terminal extension that functions as a mitochondrial targeting sequence (18). Surprisingly, sequences for fungal mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthases do not include obvious N-terminal extensions, although the actual sequences at the N termini possess the general characteristics of mitochondrial targeting sequence elements. Thus, it is unclear at present how these fungal enzymes are targeted for import into mitochondria. X-ray crystallographic analysis and mutagenesis of β-ketoacyl synthases associated with type II FAS systems have established the importance of several residues in the functioning of this type of enzyme (19–27). A multiple sequence alignment revealed that all of these residues were positionally conserved in the putative mammalian mitochondrial enzymes, as well as in the confirmed plant and fungal mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthases (Fig. 1). These residues included the cysteine nucleophile (residue 209), two catalytic histidine residues thought to be required for promoting the decarboxylation of malonyl moieties (residues 348 and 385), an essential lysine of uncertain function (residue 380), a glycine residue that allows entrance into the substrate-binding tunnel (residue 273), two threonine residues that hydrogen bond with the ACP phosphopantetheine moiety (residues 350 and 352), and a glycine-rich motif near the C terminus that contributes to the oxyanion hole (residues 443–449). This analysis provided a strong indication that mammalian nuclear genomes encode a single, type II β-ketoacyl synthase having an extended sequence at the N terminus. The coding sequence for the human enzyme is located on chromosome 3 (3p24.2) and that for the mouse counterpart on chromosome 14.

Verification That the Putative Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase Contains an N-terminal Mitochondrial Targeting Sequence—A cDNA encoding the putative human β-ketoacyl synthase mitochondrial targeting sequence (residues 1–38) fused in-frame with the coding sequence for EGFP, a red-shifted variant of green fluorescent protein, was coexpressed in HeLa cells together with a fusion protein consisting of the mitochondrial targeting sequence of cytochrome c coupled to the Discosoma sp. red fluorescent protein. Confocal fluorescence microscopy revealed that the KSmit1–38-EGFP colocalized with the red fluorescent mitochondrial marker protein (Fig. 2). In contrast, the EGFP protein lacking the putative mitochondrial targeting sequence of the β-ketoacyl synthase expressed throughout the cytoplasm. Thus, this experiment confirmed that the N-terminal region of the full-length β-ketoacyl synthase indeed is a mitochondrial targeting sequence.

Complementation of the Yeast cem1 Mutant Strain by the Human β-Ketoacyl Synthase—The in vivo function of the cDNA-encoded human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase was established by complementation of the mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase defect of a S. cerevisiae cem1 mutant (2). This mutation is characterized by a nuclear-encoded respiratory-defective petite phenotype, resulting in the inability to grow on non-fermentable carbon sources such as glycerol or lactate. Consequently, the four spores originating from a sporulated BY4743 diploid consist of two lactate-positive and two lactate-negative segregants (Fig. 3B). In accordance with the use of kanMX4 as a disruption cassette for CEM1, the two lactate-negative spores are G418-resistant (Fig. 3B). In contrast, sporulation of BY4743 cells transformed with pKSmit-GFP resulted in four respiratory-competent spores, even though two of them were again G418-resistant and hence contained the defective cem1Δ allele (Fig. 3A). Obviously, the β-ketoacyl synthase defect in these cells was compensated by the human β-ketoacyl synthase homolog expressed from pKSmit-GFP. Because this plasmid contains the yeast URA3 gene as a selection marker, the uracil-prototrophy of all four spores proved the equal distribution of the multicopy plasmid among the meiotic segregants. The C-terminal fusion of GFP to pKSmit-GFP-encoded human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase apparently did not interfere with the β-ketoacyl synthase function. Furthermore, the successful complementation of the respiratory defect implied that the mitochondrial targeting sequence at the N terminus of the human β-ketoacyl synthase was recognized in the fungal host. This conclusion was supported by the observation that in situ fluorescence elicited by the C-terminal GFP marker was not distributed throughout the cytoplasm but was limited to specific regions of the cell likely corresponding to mitochondria (data not shown).

Tissue Distribution of Human Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase—Analysis of a multiple tissue Northern blot with a radiolabeled cDNA probe revealed that mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase transcripts are most abundant in the heart and skeletal muscle, as well as the liver and kidney, tissues that contain high levels of active mitochondria (Fig. 4). Transcripts were present at relatively low levels in the placenta, brain, spleen, and lung and were barely detectable in the colon, thymus, and leukocytes. This relatively broad tissue expression contrasts with that of the type I cytosolic FAS, which is not expressed at significant levels in heart or skeletal muscle and is expressed at high levels in tissues such as liver that are involved in lipogenesis and energy homeostasis.

Expression and Purification of the Human Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase—The mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase construct KSmit38, in which the first 37 residues constituting the mitochondrial targeting sequence were replaced by a His6-tag, expressed well in E. coli, although appreciable amounts of the protein were sequestered in inclusion bodies when the cells were grown at temperatures above 20 °C. The protein could be obtained in high purity by two successive metal-ion affinity chromatography steps, and its mobility on SDS-PAGE corresponded closely to that of a species with the expected molecular mass of 45.8 kDa (Fig. 5).

Substrate Specificity and Kinetic Properties of the Human Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase—The type II FAS systems of prokaryotes and chloroplasts typically employ a specialized enzyme (β-ketoacyl synthase III) for catalysis of the first elongation step that uses acetyl-CoA, rather than acetyl-ACP, as the primer. Therefore, the possibility that the mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase could utilize acetyl-CoA directly as a substrate for elongation was evaluated using the malonyl thioester of human mitochondrial ACP (ACPmit) as the chain extender; however, no activity was observed even when high concentrations (0.725 μm) of enzyme were used.
For evaluation of catalytic activity using various acyl-ACPmit thioesters as primers, we devised a novel, simple, efficient procedure for synthesis of these substrates by exploiting the broad substrate specificity of the human phosphopantetheinyl transferase. This enzyme will transfer the phosphopantetheinyl moiety from CoA to a variety of apoACPs, essentially independent of whether the donor CoA substrate is offered as the free thiol, or as an acyl-CoA thioester. Thus, acyl-CoAs containing 2–16 C atoms were all efficiently converted to the corresponding acyl-ACPs by this enzyme. The human phosphopantetheinyl transferase has a remarkably broad tolerance not only for the acyl-S-phosphopantetheinyl donor but also for the carrier protein acceptor and can phosphopantetheinylate both peptidyl and acyl carrier proteins from prokaryotes and eukaryotes (15). Thus, the enzyme is ideally suited for routine synthesis of acyl-ACPs of any acyl chain length and ACP origin.
In the kinetic studies, care was taken to validate steady state conditions with each substrate. Typically, only 27 nm enzyme and incubation times of 2 min were used. When 40-fold higher concentrations of enzyme were used, a significant radiolabel from malonyl moieties was recovered in the toluene extract even when no priming substrate was provided, indicating that malonyl decarboxylase activity of the β-ketoacyl synthase most likely was generating acetyl moieties that were used as the primer. At steady state, using only 27 nm enzyme, no significant incorporation of radiolabel was observed in the absence of priming substrate indicating that formation of acetyl priming moieties by decarboxylation was negligible. Under these conditions, no more than 20% of the substrate was utilized during the course of the assay.
Acyl-ACPmit thioesters containing acyl moieties with 2–14 C atoms all were elongated by the mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase; only C-16-ACPmit was a very poor substrate (Fig. 6A). When compared in the acyl-ACPmit concentration range 5–10 μm, the activities ranked in the following order: C-12 > C-10 > C-6 > C-8 > C-4 > C-2 > C-14 > C-16. However, the Km values varied according to the acyl chain-length of the substrate. Thus, the enzyme exhibited Km values in the low micromolar range for C-4–C-12 ACP thioesters but had markedly lower affinity for C-2 and C-14 substrates. Although it was not possible to estimate actual kinetic parameters for C-2 because of an apparently very high Km value, the Vmax was >250 nmol·min–1 mg–1 for this substrate and values for the other substrates were in the range 100–400 nmol·min–1 mg–1, except for C-12-ACP, which was >1000 nmol·min–1 mg–1.

Inhibition of the Human Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase by Cerulenin—Cerulenin, an antibiotic produced by Cephalosporium caerulens, is a potent inhibitor of both prokaryotic type II and eukaryotic type I FAS systems (28) and acts by binding to the hydrophobic pocket formed at the β-ketoacyl synthase dimer interface and reacting with the active site cysteine through its C-2 carbon (20, 29). The human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase was also inactivated by cerulenin (Fig. 7), although sensitivity appears low compared with the prokaryotic β-ketoacyl synthases I and II for which IC50 values below 25 μm are typically reported (25).

DISCUSSION
This study establishes that the human nuclear genome encodes a single mitochondrially targeted β-ketoacyl synthase. This is the fourth nuclear-encoded component of a putative human mitochondrial FAS system to be characterized to date; the others are the ACP, malonyl transferase, and enoyl reductase. In common with the other three human mitochondrial FAS enzymes, as well as the fungal and plant mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthases, the animal β-ketoacyl synthases appear more closely related to prokaryotic and plastid counterparts than to the cytosolic type I FAS of the same species. Thus, phylogenetic analysis reveals that all of the mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthases originate from a single branch (Fig. 8), consistent with the generally accepted hypothesis that mitochondria originated from free-living prokaryotes.
Present day prokaryotes and plant plastids employ three β-ketoacyl synthases with different specificities to fulfill their fatty acid requirement. They are β-ketoacyl synthase III, which catalyzes the initial condensation step using acetyl-CoA as primer, and β-ketoacyl synthases I and II, which catalyze the remaining elongation reactions using acyl-ACPs as primers. All three types of enzyme share a similar overall fold and differ primarily in the structure at the active site, reflecting their different specificities (31). The β-ketoacyl synthases I and II have similar specificities, except that β-ketoacyl synthase II is able to elongate 16:1–18:1. Because only one type II β-ketoacyl synthase was identified in the human genome, the substrate specificity of this enzyme was of particular interest. The human mitochondrial enzyme, which appears more closely related to prokaryotic β-ketoacyl synthases I and II than to β-ketoacyl synthase III enzymes (Fig. 7), is unable to utilize acetyl-CoA as the primer. However, in contrast to the prokaryotic β-ketoacyl synthases I and II, it is able to catalyze the initial condensation reaction using a 2-carbon primer, presented as acetyl-ACP. Otherwise, the specificity of the mitochondrial enzyme (Fig. 6) is quite similar to that of the prokaryotic β-ketoacyl synthases I and II (32) in that, with all three types, enzyme activity falls off significantly with substrates containing more than 12 C atoms. However, the specific activity of the human mitochondrial enzyme is ∼20-fold higher than that reported for the E. coli β-ketoacyl synthases I and II (32). It is unclear whether the disparity reflects a true difference in catalytic efficiency or can be attributed to suboptimal assay conditions used for the prokaryotic enzymes.
Recently, the mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase from A. thaliana has been identified, cloned, and characterized (18). This enzyme too exhibits a high sequence similarity with β-ketoacyl synthases I and II of prokaryotes and is able to restore growth of the E. coli CY244 strain, which lacks both β-ketoacyl synthases I and II. The authors concluded that the A. thaliana mitochondrial enzyme does not use either acetyl-CoA or acetyl-ACP as primer but instead uses acetyl moieties derived by decarboxylation of malonyl-ACP. In this respect, the enzyme appears to differ from the human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase, which clearly is able to utilize acetyl-ACP as primer.
The major products of the prokaryotic type II FAS pathway are long chain acyl-ACPs containing 16 and 18 C atoms, but one of the intermediates, octanoyl-ACP, is siphoned off for the production of lipoyl-ACP. Experiments with plant mitochondria indicate that the major products of this mitochondrial type II FAS system also are octanoyl and long chain length acyl-ACPs (5). Furthermore, the profile of fatty acids synthesized by soluble extracts of E. coli CY244 cells supplemented with the A. thaliana mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase also showed a bimodal distribution with maxima at C-8 and C-14–16. The hypothesis that the mitochondrial FAS system might be responsible for producing both octanoyl and long chain length acyl-ACPs is supported by mutational disruption of the mitochondrial FAS system of fungi. For example, disruption of the nuclear-encoded gene for mitochondrial ACP in Neurospora crassa results in an accumulation of lysophospholipids in mitochondrial membranes and an accompanying respiratory-deficient phenotype. Disruption of the nuclear-encoded gene for either the mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase or ACP in S. cerevisiae also produces a respiratory-deficient phenotype and, in the case of the ACP-defective strain, it has been established that cellular lipoic acid concentration is reduced to <10% of that of the wild-type strain (4, 33). Furthermore, addition of lipoic acid to the growth medium could not compensate for the block in endogenous lipoic acid synthesis, suggesting that in this species lipoic acid may not readily be taken up into mitochondria (4). Our finding that the human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase is able to restore normal growth to the cem1 mutant strain implies that the substrate specificity and kinetic properties of the human enzyme are entirely compatible with those of the endogenous S. cerevisiae enzyme and allow the synthesis and release of octanoyl-ACP from the elongation cycle for conversion to lipoyl-ACP. An interesting feature of the kinetic properties of the human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase is the higher Km for octanoyl-ACP (11 μm), compared with the values for hexanoyl- and decanoyl-ACP (∼2 μm). Possibly, this property may result in a higher pool size for the C-8 intermediate that could facilitate diversion into the lipoate pathway. For many years it has been generally assumed that in mammals the requirement for lipoic acid is met by dietary intake. In this pathway, free lipoate, taken up via vitamin transporters (34, 35) is activated to lipoyl-AMP by a lipoate-activating enzyme, and then the lipoyl moiety is transferred to a lysine residue in the acceptor protein by a lipoyl-AMP:Nϵ-lysine lipoyltransferase; both enzymes have been cloned and characterized from mammalian sources (36). However, recent studies have revealed that mammalian mitochondria also contain a lipoic acid synthase, which converts octanoyl-ACP to lipoyl-ACP (37). Although a lipoyl-ACP-dependent transferase required for the lipoylation of mitochondrial proteins (performed by the lipB and LIP2 gene products of prokaryotes and plant mitochondria, respectively (38, 39)) has yet to be identified in mammalian mitochondria, this finding raised the possibility that endogenously synthesized lipoic acid may be utilized for the lipoylation of mitochondrial proteins, as it is in fungal and plant mitochondria. In mammals, all of the known lipoate-containing proteins, pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and glycine cleavage enzyme, are located in the mitochondria (40) and the presence of a lipoate-producing system in this organelle may ensure an adequate supply of this cofactor, essential for mitochondrial function, independent of dietary availability.
Collectively then, the complementation of the CEM1 knockout by the human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase, the similar substrate specificities, and close evolutionary relationship of type II human mitochondrial and prokaryotic β-ketoacyl synthases suggest that the type II enzymes fulfill similar roles in these different environments, namely the supply of octanoyl-ACP for lipoic acid production and the production of long chain length fatty acyl moieties for membrane phospholipid biosynthesis. Nevertheless, until unequivocal experimental evidence is obtained validating this hypothesis, the possibility that the FAS pathway might generate other products important for mitochondrial function, such as myristate for protein modification, should not be discounted. In this regard, the finding that ACP isolated from N. crassa mitochondria appeared to have a β-hydroxymyristoyl moiety attached to the phosphopantetheine (41) remains something of an enigma. Evaluation of the effects of down-regulation of expression of mitochondrial FAS components on mitochondrial function may resolve these questions.
In recent years the type II fatty acid-synthesizing systems of microorganisms have been identified as promising targets for the development of new therapeutic agents for the treatment of a variety of infectious diseases, based primarily on the premise that such agents likely would have little or no effect on the type I FAS system present in the cytosol of the animal host cells (31, 42, 43). Demonstration of the presence of a type II FAS system in animal mitochondria indicates that caution should be exercised in the screening of such compounds, and assurance should be sought that they have no serious side effects on mitochondrial function.

paper result.text:
Cloning, expression, and characterization of the human mitochondrial beta-ketoacyl synthase. Complementation of the yeast CEM1 knock-out strain

Abstract
A human beta-ketoacyl synthase implicated in a mitochondrial pathway for fatty acid synthesis has been identified, cloned, expressed, and characterized. Sequence analysis indicates that the protein is more closely related to freestanding counterparts found in prokaryotes and chloroplasts than it is to the beta-ketoacyl synthase domain of the human cytosolic fatty acid synthase. The full-length nuclear-encoded 459-residue protein includes an N-terminal sequence element of approximately 38 residues that functions as a mitochondrial targeting sequence. The enzyme can elongate acyl-chains containing 2-14 carbon atoms with malonyl moieties attached in thioester linkage to the human mitochondrial acyl carrier protein and is able to restore growth to the respiratory-deficient yeast mutant cem1 that lacks the endogenous mitochondrial beta-ketoacyl synthase and exhibits lowered lipoic acid levels. To date, four components of a putative type II mitochondrial fatty acid synthase pathway have been identified in humans: acyl carrier protein, malonyl transferase, beta-ketoacyl synthase, and enoyl reductase.

The substrate specificity and complementation data for the beta-ketoacyl synthase suggest that, as in plants and fungi, in humans this pathway may play an important role in the generation of octanoyl-acyl carrier protein, the lipoic acid precursor, as well as longer chain fatty acids that are required for optimal mitochondrial function.

Over the last decade, it has become clear that fungal and plant mitochondria are capable of synthesizing fatty acids de novo (1–6). The enzymes involved in the pathway are freestanding, monofunctional proteins of the type II variety and are distinct from the multifunctional polypeptide type I FASs1 present in the cytosol of fungi and animals. Thus far, the preponderance of evidence suggests that these mitochondrial FAS pathways function to produce octanoyl-ACP, the precursor of lipoic acid (4) and longer chain-length fatty acids that may be utilized for the remodeling of mitochondrial membrane phospholipids (7). The presence of a similar mitochondrial FAS system in animals has been suspected for some time, based initially on the discovery of an ACP-like protein in animal mitochondria (8, 9).

However, only recently have other components of a putative mitochondrial FAS been identified, cloned, and characterized; they include the human ACP and malonyl transferase (10) and enoyl reductase (11). In continuation of the search for other components, we have now identified and characterized a single candidate for a type II human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase, the critical enzyme required for catalysis of the chain-elongating condensation reaction.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES
Cloning of the Human Mitochondrial β-Ketoacyl Synthase—Using the sequences of several authentic type I and type II β-ketoacyl synthases as probes to BLAST search the human genome sequence data base, we identified a sequence (accession NP_060367) that also was represented in a human EST clone (IMAGE clone 3446492, ATCC MGC-4956) and appeared likely to encode a full-length human β-ketoacyl synthase, together with an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence. A cDNA from this EST clone was used as template to generate a construct for expression in Escherichia coli. Specific primers (KSmitqeT/B, Table I) with appropriate restriction sites for cloning were designed, and the cDNA encoding the putative β-ketoacyl synthase was amplified using PCR, essentially as described earlier (12). The E.

coli expression construct carried a 37-residue N-terminal deletion that we deduced, by analysis of multiple sequence alignments, might represent a mitochondrial targeting sequence. The amplified fragment was purified using a QIAquick PCR purification kit (Qiagen), cleaved with appropriate restriction enzymes and cloned into the pQE80 L (QE) E. coli expression vector (Qiagen). To facilitate purification of the recombinant protein by affinity chromatography, a His6-tag was encoded at the N terminus of the construct. The authenticity of the cloned, amplified fragments was confirmed by DNA sequencing.

Verification That the Putative N-terminal Mitochondrial Recognition Elements Direct the β-Ketoacyl Synthase into Mitochondria—A PCR-amplified fragment (primer set KSmit1–38gfpT/B, Table I) encoding the first 38 amino acid residues (putative targeting sequence) of the human mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase was directionally cloned into the EcoRI and KpnI sites of the pEGFP-N3 vector (Clontech) to facilitate expression as the N-terminal partner of a KSmit1–38-EGFP fusion protein. Authenticity of the cloned fragment was confirmed by DNA sequencing.
