Przyrembel, personal communication; details reviewed in a study by Mudd et al. [1998]). Patient BII-1, a 1.6-year-old boy, with plasma methionine of 233 μM at age 2 mo, was shown to carry the single-allelic MAT1A R264H mutation with an exon VII haplotype of 1/4 (fig. 3). Members of his immediate family were screened for plasma methionine concentrations and for the presence of the R264H allele.

Consistent with the dominant mode of inheritance, his father, BI-1, in good health at age 37 years, had moderately elevated plasma methionine levels (105 mM) and was a heterozygote for a normal allele and the R264H mutation, with exon VII haplotype 3/4 (fig. 3). The mother and a sister, with VII haplotypes 1/1 and 1/3, respectively, have wild-type MAT1A genes and normal plasma methionine levels (fig. 3).

Discussion
The MAT1A gene is expressed primarily in the liver, the organ in which synthesis of the predominant portion of AdoMet occurs (Mudd and Poole 1975; Kotb et al. 1997). AdoMet serves as the methyl donor in the biosynthesis of ⩾100 metabolites. Thus, studies of genetic, metabolic, and clinical aspects of mutations in the MAT1A gene are of interest. Current evidence establishes that deleterious MAT1A mutations cause abnormal accumulation of methionine (reviewed in the studies by Mudd et al. [1995a, 1998]). In the present study, we report characterization of MAT1A mutations in seven hypermethioninemic individuals and uncover six novel mutations: 113G→A/S38N, 255delCA/92X, 791C→T/R264C, 1006G→A/G336R, 1031A→C/E344A, and 292G↓gt→A↓gt. To date, a total of 17 MAT1A mutations have been identified among 47 hypermethioninemic individuals (Ubagai et al. 1995; Chamberlin et al.

1996, 1997; Nagao and Oyanagi 1997; Hazelwood et al. 1998; present study).

The available evidence suggests that the metabolic and the clinical effects of MAT1A mutations are highly variable. The majority (32 of 47) of the genotyped individuals carry a dominant MAT1A mutation, R264H (Chamberlin et al. 1997; Nagao and Oyanagi 1997; Mudd et al. 1998). The metabolic result of this single-allelic mutation is relatively mild elevation of plasma methionine, which, clinically, appears to be entirely benign, as exemplified by the good health of individual BI-1 at age 37 years.

The remaining genotypes, all of which behave as autosomal recessive traits, are more heterogeneous with respect to the severity of the hypermethioninemia and the clinical states of the individuals carrying the mutations (Ubagai et al. 1995; Chamberlin et al. 1996; present study). Nine individuals (G1–G4, 5, 10, 11, 13, and 14) carry only missense mutations in their MAT1A gene (table 3). Most such individuals were clinically unaffected at last report, although some were very young at that time (Gaull et al. 1981; Mudd et al. 1995b, 1998). Transient expression assays demonstrate that most mutant MATs found in these patients retain significant enzymatic activity (Ubagai et al. 1995; Chamberlin et al.

1996). Within this group, patient 5 is perhaps exceptional in that, cognitively, she functions less well than her unaffected siblings. However, she had a normal MRI of the brain at age 13 years. She carries two mutations, R264C and G336R. R264C has virtually no enzymatic activity, whereas G336R retains significant MAT activity (23% of the level of the wild-type enzyme). Nevertheless, the persistently extremely high plasma methionine concentrations observed in this patient suggest that she may have less residual MAT I/III activity in vivo than do the other eight members of this group.

Patients 9 and 1 each carry both missense and insertion or deletion mutations (table 3). The 539insTG mutation in patient 9 yields a severely truncated protein devoid of MAT activity, whereas his R199C retains 11% of wild-type activity (Chamberlin et al. 1996). At age 6 years, this patient attained a composite score on the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale that placed him in the lowest 1% of the population, but, on an MRI of his brain, white matter was termed unremarkable, and there was no evidence for gray-matter heterotopia (S. Richter, personal communication).

In patient 1, the 255delCA mutation also yields a severely truncated protein without MAT activity, but, unlike the situation in patient 9, his S38N mutation abolishes MAT activity. An MRI study of the brain of this patient at age 20 years revealed anomalies of gray matter, the first demonstrated among patients with isolated hypermethioninemia.

Four patients (C, Mr C, 3, and 8) are homozygous for deletion/insertion mutations (table 3), yielding truncated MAT mutants devoid of enzymatic activity (Chamberlin et al. 1996; Hazelwood et al. 1998). Generally, these patients have the most extreme elevations of plasma methionine (Gahl et al. 1988; Surtees et al. 1991; Mudd et al. 1995b). Patient C is homozygous for a 827insG, predicted to encode a truncated protein of 350 amino acids; patient 8 is homozygous for a 1043delTG mutation, encoding a truncated protein of 349 amino acids (table 3); and both patients had neurological problems and demyelination documented by MRI scans at ages 11 and 9 years, respectively (Surtees et al. 1991; Mudd et al. 1995b). Patient 3 and Mr C are homozygous for a 539insTG mutation, yielding a truncated polypeptide of 184 amino acids (Chamberlin et al. 1996; Hazelwood et al. 1998).

However, both are free of neurological problems and neither had suggestions of demyelination on MRI examinations at ages 43 years (Hazelwood et al. 1998) and 6.25 years (W. Wilson, personal communication), respectively. The possibility has been raised that deleterious interactions may take place between the abnormal, slightly truncated, MAT1A α1 subunits synthesized in patients 8 and C and the normal α2 subunits encoded by MAT2A, whereas similar interactions might be less likely with the more-severely truncated α1 subunits produced by patients 3 and Mr C (Hazelwood et al. 1998).

Patient 7 is the only affected individual demonstrated to be homozygous for a splicing mutation in the MAT1A gene. Although the concentration of MAT activity in the liver of this patient remains unknown, his consistently high plasma methionine concentrations, comparable to those found in patients with homozygous null mutations (Mudd et al. 1995b), suggests that his MAT I/III activity deficit may be virtually complete.

In spite of normal neurological examinations at ages 4 years and 7 years, he was found, on MRIs of the brain, to have signs of demyelination and, at age 7 years, is said, by staff at his school, to be manifesting poor cognitive skills.

Assays of enzymatic activity of mutant MAT1A cDNA constructs in transient expression studies provide only provisional estimates of the contributions of such mutations to MAT I/III activity in vivo. Interactions among subunits, changes in the state of polymerization, and other variables may all affect the actual MAT activity in the liver. Nevertheless, the observations reviewed here seem to indicate that moderate impairments in MAT I/III activity are clinically benign. Among patients with severe impairments in MAT I/III activity, however, there seems to be a clustering of neurological problems, learning disabilities, and MRI abnormalities of white matter and, in one case, gray matter. Nevertheless, clinical problems are not universal in these individuals. Thus, the question of a possible causative relationship between severe deficiency of MAT I/III activity and clinical problems remains open. Further studies that assess the genetics and the clinical status of individuals with isolated persistent hypermethioninemia may help to answer this question.

content:
Characterization of the monomethylarsonate reductase and dehydroascorbate reductase activities of Omega class glutathione transferase variants: implications for arsenic metabolism and the age-at-onset of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases

Abstract
There are two functional Omega class glutathione transferase (GST) genes in humans. GSTO1 is polymorphic with several coding region alleles, including an A140D substitution, a potential deletion of E155 and an E208K substitution. GSTO2 is also polymorphic with an N142D substitution in the coding region. We investigated the effect of these variations on the enzyme's thioltransferase, dehydroascorbate reductase, monomethylarsonate reductase and dimethylarsonate reductase activities. Variant proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli and purified by Ni-agarose affinity chromatography. GSTO2-2 was insoluble and had to be dissolved and refolded from 8 M urea. The A140D and E208K substitutions in GSTO1-1 did not alter specific activity. The deletion of E155 caused a two- to three-fold increase in the specific activity with each substrate. This deletion also caused a significant decrease in the enzyme's heat stability. The E155 deletion has been linked to abnormal arsenic excretion patterns; however, the available data do not clearly identify the cause of this abnormality. We found that GSTO2-2 has activity with the same substrates as GSTO1-1, and the dehydroascorbate reductase activity of GSTO2-2 is approximately 70–100-fold higher than that of GSTO1-1. The polymorphic N142D substitution had no effect on the specific activity of the enzyme with any substrate. The most notable feature of GSTO2-2 was its very high dehydroascorbate reductase activity, which suggests that GSTO2-2 may significantly protect against oxidative stress by recycling ascorbate. A defect in ascorbate metabolism may provide a common mechanism by which the Omega class GSTs influence the age-at-onset of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

Introduction
The glutathione transferases (GSTs) are a large family of proteins with diverse functions that range from the conjugation of xenobiotics to the modulation of signal transduction pathways and the formation and modulation of membrane ion channels [1–3]. The recently described Omega class GSTs have some unusual properties compared to other members of the GST superfamily. Omega class GSTs have a cysteine residue in the active site compared to a tyrosine or serine residue in other mammalian GSTs [4–6]. In addition, the Omega GSTs have minimal catalytic activity with many compounds that are substrates for members of other GST classes and exhibit novel thiol transferase and dehydroascorbate reductase activities [4]. In previous studies, we identified two functional Omega class GST genes in humans (GSTO1 and GSTO2) that are separated by 7.5 kb on chromosome 10q24.3 [7]. GSTO1 is transcribed in a wide range of human tissues and recombinant hGSTO1-1 has been biochemically and structurally characterized [4,7]. In addition to thiol transferase and dehydroascorbate reductase activities, hGSTO1-1 has monomethylarsonate (MMAV) reductase activity and is considered to be the rate-limiting enzyme in the biomethylation pathway of inorganic arsenic metabolism [8]. Arsenic trioxide is used in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia and some fatal adverse reactions have suggested that there may be genetically determined differences in the capacity to metabolize arsenic. Although recent studies have suggested that a genetic polymorphism in GSTO1 is associated with an unusual urinary arsenic excretion profile in individuals exposed to a high arsenic burden [9], the MMAV reductase activity of the different GSTO1-1 variants has not been determined.

A rat dehydroascorbate reductase (DHAR) has been previously cloned and sequence analysis suggests that it is an Omega class GST [4,10]. Previous studies have shown that human GSTO1-1 has significant DHAR activity [4]. Immunohistochemical and functional studies of this enzyme in the rat brain suggest that it plays a significant role in maintaining ascorbate levels [11]. A major role for ascorbate in the brain appears to be scavenging free radicals and reactive oxygen species [12]. The reduction and recycling of dehydroascorbate by Omega class GSTs protects the brain against damage caused by free radicals and the products of oxidative stress. This activity suggests that the Omega class GSTs protect against the oxidative processes that have been implicated in the pathology of degenerative neurological disease [13]. In convergent genetic mapping studies, the Omega class GST genes have been shown to be significantly associated with the age-at-onset of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease [14].

In addition to its enzymatic activities, GSTO1-1 has been reported to modulate the function of ryanodine receptor calcium release channels [15], and to play a role in the post-translational processing and release of interleukin-1β in monocytes [16]. The precise mechanisms by which GSTO1-1 mediates these effects are unclear.

In our previous studies, we identified the GSTO2 gene and a polymorphism that encodes an N142D substitution [7]. Unfortunately, recombinant hGSTO2-2 was prone to precipitate when purified and we were unable to characterize the purified protein. In view of the role of the Omega class GSTs in the metabolism of arsenic and their potential role in protection against neurological disease, it has become increasingly important to determine the properties of GSTO2-2 and to determine whether the N142D polymorphism is of functional significance. We have now developed a method of refolding recombinant GSTO2-2 that has provided sufficient stable protein to characterize the substrate preferences of both polymorphic isoforms. Our studies to date have shown that human GSTO2-2 has dehydroascorbate reductase activity that is 100-fold greater than that of GSTO1-1. Similar to GSTO1-1, GSTO2-2 also has MMAV reductase activity.

Materials and methods
Expression and purification of hGSTO1-1
The expression and purification of hGSTO1-1 isoforms was carried out from pQE30 plasmids (Qiagen, Hilden Germany) as previously described [4,7]. A glutamate to lysine substitution was introduced at position 208 in the GSTO1 clone by the use of a QuikChange Site-Directed Mutagenesis Kit (Stratagene, La Jolla, California, USA).

Expression of hGSTO2-2
Full-length cDNA fragments encoding the N142 and D142 variant isoforms of human GSTO2-2 were cloned into the expression vector pQE30 (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) and transfected into the M15-rep4 strain of Escherichia coli [7]. Bacterial cultures were grown at 37°C overnight in Luria Broth medium supplemented with 100 μg/ml ampicillin and 30 μg/ml kanamycin. A 1 : 100 dilution of overnight culture was used to inoculate 2 l subcultures that were grown at 37°C for 2 h and then chilled to 8°C. Expression of recombinant protein was induced with isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) at a final concentration of 0.1 mM. Incubation was carried out with shaking at 8°C for 24 h. Cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 4°C and stored at −20°C.

Purification and refolding of GSTO2-2
Cell pellets were resuspended in ice-cold Buffer A (8 M urea; 1 mM GSH; 50 mM NaH2PO4; 300 mM NaCl; pH 7.5) and lysed by sonication. Cell debris was removed by centrifugation at 10 000 g for 15 min at 4°C and the cleared lysates were incubated with Ni-sepharose beads equilibrated in Buffer A. Subsequent steps were performed at room temperature. Ni-sepharose beads were washed with Buffer A and collected by centrifugation twice. The beads then transferred onto a scintered funnel and washed with 500 ml of Buffer A. The Ni-sepharose beads were then packed into a column and the refolding of bound GSTO2-2 was carried out in a Pharmacia fast protein liquid chromatography (FPLC) apparatus (Pharmacia, Arlington Heights, Illinois, USA) at room temperature. A program was used to cyclically lower, and partially raise the urea concentration leading to the eventual removal of the urea from the equilibrating buffer (Table 1). The flow rate of buffers was adjusted to 0.5 ml/min. Refolded enzyme was eluted from the column using a 0–500 mM imidazole gradient. Fractions of 1 ml were collected and those containing expressed refolded GSTO2-2 were identified by gel electrophoresis and concentrated in a Centricon YM-10 centrifugal filter (Millipore, Bedford, Massachusetts, USA). Glycerol and buffer A minus urea was added to the stocks to a final glycerol concentration of 30% and a final protein concentration of 0.5 mg/ml. Protein stocks were stored at −20°C.

Assays for general GST substrates
The activity of expressed proteins towards 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, cumene hydroperoxide and trans-nonenal were performed using methods described elsewhere [4]. For each protein, four replicates from two independent preparations were assayed.

Thioltransferase
Thioltransferase activity was determined using 2-hydroxy ethyl disulfide (HEDS) as a substrate as described previously [17]. The reactions were carried out in a final volume of 1 ml containing 0.3 mM NADPH, 1 mM GSH, 4 U glutathione reductase from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Sigma-Aldrich, Castle Hill, Australia), 0.1 mg/ml bovine serum albumin, 1.5 mM EDTA, 0.75 mM HEDS, and 0.1 M Tris HCl pH 8.0. The reaction mix was preincubated at 30°C for 3 min to allow the formation of a HEDS-GSH mixed disulfide and the reaction was started by the addition of approximately 25 μg of enzyme sample. Specific activities were calculated using an extinction coefficient of 6.22/ mM/cm.

DHA reductase
Reactions were performed in a final volume of 1 ml containing 200 mM sodium phosphate; 3 mM GSH; 1.5 mM dehydroascorbate (DHA); pH 6.85. 1.5–4 μg of protein was used in each reaction. Reactions were initiated by addition of DHA, and the rate of change in absorbance at 265 nm was measured at 30°C for 2 min. Assays were generally performed in triplicate. For refolded enzymes, six replicates were assayed using proteins from three independent preparations unless otherwise indicated. Reaction rates in the absence of enzyme were subtracted from the primary data. Dehydroascorbate was prepared immediately before use by a previously described method and was used within 3 h [18]. Specific activities were calculated using an extinction coefficient of 14.7/ mM/cm.

MMAV and DMAV reductase
The enzymatic reduction of MMAV (disodium methylarsenate; Chem Service, West Chester, Pennsylvania, USA) and dimethylarsinic acid (DMAV, sodium cacodylate; BDH Chemical, Poole, UK) results in the oxidation of reduced glutathione (GSH) to its disulfide GSSG. The production of GSSG was followed spectrophotometrically at 340 nm by linking its reduction by glutathione reductase to the oxidation of NADPH. The assay was based on a previously described method [19] and contained the following reagents in a final volume of 1 ml; Bis-Tris 0.1 M pH 5.5, GSH 10 mM, NADPH 0.3 mM, EDTA 5 mM, glutathione reductase 4 U, and either MMAV or DMAV at a final concentration of 10 mM. The reaction mix was preincubated for 10 min at 30°C before the addition of the enzyme sample. The reactions were recorded for 3 min and the initial reaction rate over the first minute was used for the calculation of activity. Specific activities were calculated using an extinction coefficient of 6.22/ mM/cm.

Heat stability
The relative stability of different isoenzymes was evaluated by measuring the loss of activity after incubation at 60°C (GSTO1-1), or 53°C (GSTO2-2). Thioltransferase activity was measured for GSTO1-1 and DHAR activity was determined for GSTO2-2. The samples were placed on ice immediately after heat treatment and centrifuged briefly in a microfuge to remove precipitated protein. The results are the mean of at least three determinations and the variation between the replicates was less than 10%.

Optimum pH
The DHAR activity of GSTO2-2 was determined at a range of pH points (5–8) using previously described buffers [20]. A high rate of non-enzymatic reaction between DHA and glutathione at higher pH did not allow accurate measurement of enzyme activities at pH points higher than 8.

Genotyping
Genotyping of the 3-bp (AGG) deletion (c. 464-IVS4+1del) was carried out by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification and polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis as previously described [7]. The G>A transition that generates a glutamate to lysine substitution at position 208 (c. 619G>A) was genotyped by sequencing a 741-bp genomic DNA fragment that was amplified with the following primers (O1int5F 5′-TTACTTTTGGCATAATCTGG-3′, O1int6R 5′-ATTTGGGGGTTTTCAGCATG-3′). Before sequencing, the PCR product was treated with shrimp alkaline phosphatase (SAP) and exonuclease I (ExoI) as described in detail by the Filarial Genome Network (http://nema.cap.ed.ac.uk/fgn/methods/SAP_EXOI.html). Briefly, 15 μl of PCR product was combined with 1 μl of SAP (1 U/μl; Amersham Biosciences, Castle Hill, Australia) and 1.5 μl of ExoI (1 U/μl Amersham Biosciences, Castle Hill, Australia) and incubated for 30 min at 37°C, 10 min at 80°C and 5 min at 5°C. DNA sequences were determined by the Biomolecular Resource Facility at the John Curtin School of Medical Research.

Results
GSTO1-1
In a previous study, we noted that a relatively rare polymorphic deletion of E155 caused an increase in thioltransferase activity and a decrease in heat stability [7]. It was subsequently suggested that the deletion of E155 was possibly linked to an E208K substitution [9,21] and the effects of the E208K substitution are unclear. We have now confirmed that there is very strong linkage disequilibrium (P<0.000001) between the deletion of E155 and K208 in a sample of Australian Europeans (Table 2). In five out of six cases, the deletion of E155 was on the same haplotype as a lysine residue at position 208. In addition, lysine was never found at position 208 in the absence of the deletion of E155. We then studied the Chinese subjects with the E155 deletion that were identified in our previous study [7]. By contrast to the situation in the Europeans, the E155 deletion was on the same haplotype as the E208 allele in seven out of seven cases. It should be noted that because of our selection of subjects with the E155 deletion, the Chinese subjects tested in Table 2 are not a random sample and the data should not be used for the determination of gene frequencies. We conclude from these data that the deletion of E155 appears on different haplotypes with respect to the residue at position 208 in the European and Chinese populations. This difference presumably has its origin in the evolutionary history of the different racial groups and the possibility that the same alleles have arisen as recurrent mutations on different haplotypes.

Previous studies have shown that GSTO1-1 can catalyse the reduction of MMAV to MMAIII [8], but the effects of polymorphic amino acid substitutions on this activity have not been studied. We have therefore investigated the effects of the deletion of E155 and the E208K substitution on the activity of GSTO1-1 with a range of substrates, including the pentavalent methylated arsenic species MMAV and DMAV. The data in Table 3 show that GSTO1-1 has significant activity with both MMAV and DMAV and that the polymorphic A140D substitution has little effect on activity with a range of substrates. By contrast the deletion of E155 results in a two- to three-fold increase in specific activity with all substrates studied. This effect appears to be largely independent of the residue at position 208 because the single mutation of E208 to K208 had little effect with most substrates.

In light of the observation that the deletion of E155 is strongly linked to a lysine at 208 in some populations, we re-examined the heat stability of these proteins (Fig. 1). The data indicate that the residue at position 208 does not influence heat stability. By contrast, these data confirm that the deletion of E155 results in a significant decrease in stability at 60°C.

GSTO2-2
In previous studies, we found that recombinant hGSTO2-2 expressed in E. coli was largely insoluble and was difficult to purify in sufficient quantities to allow the characterization of its substrate preferences [7]. In subsequent experiments, we have found that hGSTO2-2 can be solubilized in 8 M urea and purified by Ni-sepharose chromatography. To remove the urea and to refold the protein, we employed a cyclic program of decreasing and increasing urea gradients that ultimately results in the refolding and stabilization of hGSTO2-2 when it is immobilized on Ni-sepharose. The refolded enzyme can be eluted from the Ni-sepharose in the absence of urea and stored in 30% glycerol at −20°C without precipitation. This purification and refolding procedure has provided sufficient material to allow the limited biochemical characterization of human GSTO2-2.

We compared the properties of two allelic GSTO2 variants that differ at residue 142 (N142, D142). Neither isoform showed detectable activities with common GST substrates such as 1-chloro-2,4-dinitro benzene, ethacrynic acid and cumene hydroperoxide. The substrate preferences of hGSTO2-2 were similar to those of hGSTO1-1 (Table 3), and there were no significant differences in the specific activities of the N142 and D142 isoforms. The thioltransferase activity of the hGSTO2-2 variants was similar in magnitude to that of the common hGSTO1-1 isoforms. By contrast, the DHAR activity of hGSTO2-2 was approximately 100-fold greater than that of hGSTO1-1. The DHAR activity of hGSTO2-2 is clearly the highest of any animal enzyme studied to date (Table 4). However, plant DHAR activities are considerably higher than even hGSTO2-2. The N142 and D142 isoforms of hGSTO2-2 had similar Km values for glutathione and DHA. The Km values for GSH were 11.8±5.7 mM and 11.4±1.1 mM for the N142 and D142 variants, respectively. Km values for DHA were 0.5±0.1 mM and 0.5±0.2 mM for the N142 and D142 enzymes, respectively.

Similar to hGSTO1-1, hGSTO2-2 was able to catalyse the reduction of MMAV and DMAV. However, the specific activity of both hGSTO2-2 isoforms with DMAV was markedly lower than the values obtained with hGSTO1-1.

To further characterize the refolded hGSTO2-2 isoforms, we compared their heat stability. At 53°C, both GSTO2-2 isoforms showed a similar loss of dehydroascorbate reductase activity over 30 min (Fig. 2). A pH/activity profile revealed a pH optimum of pH7.5 but there was no difference in the response of the hGSTO2-2 N142 and D142 isoforms (data not shown).

Discussion
Although it has been suggested that previously reported individual differences in the metabolism of arsenic and the adverse responses to arsenic trioxide therapy may have a pharmacogenetic explanation [22–24], there have been few pharmacogenetic studies of the enzymes involved in this pathway. Our previous studies have shown that GSTO1-1 catalyses the reduction of MMAV to MMAIII, the rate-limiting step in the biotransformation of arsenic in humans [8] (Fig. 3). Other studies have shown that there are several polymorphic forms of this gene in different populations, but their effects on the reduction of MMAV have not been fully investigated [7,9,21,25]. In this study, we have used a spectrophotometric method to measure the formation of oxidized glutathione during the reduction of pentavalent methylated arsenic species to trivalent forms [19]. This method is rapid and avoids the use of radio labelled MMAV that has been used in previous studies [26] and which is not commercially available. However, we note that this assay is limited to the use of low enzyme levels as the response at higher concentrations is not linear. The present study has shown that GSTO1-1 can catalyse the reduction of both MMAV and DMAV, and thus it contributes to at least two steps in the biotransformation of inorganic arsenic (Fig. 3). We found no differences in the thioltransferase, DHAR, MMAV reductase and DMAV reductase activities of the A140 or D140 isoforms of GSTO1-1. This is a common polymorphism in all populations studied to date [7,9,21]. Our previous structural studies have shown that residue 140 is positioned on the outside of helix 5 and is extremely unlikely to be involved in interactions with substrates or other interactions that could indirectly influence the structure or stability of the enzyme (Fig. 4).

In a previous study of individuals residing in the vicinity of Torreon, Mexico, who were exposed to arsenic contaminating their drinking water, two related subjects (mother and son) were shown to have a decreased capacity to metabolize inorganic arsenic [9]. Both subjects were shown to be heterozygous for a GSTO1 haplotype that encoded a deletion of a glutamate residue at position 155 and encoded a lysine at position 208 [9]. This study suggested that one or both of these changes significantly affects the capacity of GSTO1-1 to reduce pentavalent methylated arsenic species. We have now confirmed the tight linkage between these two sites in European subjects. However, in Chinese subjects, we have found the deletion of E155 is linked to a glutamate at position 208. We were therefore interested to determine whether the E208K substitution and/or the deletion of E155 altered the reductase activity of the enzyme with methylated arsenic species. In the present study, we have shown that the E208K substitution has little effect on the capacity of the enzyme to reduce pentavalent forms of methylated arsenic. This experimental result is consistent with the position of residue 208 on the outside of helix 7, where there is little likelihood of interaction with substrates or an indirect effect on structure and stability (Fig. 4). By contrast, the deletion of E155 increases the specific activity of the enzyme with both MMAV and DMAV. Glutamate 155 is positioned on the outside of the C-terminal end of helix 5 (Fig. 4) and its deletion could conceivably influence the position of helix 4 or helix 6, which form the back of the substrate binding pocket. This increase in specific activity may be countered in vivo by a decrease in the stability of the enzyme that is suggested by its low heat stability in vitro. Further studies to evaluate the stability of this isoform in a cellular environment are in progress. Alternatively, because the deletion of E155 results from the reformation of the exon 4/intron 4 splice site [7], it is possible that a decrease in the efficiency of correct splicing could cause a deficiency of GSTO1-1. It is also of interest that the mother and son with the variant urinary arsenic excretion phenotype are only heterozygous for the E155 deletion [9]. If this allele does result in a deficiency of GSTO1-1, the activity in heterozygotes should only be diminished to 50% unless a dominant negative effect arises from the dimerization of the deleted and normal subunits. In most cases of enzyme deficiency arising from autosomal genes, heterozygotes are phenotypically normal. The abnormal phenotype of these GSTO1-1 heterozygotes suggests that GSTO1-1 activity is critical for the arsenic-methylation biotransformation pathway when subjects are exposed to a high arsenic burden. Given the low frequency of the E155 deletion allele in the populations studied to date, homozygotes are likely to be rare and we identified only one such Chinese individual in a previous study of African, Chinese and European subjects [7]. However, given the significant disturbance in inorganic arsenic metabolism that appears to occur in heterozygotes [9], and the report of adverse reactions in some patients treated with arsenic trioxide [24], the efficacy and toxicity of arsenic trioxide therapy for acute promyelocytic leukemia requires further investigation in heterozygotes with the E155 deletion allele.

A previous study has shown that a T217N substitution causes a significant decrease in the MMAV reductase activity of GSTO1-1 [25]. However, the relevance of this observation is currently unclear. Although this substitution is reported in SNP databases, it has never been observed in any population studies and may be either a very rare allele or the product of an EST sequencing error [7,9,21].

The substrate preferences of GSTO2-2 have not previously been reported because of the difficulty in purifying the recombinant enzyme [7]. The present study has successfully solved this problem by refolding the enzyme from 8 M urea. It is interesting to note that, compared to GSTO1-1, GSTO2-2 has a similar capacity to reduce MMAV but a much lower activity with DMAV. These data indicate that GSTO2-2 also plays a role in arsenic metabolism and differing levels of expression of these two enzymes in tissues may result in varying capacities of tissues and organs to process arsenic through the different steps of arsenic biotransformation. The relative levels of expression of GSTO1-1 and GSTO2-2 in different human tissues and cell types therefore warrants further detailed study. We have previously reported a polymorphism in GSTO2 that results in an N142D substitution [7]. The data obtained in the present study suggest that this polymorphism is unlikely to have any significant effect on arsenic biotransformation.

The most interesting property of GSTO2-2 appears to be its high dehydroascorbate reductase (DHAR) activity. DHAR activity is a minor property of several enzymes including glutaredoxin and protein disulfide isomerase [27]. A survey of published DHAR activities from a range of species suggests that the activity of hGSTO2-2 is far in excess of the levels achieved by other enzymes from animals (Table 4) and suggests a specific role for GSTO2-2 in recycling ascorbate.

Recent studies have implied a role for an Omega class GST gene in the age-at-onset of both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases [14], although this has not been confirmed in all studies of Parkinson's patients [28]. Because ascorbate is considered an important antioxidant in the brain [12] and oxidative stress has been implicated in the pathogenesis of both diseases [13,29,30], a defect in GSTO2-2 expression or function that diminishes anti-oxidant protection in the brain could be consistent with the early manifestation of both diseases. Clearly, further studies of the expression of GSTO2-2 in different tissues and cell types, particularly in the brain, are important. Our previous immunohistochemical studies of hGSTO1-1 used an antiserum that is now known to cross-react weakly with GSTO2-2 and may need to be reinterpreted. The extensive studies of rat DHAR (rGSTO1-1) in the brain may require similar consideration. In unpublished studies, we have identified a GSTO2-2 isoform in mice and this suggests a similar genomic arrangement is likely to be present in rats. The expression of Omega GSTs in the rat brain is of particular interest given the reported association with the age-at-onset of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases [14]. In particular, rat DHAR was found to be abundant in the cerebellum, striatum and hippocampus [11,31]. Detailed evaluation indicates that an Omega GST is expressed in several parts of the substantia nigra including the pars compacta, which is affected in Parkinson's disease [32].

Genetic variants of omega class GSTs, particularly GSTO2-2, could have an impact on redox sensitive processes. Clearly, the N142D polymorphism of hGSTO2 does not significantly affect DHAR activity, and thus, this polymorphism is unlikely to be directly related to the age-at-onset of these important neurological diseases. Further studies of promoter polymorphisms that may alter expression levels are currently in progress.

paper result.text:
Characterization of the monomethylarsonate reductase and dehydroascorbate reductase activities of Omega class glutathione transferase variants: implications for arsenic metabolism and the age-at-onset of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases

Abstract
There are two functional Omega class glutathione transferase (GST) genes in humans. GSTO1 is polymorphic with several coding region alleles, including an A140D substitution, a potential deletion of E155 and an E208K substitution. GSTO2 is also polymorphic with an N142D substitution in the coding region. We investigated the effect of these variations on the enzyme's thioltransferase, dehydroascorbate reductase, monomethylarsonate reductase and dimethylarsonate reductase activities. Variant proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli and purified by Ni-agarose affinity chromatography. GSTO2-2 was insoluble and had to be dissolved and refolded from 8 M urea. The A140D and E208K substitutions in GSTO1-1 did not alter specific activity. The deletion of E155 caused a two- to three-fold increase in the specific activity with each substrate. This deletion also caused a significant decrease in the enzyme's heat stability. The E155 deletion has been linked to abnormal arsenic excretion patterns; however, the available data do not clearly identify the cause of this abnormality.

We found that GSTO2-2 has activity with the same substrates as GSTO1-1, and the dehydroascorbate reductase activity of GSTO2-2 is approximately 70–100-fold higher than that of GSTO1-1. The polymorphic N142D substitution had no effect on the specific activity of the enzyme with any substrate. The most notable feature of GSTO2-2 was its very high dehydroascorbate reductase activity, which suggests that GSTO2-2 may significantly protect against oxidative stress by recycling ascorbate. A defect in ascorbate metabolism may provide a common mechanism by which the Omega class GSTs influence the age-at-onset of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

Introduction
The glutathione transferases (GSTs) are a large family of proteins with diverse functions that range from the conjugation of xenobiotics to the modulation of signal transduction pathways and the formation and modulation of membrane ion channels [1–3]. The recently described Omega class GSTs have some unusual properties compared to other members of the GST superfamily. Omega class GSTs have a cysteine residue in the active site compared to a tyrosine or serine residue in other mammalian GSTs [4–6].

In addition, the Omega GSTs have minimal catalytic activity with many compounds that are substrates for members of other GST classes and exhibit novel thiol transferase and dehydroascorbate reductase activities [4]. In previous studies, we identified two functional Omega class GST genes in humans (GSTO1 and GSTO2) that are separated by 7.5 kb on chromosome 10q24.3 [7]. GSTO1 is transcribed in a wide range of human tissues and recombinant hGSTO1-1 has been biochemically and structurally characterized [4,7]. In addition to thiol transferase and dehydroascorbate reductase activities, hGSTO1-1 has monomethylarsonate (MMAV) reductase activity and is considered to be the rate-limiting enzyme in the biomethylation pathway of inorganic arsenic metabolism [8]. Arsenic trioxide is used in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia and some fatal adverse reactions have suggested that there may be genetically determined differences in the capacity to metabolize arsenic.

Although recent studies have suggested that a genetic polymorphism in GSTO1 is associated with an unusual urinary arsenic excretion profile in individuals exposed to a high arsenic burden [9], the MMAV reductase activity of the different GSTO1-1 variants has not been determined.

A rat dehydroascorbate reductase (DHAR) has been previously cloned and sequence analysis suggests that it is an Omega class GST [4,10]. Previous studies have shown that human GSTO1-1 has significant DHAR activity [4]. Immunohistochemical and functional studies of this enzyme in the rat brain suggest that it plays a significant role in maintaining ascorbate levels [11]. A major role for ascorbate in the brain appears to be scavenging free radicals and reactive oxygen species [12]. The reduction and recycling of dehydroascorbate by Omega class GSTs protects the brain against damage caused by free radicals and the products of oxidative stress. This activity suggests that the Omega class GSTs protect against the oxidative processes that have been implicated in the pathology of degenerative neurological disease [13].

In convergent genetic mapping studies, the Omega class GST genes have been shown to be significantly associated with the age-at-onset of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease [14].

In addition to its enzymatic activities, GSTO1-1 has been reported to modulate the function of ryanodine receptor calcium release channels [15], and to play a role in the post-translational processing and release of interleukin-1β in monocytes [16]. The precise mechanisms by which GSTO1-1 mediates these effects are unclear.

In our previous studies, we identified the GSTO2 gene and a polymorphism that encodes an N142D substitution [7]. Unfortunately, recombinant hGSTO2-2 was prone to precipitate when purified and we were unable to characterize the purified protein. In view of the role of the Omega class GSTs in the metabolism of arsenic and their potential role in protection against neurological disease, it has become increasingly important to determine the properties of GSTO2-2 and to determine whether the N142D polymorphism is of functional significance. We have now developed a method of refolding recombinant GSTO2-2 that has provided sufficient stable protein to characterize the substrate preferences of both polymorphic isoforms.

Our studies to date have shown that human GSTO2-2 has dehydroascorbate reductase activity that is 100-fold greater than that of GSTO1-1. Similar to GSTO1-1, GSTO2-2 also has MMAV reductase activity.

Materials and methods
Expression and purification of hGSTO1-1
The expression and purification of hGSTO1-1 isoforms was carried out from pQE30 plasmids (Qiagen, Hilden Germany) as previously described [4,7]. A glutamate to lysine substitution was introduced at position 208 in the GSTO1 clone by the use of a QuikChange Site-Directed Mutagenesis Kit (Stratagene, La Jolla, California, USA).

Expression of hGSTO2-2
Full-length cDNA fragments encoding the N142 and D142 variant isoforms of human GSTO2-2 were cloned into the expression vector pQE30 (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) and transfected into the M15-rep4 strain of Escherichia coli [7]. Bacterial cultures were grown at 37°C overnight in Luria Broth medium supplemented with 100 μg/ml ampicillin and 30 μg/ml kanamycin. A 1 : 100 dilution of overnight culture was used to inoculate 2 l subcultures that were grown at 37°C for 2 h and then chilled to 8°C. Expression of recombinant protein was induced with isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) at a final concentration of 0.1 mM. Incubation was carried out with shaking at 8°C for 24 h.

Cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 4°C and stored at −20°C.

Purification and refolding of GSTO2-2
Cell pellets were resuspended in ice-cold Buffer A (8 M urea; 1 mM GSH; 50 mM NaH2PO4; 300 mM NaCl; pH 7.5) and lysed by sonication. Cell debris was removed by centrifugation at 10 000 g for 15 min at 4°C and the cleared lysates were incubated with Ni-sepharose beads equilibrated in Buffer A. Subsequent steps were performed at room temperature. Ni-sepharose beads were washed with Buffer A and collected by centrifugation twice. The beads then transferred onto a scintered funnel and washed with 500 ml of Buffer A. The Ni-sepharose beads were then packed into a column and the refolding of bound GSTO2-2 was carried out in a Pharmacia fast protein liquid chromatography (FPLC) apparatus (Pharmacia, Arlington Heights, Illinois, USA) at room temperature. A program was used to cyclically lower, and partially raise the urea concentration leading to the eventual removal of the urea from the equilibrating buffer (Table 1). The flow rate of buffers was adjusted to 0.5 ml/min. Refolded enzyme was eluted from the column using a 0–500 mM imidazole gradient.

Fractions of 1 ml were collected and those containing expressed refolded GSTO2-2 were identified by gel electrophoresis and concentrated in a Centricon YM-10 centrifugal filter (Millipore, Bedford, Massachusetts, USA). Glycerol and buffer A minus urea was added to the stocks to a final glycerol concentration of 30% and a final protein concentration of 0.5 mg/ml. Protein stocks were stored at −20°C.

Assays for general GST substrates
The activity of expressed proteins towards 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, cumene hydroperoxide and trans-nonenal were performed using methods described elsewhere [4]. For each protein, four replicates from two independent preparations were assayed.

Thioltransferase
Thioltransferase activity was determined using 2-hydroxy ethyl disulfide (HEDS) as a substrate as described previously [17]. The reactions were carried out in a final volume of 1 ml containing 0.3 mM NADPH, 1 mM GSH, 4 U glutathione reductase from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Sigma-Aldrich, Castle Hill, Australia), 0.1 mg/ml bovine serum albumin, 1.5 mM EDTA, 0.75 mM HEDS, and 0.1 M Tris HCl pH 8.0. The reaction mix was preincubated at 30°C for 3 min to allow the formation of a HEDS-GSH mixed disulfide and the reaction was started by the addition of approximately 25 μg of enzyme sample.

Specific activities were calculated using an extinction coefficient of 6.22/ mM/cm.

DHA reductase
Reactions were performed in a final volume of 1 ml containing 200 mM sodium phosphate; 3 mM GSH; 1.5 mM dehydroascorbate (DHA); pH 6.85. 1.5–4 μg of protein was used in each reaction. Reactions were initiated by addition of DHA, and the rate of change in absorbance at 265 nm was measured at 30°C for 2 min. Assays were generally performed in triplicate. For refolded enzymes, six replicates were assayed using proteins from three independent preparations unless otherwise indicated. Reaction rates in the absence of enzyme were subtracted from the primary data. Dehydroascorbate was prepared immediately before use by a previously described method and was used within 3 h [18]. Specific activities were calculated using an extinction coefficient of 14.7/ mM/cm.

MMAV and DMAV reductase
The enzymatic reduction of MMAV (disodium methylarsenate; Chem Service, West Chester, Pennsylvania, USA) and dimethylarsinic acid (DMAV, sodium cacodylate; BDH Chemical, Poole, UK) results in the oxidation of reduced glutathione (GSH) to its disulfide GSSG. The production of GSSG was followed spectrophotometrically at 340 nm by linking its reduction by glutathione reductase to the oxidation of NADPH.

The assay was based on a previously described method [19] and contained the following reagents in a final volume of 1 ml; Bis-Tris 0.1 M pH 5.5, GSH 10 mM, NADPH 0.3 mM, EDTA 5 mM, glutathione reductase 4 U, and either MMAV or DMAV at a final concentration of 10 mM. The reaction mix was preincubated for 10 min at 30°C before the addition of the enzyme sample. The reactions were recorded for 3 min and the initial reaction rate over the first minute was used for the calculation of activity. Specific activities were calculated using an extinction coefficient of 6.22/ mM/cm.

Heat stability
The relative stability of different isoenzymes was evaluated by measuring the loss of activity after incubation at 60°C (GSTO1-1), or 53°C (GSTO2-2). Thioltransferase activity was measured for GSTO1-1 and DHAR activity was determined for GSTO2-2. The samples were placed on ice immediately after heat treatment and centrifuged briefly in a microfuge to remove precipitated protein.

The results are the mean of at least three determinations and the variation between the replicates was less than 10%.

Optimum pH
The DHAR activity of GSTO2-2 was determined at a range of pH points (5–8) using previously described buffers [20]. A high rate of non-enzymatic reaction between DHA and glutathione at higher pH did not allow accurate measurement of enzyme activities at pH points higher than 8.

Genotyping
Genotyping of the 3-bp (AGG) deletion (c. 464-IVS4+1del) was carried out by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification and polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis as previously described [7]. The G>A transition that generates a glutamate to lysine substitution at position 208 (c. 619G>A) was genotyped by sequencing a 741-bp genomic DNA fragment that was amplified with the following primers (O1int5F 5′-TTACTTTTGGCATAATCTGG-3′, O1int6R 5′-ATTTGGGGGTTTTCAGCATG-3′). Before sequencing, the PCR product was treated with shrimp alkaline phosphatase (SAP) and exonuclease I (ExoI) as described in detail by the Filarial Genome Network (http://nema.cap.ed.ac.uk/fgn/methods/SAP_EXOI.html).

Briefly, 15 μl of PCR product was combined with 1 μl of SAP (1 U/μl; Amersham Biosciences, Castle Hill, Australia) and 1.5 μl of ExoI (1 U/μl Amersham Biosciences, Castle Hill, Australia) and incubated for 30 min at 37°C, 10 min at 80°C and 5 min at 5°C. DNA sequences were determined by the Biomolecular Resource Facility at the John Curtin School of Medical Research.

Results
GSTO1-1
In a previous study, we noted that a relatively rare polymorphic deletion of E155 caused an increase in thioltransferase activity and a decrease in heat stability [7]. It was subsequently suggested that the deletion of E155 was possibly linked to an E208K substitution [9,21] and the effects of the E208K substitution are unclear. We have now confirmed that there is very strong linkage disequilibrium (P<0.000001) between the deletion of E155 and K208 in a sample of Australian Europeans (Table 2). In five out of six cases, the deletion of E155 was on the same haplotype as a lysine residue at position 208. In addition, lysine was never found at position 208 in the absence of the deletion of E155.

We then studied the Chinese subjects with the E155 deletion that were identified in our previous study [7]. By contrast to the situation in the Europeans, the E155 deletion was on the same haplotype as the E208 allele in seven out of seven cases. It should be noted that because of our selection of subjects with the E155 deletion, the Chinese subjects tested in Table 2 are not a random sample and the data should not be used for the determination of gene frequencies. We conclude from these data that the deletion of E155 appears on different haplotypes with respect to the residue at position 208 in the European and Chinese populations. This difference presumably has its origin in the evolutionary history of the different racial groups and the possibility that the same alleles have arisen as recurrent mutations on different haplotypes.

Previous studies have shown that GSTO1-1 can catalyse the reduction of MMAV to MMAIII [8], but the effects of polymorphic amino acid substitutions on this activity have not been studied.

We have therefore investigated the effects of the deletion of E155 and the E208K substitution on the activity of GSTO1-1 with a range of substrates, including the pentavalent methylated arsenic species MMAV and DMAV. The data in Table 3 show that GSTO1-1 has significant activity with both MMAV and DMAV and that the polymorphic A140D substitution has little effect on activity with a range of substrates. By contrast the deletion of E155 results in a two- to three-fold increase in specific activity with all substrates studied. This effect appears to be largely independent of the residue at position 208 because the single mutation of E208 to K208 had little effect with most substrates.

In light of the observation that the deletion of E155 is strongly linked to a lysine at 208 in some populations, we re-examined the heat stability of these proteins (Fig. 1). The data indicate that the residue at position 208 does not influence heat stability. By contrast, these data confirm that the deletion of E155 results in a significant decrease in stability at 60°C.

GSTO2-2
In previous studies, we found that recombinant hGSTO2-2 expressed in E.

coli was largely insoluble and was difficult to purify in sufficient quantities to allow the characterization of its substrate preferences [7]. In subsequent experiments, we have found that hGSTO2-2 can be solubilized in 8 M urea and purified by Ni-sepharose chromatography. To remove the urea and to refold the protein, we employed a cyclic program of decreasing and increasing urea gradients that ultimately results in the refolding and stabilization of hGSTO2-2 when it is immobilized on Ni-sepharose. The refolded enzyme can be eluted from the Ni-sepharose in the absence of urea and stored in 30% glycerol at −20°C without precipitation. This purification and refolding procedure has provided sufficient material to allow the limited biochemical characterization of human GSTO2-2.

We compared the properties of two allelic GSTO2 variants that differ at residue 142 (N142, D142). Neither isoform showed detectable activities with common GST substrates such as 1-chloro-2,4-dinitro benzene, ethacrynic acid and cumene hydroperoxide. The substrate preferences of hGSTO2-2 were similar to those of hGSTO1-1 (Table 3), and there were no significant differences in the specific activities of the N142 and D142 isoforms. The thioltransferase activity of the hGSTO2-2 variants was similar in magnitude to that of the common hGSTO1-1 isoforms.

By contrast, the DHAR activity of hGSTO2-2 was approximately 100-fold greater than that of hGSTO1-1. The DHAR activity of hGSTO2-2 is clearly the highest of any animal enzyme studied to date (Table 4). However, plant DHAR activities are considerably higher than even hGSTO2-2. The N142 and D142 isoforms of hGSTO2-2 had similar Km values for glutathione and DHA. The Km values for GSH were 11.8±5.7 mM and 11.4±1.1 mM for the N142 and D142 variants, respectively. Km values for DHA were 0.5±0.1 mM and 0.5±0.2 mM for the N142 and D142 enzymes, respectively.

Similar to hGSTO1-1, hGSTO2-2 was able to catalyse the reduction of MMAV and DMAV. However, the specific activity of both hGSTO2-2 isoforms with DMAV was markedly lower than the values obtained with hGSTO1-1.

To further characterize the refolded hGSTO2-2 isoforms, we compared their heat stability. At 53°C, both GSTO2-2 isoforms showed a similar loss of dehydroascorbate reductase activity over 30 min (Fig. 2).

A pH/activity profile revealed a pH optimum of pH7.5 but there was no difference in the response of the hGSTO2-2 N142 and D142 isoforms (data not shown).

Discussion
Although it has been suggested that previously reported individual differences in the metabolism of arsenic and the adverse responses to arsenic trioxide therapy may have a pharmacogenetic explanation [22–24], there have been few pharmacogenetic studies of the enzymes involved in this pathway. Our previous studies have shown that GSTO1-1 catalyses the reduction of MMAV to MMAIII, the rate-limiting step in the biotransformation of arsenic in humans [8] (Fig. 3). Other studies have shown that there are several polymorphic forms of this gene in different populations, but their effects on the reduction of MMAV have not been fully investigated [7,9,21,25]. In this study, we have used a spectrophotometric method to measure the formation of oxidized glutathione during the reduction of pentavalent methylated arsenic species to trivalent forms [19]. This method is rapid and avoids the use of radio labelled MMAV that has been used in previous studies [26] and which is not commercially available.

However, we note that this assay is limited to the use of low enzyme levels as the response at higher concentrations is not linear. The present study has shown that GSTO1-1 can catalyse the reduction of both MMAV and DMAV, and thus it contributes to at least two steps in the biotransformation of inorganic arsenic (Fig. 3). We found no differences in the thioltransferase, DHAR, MMAV reductase and DMAV reductase activities of the A140 or D140 isoforms of GSTO1-1. This is a common polymorphism in all populations studied to date [7,9,21]. Our previous structural studies have shown that residue 140 is positioned on the outside of helix 5 and is extremely unlikely to be involved in interactions with substrates or other interactions that could indirectly influence the structure or stability of the enzyme (Fig. 4).

In a previous study of individuals residing in the vicinity of Torreon, Mexico, who were exposed to arsenic contaminating their drinking water, two related subjects (mother and son) were shown to have a decreased capacity to metabolize inorganic arsenic [9].

Both subjects were shown to be heterozygous for a GSTO1 haplotype that encoded a deletion of a glutamate residue at position 155 and encoded a lysine at position 208 [9]. This study suggested that one or both of these changes significantly affects the capacity of GSTO1-1 to reduce pentavalent methylated arsenic species. We have now confirmed the tight linkage between these two sites in European subjects. However, in Chinese subjects, we have found the deletion of E155 is linked to a glutamate at position 208. We were therefore interested to determine whether the E208K substitution and/or the deletion of E155 altered the reductase activity of the enzyme with methylated arsenic species. In the present study, we have shown that the E208K substitution has little effect on the capacity of the enzyme to reduce pentavalent forms of methylated arsenic. This experimental result is consistent with the position of residue 208 on the outside of helix 7, where there is little likelihood of interaction with substrates or an indirect effect on structure and stability (Fig. 4). By contrast, the deletion of E155 increases the specific activity of the enzyme with both MMAV and DMAV.

Glutamate 155 is positioned on the outside of the C-terminal end of helix 5 (Fig. 4) and its deletion could conceivably influence the position of helix 4 or helix 6, which form the back of the substrate binding pocket. This increase in specific activity may be countered in vivo by a decrease in the stability of the enzyme that is suggested by its low heat stability in vitro. Further studies to evaluate the stability of this isoform in a cellular environment are in progress. Alternatively, because the deletion of E155 results from the reformation of the exon 4/intron 4 splice site [7], it is possible that a decrease in the efficiency of correct splicing could cause a deficiency of GSTO1-1. It is also of interest that the mother and son with the variant urinary arsenic excretion phenotype are only heterozygous for the E155 deletion [9]. If this allele does result in a deficiency of GSTO1-1, the activity in heterozygotes should only be diminished to 50% unless a dominant negative effect arises from the dimerization of the deleted and normal subunits. In most cases of enzyme deficiency arising from autosomal genes, heterozygotes are phenotypically normal.

The abnormal phenotype of these GSTO1-1 heterozygotes suggests that GSTO1-1 activity is critical for the arsenic-methylation biotransformation pathway when subjects are exposed to a high arsenic burden. Given the low frequency of the E155 deletion allele in the populations studied to date, homozygotes are likely to be rare and we identified only one such Chinese individual in a previous study of African, Chinese and European subjects [7]. However, given the significant disturbance in inorganic arsenic metabolism that appears to occur in heterozygotes [9], and the report of adverse reactions in some patients treated with arsenic trioxide [24], the efficacy and toxicity of arsenic trioxide therapy for acute promyelocytic leukemia requires further investigation in heterozygotes with the E155 deletion allele.

A previous study has shown that a T217N substitution causes a significant decrease in the MMAV reductase activity of GSTO1-1 [25]. However, the relevance of this observation is currently unclear.

Although this substitution is reported in SNP databases, it has never been observed in any population studies and may be either a very rare allele or the product of an EST sequencing error [7,9,21].

The substrate preferences of GSTO2-2 have not previously been reported because of the difficulty in purifying the recombinant enzyme [7]. The present study has successfully solved this problem by refolding the enzyme from 8 M urea. It is interesting to note that, compared to GSTO1-1, GSTO2-2 has a similar capacity to reduce MMAV but a much lower activity with DMAV. These data indicate that GSTO2-2 also plays a role in arsenic metabolism and differing levels of expression of these two enzymes in tissues may result in varying capacities of tissues and organs to process arsenic through the different steps of arsenic biotransformation. The relative levels of expression of GSTO1-1 and GSTO2-2 in different human tissues and cell types therefore warrants further detailed study. We have previously reported a polymorphism in GSTO2 that results in an N142D substitution [7].

The data obtained in the present study suggest that this polymorphism is unlikely to have any significant effect on arsenic biotransformation.

The most interesting property of GSTO2-2 appears to be its high dehydroascorbate reductase (DHAR) activity. DHAR activity is a minor property of several enzymes including glutaredoxin and protein disulfide isomerase [27]. A survey of published DHAR activities from a range of species suggests that the activity of hGSTO2-2 is far in excess of the levels achieved by other enzymes from animals (Table 4) and suggests a specific role for GSTO2-2 in recycling ascorbate.

Recent studies have implied a role for an Omega class GST gene in the age-at-onset of both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases [14], although this has not been confirmed in all studies of Parkinson's patients [28]. Because ascorbate is considered an important antioxidant in the brain [12] and oxidative stress has been implicated in the pathogenesis of both diseases [13,29,30], a defect in GSTO2-2 expression or function that diminishes anti-oxidant protection in the brain could be consistent with the early manifestation of both diseases. Clearly, further studies of the expression of GSTO2-2 in different tissues and cell types, particularly in the brain, are important.

Our previous immunohistochemical studies of hGSTO1-1 used an antiserum that is now known to cross-react weakly with GSTO2-2 and may need to be reinterpreted. The extensive studies of rat DHAR (rGSTO1-1) in the brain may require similar consideration. In unpublished studies, we have identified a GSTO2-2 isoform in mice and this suggests a similar genomic arrangement is likely to be present in rats. The expression of Omega GSTs in the rat brain is of particular interest given the reported association with the age-at-onset of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases [14]. In particular, rat DHAR was found to be abundant in the cerebellum, striatum and hippocampus [11,31]. Detailed evaluation indicates that an Omega GST is expressed in several parts of the substantia nigra including the pars compacta, which is affected in Parkinson's disease [32].

Genetic variants of omega class GSTs, particularly GSTO2-2, could have an impact on redox sensitive processes. Clearly, the N142D polymorphism of hGSTO2 does not significantly affect DHAR activity, and thus, this polymorphism is unlikely to be directly related to the age-at-onset of these important neurological diseases. Further studies of promoter polymorphisms that may alter expression levels are currently in progress.
