Discovery of a functional polymorphism in human glutathione transferase zeta by expressed sequence tag database analysis

Abstract
Analysis of the expressed sequence tag (EST) database by sequence alignment allows a rapid screen for polymorphisms in proteins of physiological interest. The human zeta class glutathione transferase GSTZ1 has recently been characterized and analysis of expressed sequence tag clones suggested that this gene may be polymorphic. This report identifies three GSTZ1 alleles resulting from A to G transitions at nucleotides 94 and 124 of the coding region, GSTZ1*A  – A94A124;GSTZ1*B  – A94G124;GSTZ1*C  – G94G124. Polymerase chain reaction/restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis of a control Caucasian population (n  = 141) showed that all three alleles were present, with frequencies of 0.09, 0.28 and 0.63 for Z1*A, Z1*B and Z1*C, respectively. These nucleotide substitutions are non-synonymous, with A to G at positions 94 and 124 encoding Lys32 to Glu and Arg42 to Gly substitutions, respectively. The variant proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli as 6X His-tagged proteins and purified by Ni-agarose column chromatography. Examination of the activities of recombinant proteins revealed that GSTZ1a–1a displayed differences in activity towards several substrates compared with GSTZ1b–1b and GSTZ1c–1c, including 3.6-fold higher activity towards dichloroacetate.

This report demonstrates the discovery of a functional polymorphism by analysis of the EST database.

Introduction
The expressed sequence tag (EST) database for humans contains over one million entries of partial cDNA sequences that are expressed in a broad range of tissues and are derived from many individuals (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/dbEST/). The information in this database has been used for several purposes (Boguski, 1995), including finding human homologues of genes identified in other species (Board et al., 1997;Fernandez-Canon & Penalva, 1998), and the discovery of new members of multigene families (Board, 1998). The clones from which a sequence entry was derived can be readily obtained, allowing laboratory confirmation of the sequence data and further experimental investigation. In this study, we demonstrate that the information in the EST database can also be used for identification of novel polymorphisms in proteins of physiological interest.

Glutathione transferases (GSTs) are a large family of detoxication enzymes that contribute to the metabolism of a range of xenobiotics including many carcinogens and therapeutic drugs. There are five classes of cytosolic GSTs in mammalian cells, termed alpha, mu, pi, theta and zeta (Hayes & Pulford, 1995;Board et al., 1997).

Allelic variation in members of the mu, pi and theta classes has been described, including null alleles for GSTM1 and GSTT1 which result in the absence of functional protein in homozygotes (Board, 1981;Seidegard et al., 1988;Pemble et al., 1994), and point mutations in GSTP1 which result in altered substrate specificity (Board et al., 1989;Ali-Osman et al., 1997;Hu et al., 1997).

The zeta class of cytosolic GSTs, which spans a range of species from plants to humans, has recently been identified (Board et al., 1997) and several novel functions have been assigned to the proteins. Human GSTZ1 has been described as maleylacetoacetate isomerase, a fundamental enzyme of the phenylalanine catabolism pathway responsible for the glutathione-dependent isomerization of maleylaceto-acetate to fumarylacetoacetate (Fernandez-Canon & Penalva, 1998). Rat and human GSTZ1 catalyse the metabolism of dichloroacetate to glyoxylate (Tong et al., 1998a).

Dichloroacetate is a common contaminant in chlorinated drinking water (Uden & Miller, 1983), is hepatocarcinogenic in rodents (Bull et al., 1990;DeAngelo et al., 1996), and is used clinically in the management of lactic acidosis (Stacpoole, 1989).

During the characterization of the human GSTZ1 cDNA, an analysis of GSTZ1 expressed sequence tag clones revealed variation at two positions, nucleotides 94 and 124 of the coding region (Board et al., 1997). Allelic variation in the human population was further suggested when the gene was characterized, and differences in the coding sequence of the cDNA and gene were identified at these same two positions (Blackburn et al., 1998). The variable nucleotides were both found within exon 3 of GSTZ1 gene (Blackburn et al., 1998). We confirmed the existence of three GSTZ1 alleles by developing a polymerase chain reaction (PCR)/restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) method for identifying the variants at nucleotides 94 and 124 and determining the allele frequencies in a control sample.

Furthermore, the proteins encoded by the variant alleles were heterologously expressed and purified to examine the effects of these substitutions on enzyme function.

Materials and methods
Materials
Oligonucleotides were synthesized on an Applied Biosystems 380B DNA Synthesizer (Applied Biosystems Inc., Foster City, CA, USA). Restriction enzymes and their buffers were obtained from MBI Fermentas (NY, USA) (Alw 26I), New England Biolabs (Beverly, MA, USA) (Fok I, Bsp MI, Stu I, Mlu I, Ase I), Pharmacia Biotech (Uppsala, Sweden) (Bam HI) and Boehringer Mannheim (Mannheim, Germany) (Hin dIII). Sequencing was performed using the ThermoSequenase cycle sequencing kit (Amersham Life Science, Sydney, Australia). [α-33P]dATP was obtained from Amersham (Bucks., UK).

EST database screening
The EST database is accessible through the National Centre for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) web page (http://www.ncbi.nlm.gov/). Database screening was carried out by application of the BLAST alignment tool (Altschul et al., 1997), accessed through the home page of the NCBI. The human EST database was searched using the GSTZ1 cDNA sequence (accession number U86529). An advanced BLAST search using the `flat master-slave with identities' alignment view option presents the EST sequences as a multiple alignment as displayed in Fig. 1.

EST clones were obtained from the IMAGE consortium through Genome Systems, Inc. (St Louis, MI, USA).

Fig. 1.: The alignment of human EST sequences matching exon 3 of GSTZ1. Nucleotides are represented by dots for identical, n for ambiguous and spaces for gaps (or where there was no sequence information). N31040 is the original clone characterized as the GSTZ1 cDNA.
Analysis of polymorphisms in a control population
DNA was extracted from blood samples by standard methods. The control population consisted of unselected Australian European blood donors (Harris et al., 1998). The average age of the 141 individuals analysed in this study was 40 years (range 16–69 years) with 68 women and 73 men.

The polymorphic region of the GSTZ1 gene was amplified from genomic DNA samples using the primers ZseqA8 and Zexon3B, designed from the flanking intronic regions of exon 3 such that both variable nucleotides could be investigated within the one PCR product. The primer sequences are presented in Table 1.

PCR was performed with 25–50 ng genomic DNA with 300 pmol/ml of each primer in a 20 μl reaction volume containing 1X Advanced Biotechnologies (Epsom, UK) buffer IV (20 mm (NH4)2SO4, 75 mm Tris-HCl pH 9.0, 0.01% Tween), 1.5 mm MgCl2 (Advanced Biotechnologies) 200 μm dNTPs and 0.5 U of Taq polymerase. The cycling conditions were 95 °C 2 min, followed by 35 cycles of 95 °C 20 s, 60 °C 15 s, 72 °C 30 s with a final cycle of 72 °C for 3 min.

An A to G transition at nucleotide position 94 was detected by digestion of the PCR product with Alw 26I and analysis of the digestion products by 10% polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE). An A to G transition at nucleotide position 124 was detected by digestion of the PCR product with Fok I and analysis of the digestion products by 8% PAGE. Alw 26I was used at 0.1 U/μl in 1X MBI buffer Y with 0.1 mg/ml BSA, while Fok I was used at 0.05 U/μl in 1X NEB buffer 4. In each case, 2–4 μl of the PCR product was digested in a 15 μl volume at 37 °C overnight.

PAGE was performed using Accugel (29:1, National Diagnostics, Atlanta, GA, USA) with 1X TBE (0.09 m Tris-borate, 2 mm EDTA) gel and running buffer.

In individuals heterozygous at both polymorphic sites, allele-specific PCR for nucleotide 124 was performed followed by digestion with Alw 26I to determine the haplotypes present. PCR was performed as described above, using the primer ZseqA8 in combination with one of the allele-specific primers, Zeta124G or Zeta124A (Table 1), at 200 pmol/ml. The allele-specific primers were designed with the polymorphic nucleotide in the terminal 3′ position and with a mismatch at the adjacent nucleotide (Newton et al., 1989;Kwok et al., 1990). The cycling conditions were 95 °C 2 min, followed by 35 cycles of 95 °C 20 s, 55 °C 20 s, 72 °C 30 s with a final cycle of 72 °C for 2 min.

The 202 bp product was digested with Alw 26I overnight, and the fragments were separated by 10% PAGE.

Chi-squared analysis was performed to test for linkage disequilibrium between the two polymorphic sites, and for agreement with Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

Bacterial expression and purification of variant GSTZ1 proteins
The GSTZ1 proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli as 6X His-tagged proteins and were purified by Ni-agarose column chromatography. The coding region of GSTZ1 was PCR-amplified as a 686 bp product from EST clones containing the appropriate sequence variations at nucleotides 94 and 124: N31040 A94A124 (Board et al., 1997); T35781 A94G124; R67650 G94G124. The forward primer (PQEZ1) was designed to replace the initiating methionine with a Bam HI restriction site, and the reverse primer (Z1exB2) introduced a Hin dIII restriction site 18 bp beyond the stop codon (Table 1). The amplified product was digested with Bam HI and Hin dIII, and ligated into the pQE30 vector (Qiagen, Clifton Hill, Australia), which encodes the 6X His-tag at the N-terminus of the protein, and transformed into E. coli JM103. After selection of expressing clones and nucleotide sequencing to ensure the absence of PCR-induced errors, the constructs were transformed into E.

coli M15[pREP4] for large scale expression.

During sequencing of the pQEZ1 constructs, a sequence variation was found in the G94G124 clone, pQC21. Sequencing of the EST clone R67650 showed that this variation, a C to T transition at nucleotide 245 of the coding region, was present in the PCR template. To create a pQEZ1C without this variation, a 419 bp Bsp MI/ Stu I fragment from nucleotides 171–590 of the cDNA was excised from pQC21 and replaced with the same fragment from pQEZ1B. The presence of the C at nucleotide 245, which introduces a Mlu I restriction site, was detected by digestion of the plasmid DNA with Mlu I and Ase I. The new pQEZ1C construct was sequenced in the modified region to confirm that no other variations had been introduced. The constructs were now identical in sequence to the coding region of pGSTZ1 (Board et al., 1997) except for the variations at nucleotides 94 and 124 as follows: pQEZ1A – A94A124; pQEZ1B – A94G124; pQEZ1C – G94G124.

Cultures of M15[pREP4] containing pQEZ1 plasmids were grown in LB broth supplemented with 100 μg/ml ampicillin and 25 μg/ml kanamycin at 37 °C.

To induce protein expression, cultures were grown overnight in the presence of 0.1 mm isopropyl thio-β-d-galactoside. Purification procedures followed the QIA expressionist protocol for purification of 6X His-tagged proteins under native conditions (Qiagen). To prepare cleared bacterial lysates, bacteria were pelleted by centrifugation, resuspended in buffer A (50 mm sodium phosphate, 300 mm NaCl pH 7.5), lysed either by incubation with 1 mg/ml lysozyme on ice for 1 h followed by sonication, or by passage through a Ribi cell fractionator model RF-1 (Sorvall, Newton, VA, USA), and the lysates cleared by centrifugation at 10 000 g for 15 min at 4 °C. Cleared lysates were incubated with Ni-agarose resin (Porath & Olin, 1983) for 1–2 h at 4 °C on a rotary mixer. The resin was collected by centrifugation and washed extensively with buffer A, and then packed under gravity into a small column. The column was equilibrated with several volumes of buffer A containing 10% glycerol and proteins were eluted with 50 mm and 500 mm imidazole in buffer A containing 10% glycerol.

Fractions containing recombinant GSTZ1 were identified by SDS-PAGE, pooled and dialysed overnight against buffer consisting of 5 mm Hepes pH 7.0, 1 mm dithiothreitol and 10% glycerol. The proteins were stored at −20 °C, and the protein concentration was determined by the Lowry method after thawing of aliquots.

Enzyme assays
The formation of glyoxylate from dichloroacetate and chlorofluoroacetate was measured spectrophotometrically as previously described (Tong et al., 1998a). Reaction mixtures for these assays contained 1 μg purified GSTZ1 and were incubated at 37 °C for 20 min. The measurement by HPLC of S-carboxymethylglutathione and S-(α-methylcarboxymethyl)glutathione formation from fluoroacetate and 2-halopropionates, respectively, has also been described elsewhere (Tong et al., 1998b). The amount of purified GSTZ1 and incubation time at 37 °C for the reaction mixtures were as follows: 11–13 μg and 80 min with fluoroacetate; 2 μg and 45 min with R-2-chloropropionate; and 4–13 μg and 45 min with S-2-chloropropionate.

Glutathione conjugating activity towards a range of electrophilic substrates was measured spectrophotometrically under the following previously described conditions: 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, 1,2-dichloro-4-nitrobenzene, ethacrynic acid, p-nitrophenyl acetate, 1,2-epoxy-3-(4-nitrophenoxy)propane (Habig et al., 1974;Mannervik & Widersten, 1995); 7-chloro-4-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazole (Ricci et al., 1994);trans-alk-2-enals and trans,trans-deca-2,4-dienal (Brophy et al., 1989).

Results
When GSTZ1 was first characterized, the available sequence from 13 ESTs encoding GSTZ1 was examined by alignment for evidence of polymorphism. This revealed consistent variability at two sites, with an A or G variably found at both nucleotide positions 94 and 124 (Board et al., 1997). A more recent BLAST search of the human EST database retrieved 90 sequences matching some part of the GSTZ1 cDNA, of which 84 were clearly clones of the GSTZ1 cDNA. Of these, 26 entries matched some part of the sequence of exon 3 of GSTZ1, with 23 sequences containing both nucleotides 94 and 124. These sequences are aligned in Fig. 1.

Numerous sequence variations are observed in such an alignment of EST sequence data. In looking for polymorphisms in these sequences, the occurrence of errors due to single pass automated sequencing must be considered, and attention focused on variations that occur in multiple ESTs.

The nucleotides found at position 94 were 11 As and 15 Gs, which is a ratio unlikely to be due to random sequencing errors. At position 124, only four As were found, matching pGSTZ1, while 17 sequences contained G, matching the gene sequence. While variation at this site is far less common than at nucleotide 94, no other positions display variation at this frequency (Fig. 1), thus supporting the possibility that the sequence variation is due to allelic variation rather than random sequencing errors.

Both polymorphic sites are found within exon 3 (nucleotides 68–135) of the GSTZ1 gene (Blackburn et al., 1998) and result in changes in restriction enzyme sites. Thus amplification of a single 308 bp segment of the gene, covering exon 3 and its flanking intronic regions, followed by digestion with the appropriate restriction enzyme allows determination of the nucleotides present at the polymorphic sites. The A to G polymorphism at position 94 results in the presence (G) or absence (A) of an Alw 26I site in the 308 bp PCR product, in addition to an invariant Alw 26I site which yields a 125 bp fragment. This invariant site serves as an internal control for digestion efficiency.

Three possible genotypes are defined by three distinct banding patterns as displayed in Fig. 2 a: A94/A94 (186 and 125 bp fragments), A94/G94 (186, 159, 125 and 26 bp fragments), and G94/G94 (159, 125 and 26 bp fragments). Similarly, the A to G polymorphism at position 124 results in the presence (G) or absence (A) of a Fok I site, resulting in the banding patterns seen in Fig. 2 b: A124/A124 (308 bp fragment only), A124/G124 (308, 193 and 115 bp fragments), and G124/G124 (193 and 115 bp fragments). This method was used to determine the frequency of the variants in a control population consisting of 141 unselected controls of Caucasian origin (Table 2). G was more common than A at both positions 94 and 124, and the distribution of G or A at each position was in agreement with that expected in a Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

The presence of two polymorphic sites results in four possible haplotypes: A94A124, A94G124, G94G124 and G94A124. Of the 21 EST sequences which included unambiguous bases at both nucleotide 94 and 124, four were A94A124, six were A94G124 and 11 were G94G124 (Fig. 1).

There was no evidence in the EST database for the occurrence of a variant G94A124. In the control population, examination of the genotypes at both nucleotide positions allowed the determination of the alleles present in the majority of individuals. Fifteen people were heterozygous at both nucleotides 94 and 124, and therefore their genotypes could not be determined by this approach. Allele-specific PCR for nucleotide 124 was conducted on these samples, generating a 202 bp product which was digested with Alw 26I to determine the base present at nucleotide 94. The 202 bp product contained both the invariant and polymorphic Alw 26I sites, such that an A at nucleotide 94 produced fragments of 122 and 80 bp, while a G at nucleotide 94 produced fragments of 122, 54 and 26 bp (Fig. 3). It was found that all alleles containing an A at nucleotide 124 also contained an A at nucleotide 94.

Thus all double heterozygotes were of genotype A94A124/G94G124 and the fourth possible variant, G94A124, was not present in our control population.

Based on this data, three variants of GSTZ1 were designated GSTZ1*A, GSTZ1*B and GSTZ1*C in accordance with the proposed nomenclature for allelic GST gene variants (Mannervik et al., 1992). GSTZ1*A refers to pGSTZ1, which has an A at both variant positions (A94A124) (Board et al., 1997). GSTZ1*B differs from GSTZ1*A by having an A to G transition at nucleotide 124 (A94G124) while GSTZ1*C differs from GSTZ1*B by having an A to G transition at nucleotide 94 (G94G124). The frequencies of the alleles Z1*A, Z1*B and Z1*C in the control population were determined (Table 2). Chi-squared analysis of these alleles indicated there is significant linkage disequilibrium between the two loci (P  < 0.005), caused by the absence of the fourth variant. The frequency of the three alleles is in agreement with that expected in a Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

The nucleotide variations identified at positions 94 and 124 are both non-synonymous, and thus result in variation of the amino acids encoded by codons 32 and 42, respectively, in the three alleles as follows:Z1*A Lys32, Arg42;Z1*B Lys32, Gly42;Z1*C Glu32, Gly42.

The three variant proteins corresponding to the three identified alleles were expressed in E. coli and purified to investigate their activity towards a range of GST substrates. The activities of the enzymes towards dichloroacetate and several other α-haloacids were investigated (Table 3). There was no difference in activity between GSTZ1b-1b and GSTZ1c-1c, however, the activity of GSTZ1a-1a was markedly different from GSTZ1b-1b and GSTZ1c-1c towards four of the five α-haloacids tested. GSTZ1a-1a possessed higher activity towards dichloroacetate (3.6-fold) and R-2-chloropropionate (3.8-fold), and lower activity towards fluoroacetate (0.26-fold) and S-2-chloropropionate (0.3-fold). All three proteins possessed similar activity towards chlorofluoroacetate. For comparison, the activity of purified rat liver GST Zeta towards these substrates, as reported by Tong et al., 1998b, is also included in Table 3. The activity of GSTZ1a-1a towards R-2-chloropropionate and dichloroacetate was higher than rat GSTZ (3.5- and 1.6-fold, respectively), while GSTZ1b-1b and GSTZ1c-1c possessed very similar activity towards R-2-chloropropionate. In all other cases, the rat enzyme was more active than the human enzymes with 2–8-fold the activity of GSTZ1c-1c.

Interestingly, human GSTZ1 enzymes showed higher activity towards the R enantiomer of 2-chloropropionic acid while activity of rat GSTZ1 was greater with the S-enantiomer (Tong et al., 1998b).

Activity of human GSTZ1 was previously observed towards the substrates ethacrynic acid, 7-chloro-4-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazole and p-nitrophenyl acetate (Board et al., 1997). Comparing the variant proteins, GSTZ1a-1a possessed higher activity towards ethacrynic acid and 7-chloro-4-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazole compared with GSTZ1b-1b and GSTZ1c-1c, while there was no difference between the three enzymes towards p-nitrophenyl acetate (Table 3). The activities towards these substrates were much lower than for dichloroacetate. No activity was detected for the variant proteins towards 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, 1,2-dichloro-4-nitrobenzene, trans-non-2-enal, trans-oct-2-enal, trans,trans-deca-2,4-dienal, and 1,2-epoxy-3-(4-nitrophenoxy)propane.

Discussion
As our appreciation grows of the subtle contributions many genes can make to complex genetic disorders and disease susceptibility, a systematic approach to discovering polymorphisms and understanding their consequences is required. This study has demonstrated how analysis of the human EST database can be used to facilitate the identification and investigation of genetic polymorphisms in enzymes and proteins of physiological interest.

This approach provides a convenient first step in the detection of variant alleles compared to previous approaches, which have depended on isolating clones of interest from cDNA libraries of many individuals (Ali-Osman et al., 1997) or on the observation of phenotypic differences between individuals (Board, 1981;Seidegard et al., 1988;Blum et al., 1991;Pemble et al., 1994).

The availability of sequence information in the human EST database for any given cDNA will depend on the tissue expression patterns of the gene, the stability of the mRNA and the size of the cDNA. For each clone, the sequence data are incomplete because they are sequenced from the ends only. However, as the ESTs vary in length at the 5′ end, this sequence information may extend considerably into the centre of the cDNA of interest. GSTZ1 is very widely expressed, resulting in a large number of ESTs being identified from different libraries by the BLAST search. The 5′ and 3′ ends of the 1162 bp cDNA were represented by 25 and 34 ESTs, respectively.

The least well represented portion of the cDNA, a 200 bp region around nucleotides 400–600 of the coding sequence, was present in eight EST sequences, thus keeping open the possibility of identifying common variable nucleotides in this region. In the case of GSTZ1, this information was sufficient to detect the nucleotide 124 polymorphism, which occurred at a frequency of only 9% in controls. Since the EST database is accumulating partial cDNA sequences from an increasing number of individuals, it is clearly a valuable tool for the investigation of genes where there is some expectation of polymorphism.

Many members of the GST gene family have been found to be polymorphic in human populations, thus when the human GSTZ1 cDNA was characterized, the possibility of variants of this gene occurring was considered. Examination of the EST sequences for GSTZ1 revealed two sites which are variable in numerous clones. Development of PCR/RFLP methods and population analysis of the variant nucleotides have shown that the variations identified in the EST database are genuine polymorphisms, and that the three alleles identified are present at significant frequencies in the Australian European population.

The three alleles characterized have been designated GSTZ1*A, GSTZ1*B and GSTZ1*C.

The investigation of the activities of the recombinant proteins encoded by these alleles indicates that GSTZ1a-1a has different catalytic properties from GSTZ1b-1b and GSTZ1c-1c (Table 3). Thus, while the Glu32 to Lys substitution has little effect on protein activity, the Gly42 to Arg alters enzyme function considerably. Molecular modelling of the N-terminal domain of GSTZ1 was performed when the protein was originally characterized (Board et al., 1997). Based on the Lucilia cuprina GST structure, it was predicted that residue 32 would not interact directly with the active site. The enzyme activities presented here support that prediction, as the substitution of a 4-carbon, positive residue for a 2-carbon, negative residue made little difference to enzyme activity towards the diverse range of substrates tested.

The effect of the Gly42 to Arg substitution was not predictable from the molecular modelling as residue 42 fell in the β2 to α2 loop region which varies significantly in the solved GST structures (Board et al., 1997).

The results in Table 3 suggest that residue 42 influences the active site, with the Gly42 to Arg substitution resulting in higher activity towards dichloroacetate, R-2-chloropropionate and lower activity towards fluoroacetate and S-2-chloropropionate. The arginine residue introduces both a positive charge and a much larger side chain, factors which may contribute to both the electrostatic interactions and the architecture of the active site. It is interesting to compare the enantioselectivity of the human and rat enzymes towards 2-chloropropionate, with the relative activities of GSTZ1a-1a, GSTZ1b-1b and rat (Tong et al., 1998b) being R  > S, R  ∼ S, R  < S, respectively, suggesting that the active site of the rat enzyme has features different from both GSTZ1a-1a and GSTZ1b-1b.

GSTZ1 has been demonstrated to have activity towards both xenobiotic and endogenous substrates. GSTZ1 was identified as the major enzyme in rat liver responsible for the metabolism of dichloroacetate (Tong et al., 1998a), a compound which has therapeutic applications but is also hepatocarcinogenic in rodents (Stacpoole, 1989;Bull et al., 1990;DeAngelo et al., 1996). The discovery of genetic variants in GSTZ1 which have variable ability to metabolize this compound may be important in understanding the clinical efficacy and toxicity of this compound.

GSTZ1 has also been identified as maleylacetoacetate isomerase, converting maleylacetoacetate to fumarylacetoacetate in the catabolism of aromatic amino acids (Fernandez-Canon & Penalva, 1998). In the absence of readily available maleylacetoacetate, we have been unable to investigate the activity of these variant enzymes towards the endogenous substrate. While many diseases, including alkaptonuria and phenylketonuria, have been identified where a complete block in this metabolic pathway occurs, it is not known what the consequences of a partial block or altered flux through this pathway may be. Accumulation of maleylacetoacetate, fumarylacetoacetate and their reduced counterpart succinylacetoacetate are thought responsible for the pathology of hereditary tyrosinemia type 1, a severe genetic disease resulting from complete lack of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, although the mechanism by which these metabolites are toxic is not well understood (Tanguay et al., 1996). The use of the EST database to find novel genetic variations opens the opportunity to investigate the consequences of subtle variations in enzyme activity which may not have been discovered by phenotypic approaches for the discovery of genetic variation.

Analysis of the mouse and human acyl-CoA thioesterase(ACOT) gene clusters shows that convergent,functional evolution results in a reduced number ofhuman peroxisomal ACOTs

ABSTRACT The maintenance of cellular levels offree fatty acids and acyl-CoAs, the activated form offree fatty acids, is extremely important, as imbalancesin lipid metabolism have serious consequences forhuman health. Acyl-coenzyme A (CoA) thioesterases(ACOTs) hydrolyze acyl-CoAs to the free fatty acid andCoASH, and thereby have the potential to regulateintracellular levels of these compounds. We previouslyidentiﬁed and characterized a mouse ACOT gene clus-ter comprised of six genes that apparently arose bygene duplications encoding acyl-CoA thioesterases withlocalizations in cytosol (ACOT1), mitochondria(ACOT2), and peroxisomes (ACOT3– 6). However, thecorresponding human gene cluster contains only threegenes (ACOT1, ACOT2, and ACOT4) coding for full-length thioesterase proteins, of which only one isperoxisomal (ACOT4). We therefore set out to charac-terize the human genes, and we show here that thehuman ACOT4 protein catalyzes the activities of threemouse peroxisomal ACOTs (ACOT3, 4, and 5), beingactive on succinyl-CoA and medium to long chainacyl-CoAs, while ACOT1 and ACOT2 carry out similarfunctions to the corresponding mouse genes. Thesedata strongly suggest that the human ACOT4 gene hasacquired the functions of three mouse genes by afunctional convergent evolution that also provides anexplanation for the unexpectedly low number of hu-man genes.—Hunt, M. C., Rautanen, A., Westin,M. A. K., Svensson, L. T., Alexson, S. E. H. Analysis ofthe mouse and human acyl-CoA thioesterase (ACOT)gene clusters shows that convergent, functional evolu-tion results in a reduced number of human peroxiso-mal ACOTs. FASEB J. 20, 1855–1864 (2006)

Key Words:-oxidation  acyl-coenzyme A  peroxisome fatty acids

Imbalances in fatty acid metabolism have seriousconsequences for human health and the onset andprogression of several chronic diseases, such as coro-nary artery disease and atherosclerosis, dyslipidemia, obesity, and diabetes. The central role of free fatty acidsand acyl-CoAs (the activated form of fatty acids) isevident by the numerous intracellular processes inwhich these molecules are key components. Theseprocesses (reviewed in ref. 1) include oxidation of fattyacids (, , and -oxidation), biosynthesis of lipids, andallosteric regulation of a number of enzymes (2– 4) andopening of KATP channels in human pancreatic betacells (5). There are, however, many processes that areactivated by acyl-CoAs and inhibited by the free fattyacids or vice versa, showing the importance of maintain-ing the balance of these compounds in vivo. It wasrecently shown that palmitoyl-coenzyme A (CoA) inhib-its AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) indirectly by aspeciﬁc and concentration-dependent inactivation ofits upstream kinase (6). Another example where thebalance of free fatty acids vs. acyl-CoAs is important is inthe activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activatedreceptors (PPARs) by free fatty acids (7–10) and, morerecently, by CoA esters of long chain fatty acids (acyl-CoAs) (11). One way in which the cell can control theintracellular acyl-CoA and free fatty acid levels is via theactivity of enzymes named acyl-CoA thioesterases(ACOTs), which can hydrolyze acyl-CoAs to the corre-sponding free fatty acid and CoA (CoASH) (for reviews,see refs. 12, 13). These acyl-CoA thioesterases areexpressed in several cellular compartments that coin-cide with metabolic processes involving acyl-CoAs.In 1995, a particular family of acyl-CoA thioesteraseswas identiﬁed in rat and was named Type-I acyl-CoA thioesterases (14). In the past few years, the cloning ofcDNAs and genes has identiﬁed the Type-I acyl-CoAthioesterases to be a novel gene family with six mem-bers in the mouse: a cytosolic isoform (Acot1, previ-ously CTE-I), a mitochondrial isoform (Acot2, previ-ously MTE-I), and four peroxisomal isoforms (Acot3, 4,5, and 6, previously PTE-Ia, -Ib, -Ic, and -Id) (15–17).Both the sequence similarity and the gene organizationshow a high degree of conservation, suggesting thatthese genes have evolved by gene duplications. Theidentiﬁcation of four peroxisomal ACOTs was surpris-ing, but characterization of their acyl-CoA substratespeciﬁcities showed that they catalyze distinct activitiesand also show individual tissue expression. However,based on the multiple and important functions thatperoxisomes play in degrading a variety of lipids, whichis reﬂected in the severity of peroxisomal disorders (forreviews, see 18, 19), it is tempting to speculate thatthese ACOTs participate in regulation of -oxidationand release of -oxidation products. In the mouse thisType-I gene cluster is located on mouse chromosome12 D3 within 120 kb of DNA. We have now character-ized the genes in the corresponding gene cluster ofType-I ACOTs in humans, which is localized on humanchromosome 14q24.3. However, this cluster containsfour genes, of which three are transcribed to encodefull-length ACOTs, and only one gene encodes a per-oxisomal acyl-CoA thioesterase (ACOT4). We show herethat the human ACOT4 gene apparently has evolvedinto a multifunctional protein that catalyzes the com-bined activities of mouse ACOT3, 4, and 5, whilehuman ACOT1 and ACOT2 have functions similar tothe mouse orthologs.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
Cloning and expression of acyl-CoA thioesterases
Oligonucleotides were designed based on the sequence of theORFs for human ACOT1, ACOT2, and ACOT4. Due to thehigh sequence identity between ACOT1 and ACOT2, it wasnot possible to polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifyindividual transcripts of ACOT1 and ACOT2. We obtainedthe ACOT2 ORF using PCR ampliﬁcation from human liverand purchased a clone containing the cDNA for ACOT1,Accession No. BM543491 (Image clone No. 5726581, UKHMGP Resource center, Hinxton, UK), and used this as atemplate for PCR ampliﬁcation of ACOT1. ACOT1 andACOT2 were cloned into pET16b (Novagen Inc., Darmstadt,Germany) using the following primers: 5-CATATGT-CACTTTTGATGGGATTGTC-3 and 5-CATATGGCGGC-GACGCTGAT-3 with NdeI sites indicated in boldface. TheACOT4 was cloned into the pET102 (Invitrogen Corp., CA,USA), in-frame with thioredoxin. The 5 primer sequence was5-CACCATGTCAGCAACGCTGATCCTG-3 and was con-structed to contain an overhang of CACC for cloning intopET102. The 3 primer sequence was 5-CAATTTAGGGA-CAGCTGTTTTCTG-3. The ORF for ACOT4 was ampliﬁedby reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) from human livertotal RNA. RT-PCR was performed in a Perkin-Elmer 2600using the One Step RT-PCR kit (Takara Biomedicals, Shiga,Japan). Thermal cycling was performed at 50°C for 30 min and 94°C for 2 min, followed by 35 cycles of 94°C for 30 s,51.5°C for 30 s (ACOT2) or 60°C for 30 s (ACOT4) and 72°Cfor 3 min. The resultant PCR products were cloned intopET16b or pET102, respectively, and sequenced (CybergeneAB, Huddinge, Sweden).The plasmids containing the human ACOT1, 2, and 4 werethen used to transform BL21(DES3)pLysS cells (NovagenInc., Darmstadt, Germany). Bacteria were cultured in 500 mlLuria-Bertani medium at 37°C with the addition of ampicillin(50 g/ml) and chloramphenicol (34 g/ml) until theoptical density (OD)600nm was 0.6. Protein expression wasinduced by addition of 1 mM isopropyl-1-thio--D-galactopy-ranoside and cells were grown for 3 h at 37°C (ACOT1 andACOT2) or at 30°C for 5 h (ACOT4). The recombinantproteins were puriﬁed as described previously and elutedusing 500 mM imidazole (20). The purity of the expressedproteins was examined using SDS/PAGE analysis and Coo-massie Brilliant blue staining, and these puriﬁed proteinswere used to measure acyl-CoA thioesterase activity. MouseACOT3, 4, and 5 recombinant proteins were produced asoutlined in ref. 16, 17 and activity was measured with variousacyl-CoA substrates.
Northern blot analysisHuman Multiple Tissue blots were purchased from ClontechInc (Palo Alto, CA, USA) and analysis was carried outaccording to the manufacturer’s instructions, using - 32 P-labeled cDNA probes. The cDNA probes for the humanACOTs were constructed using RT-PCR from human livertotal RNA. For ACOT1 and ACOT2, a cDNA probe wasampliﬁed corresponding to amino acids 167–371 of the openreading frame (ORF) (shown in Fig. 2). The ACOT4 cDNAprobe was ampliﬁed corresponding to amino acids 215 to 405of the ORF, and a speciﬁc probe located in the mitochondrialtargeting signal of ACOT2 was ampliﬁed corresponding toamino acids 21 to 59 of the ORF.Enzyme activity measurementsACOT activity was measured spectrophotometrically at 412nm with 5,5-dithiobis(2-nitrobenzoic acid) (DTNB). Themedium contained 200 mM potassium chloride, 10 mMHEPES, and 0.05 mM DTNB (pH 7.4). An E 412   13,600 M –1cm–1 was used to calculate the activity. The acyl-CoA sub-strates used were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich Inc. (St. Louis,MO, USA). The addition of BSA to prevent substrate inhibi-tion with CoA esters was titrated for long chain acyl-CoAs(C16-C20-CoA). A BSA:C18-CoA molar ratio of  1:10 wasused to measure ACOT1 and ACOT2 activities. Otherwiseaddition of BSA was not required for measurement of acyl-CoA thioesterase activity.Cellular localization of human ACOTs using greenﬂuorescent fusion proteinThe ORFs for the human ACOT1, 2, 4, and 6 were cloned asfusion proteins with green ﬂuorescent protein (GFP) toexamine the intracellular localization of the proteins. ACOT6was ampliﬁed using primers 5-ATGCTGCAGCATCCAAAG-GTG-3 and 5-TCTGTCAAGCACAGCAAAATATAA-3. TheORFs were ampliﬁed using PCR and the PCR products forACOT1, ACOT4, and ACOT6 were cloned into thepcDNA3.1/NT-GFP vector (Invitrogen Corp., CA, USA), in-frame with the GFP, leaving the carboxyl-terminal end acces-sible. The ACOT2 was cloned in-frame with the pcDNA3.1/CT-GFP (Invitrogen Corp., CA, USA), leaving the N-terminalend accessible. Sequence analysis was performed using Big
Dye Terminator Ready Reaction kit (Perkin Elmer Inc.,Wellesley, MA, USA) and sequenced by Cybergene AB (Hud-dinge, Sweden).Human skin ﬁbroblasts or HepG2 cells were grown inEagles MEM (Sigma-Aldrich Inc.), supplemented with 10%fetal calf serum (Invitrogen Corp., CA, USA) and 100 Upenicillin/100 g streptomycin in an atmosphere of 5% CO2 .Cells were grown overnight in 60 mm dishes on glass cover-slips and transfected with 10 g of the various plasmids usingcalcium phosphate method as described (20). The localiza-tion of ACOT1, ACOT4, and ACOT6 was investigated inﬁbroblasts, and in the case of ACOT4, skin ﬁbroblasts from aZellweger patient were also used. The localization of ACOT2was investigated in HepG2 cells and Mitotracker® OrangeCMTMRos (Invitrogen Corp., CA, USA) was used to conﬁrmmitochondrial structures. Transfected cells were grown for48 h and ﬁbroblasts were treated for immunoﬂuorescence asdescribed (20). HepG2 cells treated with 200 nM Mito-tracker® Orange for 30 min before immunoﬂuorescencemicroscopy was carried out as described previously (20), butwithout use of the Tritc-labeled antibody (Ab).

RESULTS
Identiﬁcation of a human ACOT gene cluster
Previous data had identiﬁed six mouse Acot genes in acluster located within 120 kb on mouse chromosome 12 D3 (15–17). Database searches using the cDNA se-quences for the mouse Type-I Acot genes identiﬁedfour putative human ACOT genes on chromosome14q24.3 located within 80 kb of genomic sequence (Fig.1). Based on homology to the mouse genes, we identi-ﬁed the putative human orthologs of Acot1, Acot2,Acot4, and Acot6 in the human gene cluster. Thedistance between the genes is 25.7 kb betweenACOT1 and ACOT2, 16.5 kb between ACOT2 andACOT4, and 16.9 kb between ACOT4 and ACOT6.Comparison of the two gene clusters reveals two strik-ing differences: ﬁrst, that the order of the ACOT1 andACOT2 genes are different in the human genomecompared to mouse, and second, that the human genecluster contains only one gene encoding a putativeperoxisomal ACOT. Similar to the mouse genes, theopen reading frames for three of these genes are codedfor by three exons (ACOT1, ACOT2, and ACOT4)whereas the fourth gene identiﬁed in the cluster,ACOT6, contained the genomic information for allthree exons (which would result in a full-length ACOTprotein), but apparently is translated from a methio-nine at the end of exon 2 through exon 3. This is basedon expressed sequence tag (EST) sequences, the esti-mated size of the transcript detected by Northern blot(data not shown), and by the fact that we could not amplify the predicted full-length open reading framebut could amplify a transcript that covered part of exon2 and exon 3.Database searches in the entire human genome didnot indicate the presence of any other genes that wouldcorrespond to mouse Acot3 or Acot5, but another genewas identiﬁed on chromosome 19q13.12 that shows91% sequence identity at nucleotide level to theACOT4 gene on chromosome 14. However, this geneon chromosome 19 lacks introns and contains severalstop codons that will not result in active protein.Searches in EST databases show that the pseudogene isexpressed in puriﬁed pancreatic islets (EST No.CA843741, CB177282, and CA843493), brain (EST No.BI827748 and AW090080), and placenta (EST No.DB328688 and DA849162).Alignment of the deduced amino acid sequences forthe open reading frames of the ACOT1, ACOT2, andACOT4 genes shows the striking conservation betweenthe various ACOTs (Fig. 2). The ACOT1 and ACOT4genes encode proteins of 421 amino acids, with thelatter containing –PKL at its carboxyl terminal, which isa variant of the peroxisomal type-1 targeting signal(PTS1) that can target proteins to peroxisomes (21).ACOT2 encodes a protein of 483 amino acids andcontains a 62 amino acid leader sequence at theN-terminal that targets the protein to mitochondria(see below). The 421 amino acids of ACOT2 that align to ACOT1 show 98.6% sequence identity, with only 5amino acids being different. The three amino acidsidentiﬁed to be the catalytic triad of the active site inthe mouse ACOT enzymes (22), a serine (acting as thenucleophile) in a Gly-X-Ser-X-Gly motif common toserine esterases, a histidine, and an aspartic acid are allconserved in the human enzymes (indicated in Fig. 2).The serine is located at position 232 of ACOT1, theaspartic acid at 326, and the histidine at 360.Subcellular localization of the human ACOTsThe subcellular localization of the four human ACOTsidentiﬁed in this study was examined by expression ofthe ACOTs in human skin ﬁbroblasts and HepG2 cellsas GFP fusion proteins. The rationale for choosingeither N-terminal or C-terminal GFP was based on thepresence of putative targeting signals at the N- orC-terminal ends, and also on previous data obtained forlocalization of the mouse orthologs. The ACOT1 (ho-mologous to the mouse ACOT1, which is cytosolic; ref.23) contains no apparent targeting signal but containsa PTS1-like sequence of –SKV at its C-terminal end.However, transfection of this GFP fusion protein intohuman ﬁbroblasts resulted in a protein with a diffusepattern of expression with no visible punctate staining,in line with a cytosolic localization (Fig. 3A). ACOT6also contains a PTS1-like sequence of –SKI at its Cterminal end, but this GFP fusion protein was also local-ized in cytosol (Fig. 3B). The ACOT2 protein contains aputative mitochondrial targeting signal at its N-terminalend. This GFP fusion protein showed a typical pattern formitochondrial localization as judged by immunoﬂuores-cence microscopy (Fig. 3C). Use of a mitotracker con-ﬁrmed that the ACOT2 fusion protein was localized inmitochondria (Fig. 3D). The human ACOT4 contains anear-consensus PTS1 of –PKL at its C-terminal, which isalso present in C. tropicalis sterol carrier protein (POX18)and has been shown to target proteins to peroxisomes(24). We transfected the ACOT4/NT-GFP vector intoboth control ﬁbroblasts and ﬁbroblasts from a Zellwegerpatient, which are unable to import peroxisomal matrixproteins. Using immunoﬂuorescence microscopy for GFPdetection, ACOT4 showed a punctate pattern of expres-sion in control ﬁbroblasts indicative of a peroxisomallocalization (Fig. 3E). However, in Zellweger ﬁbroblasts,transfection of ACOT4 resulted in a diffuse GFP expres-sion, showing an inability of the protein to be importedinto peroxisomes (Fig. 3F).Recombinant expression and characterization ofhuman and mouse ACOT proteinsCloning of the open reading frames of ACOT1 andACOT2 into pET16b and ACOT4 into pET102 vectors resulted in expression of these proteins as His-taggedfusion proteins, to allow for puriﬁcation using afﬁnitychromatography. After puriﬁcation on a HiTrap™ col-umn, the puriﬁed ACOT1 and ACOT2 were detected assingle bands of 46 kDa in mass on SDS/PAGE gelstained with Coomassie Brilliant blue, whereas ACOT4was detected as an 60 kDa band as a thioredoxinfusion protein (data not shown).The human ACOT4 gene shows the strongest similar-ity to ACOT4 in the mouse, and is therefore likely to bethe human ortholog of mouse ACOT4. The mouseACOT4 enzyme was recently shown to be a highlyspeciﬁc succinyl-CoA thioesterase, with only low activitywith glutaryl-CoA and no activity with any othertested acyl-CoAs (17). In line with this, characterizationof recombinant human ACOT4 indeed showed thehighest activity with succinyl-CoA (Vmax 581 nmol/min/mg protein, K m 14 M), with much lower Vmaxand higher K m with glutaryl-CoA (132 nmol/min/mgprotein and 147 M, respectively). Surprisingly,ACOT4 was also active on all long chain saturatedacyl-CoAs of 8 carbon atoms as well as on all unsat-urated acyl-CoAs tested (C18:1, C18:2, and C20:4). Thecalculated Vmax and Km values of ACOT4 with C14-CoA(which was the best long chain acyl-CoA substrate) were137 nmol/min/mg protein and 3.4 M, respectively. Figure 4A summarizes the activity of human ACOT4with all acyl-CoAs tested, demonstrating that humanACOT4 is a succinyl-CoA thioesterase that also hydro-lyzes long chain saturated and unsaturated monocar-boxylic acyl-CoAs. The pattern of activity of humanACOT4 mirrors the combined activities of the recentlycharacterized mouse ACOT3, ACOT4, and ACOT5proteins (summarized in Fig. 4B). Therefore, the hu-man peroxisomal ACOT4 can replace the function ofthree distinct peroxisomal enzymes in mouse. Althoughsuccinyl-CoA (C4-dicarboxylyl-CoA) was the best sub-strate for ACOT4, the corresponding C4-monocarboxy-lyl-CoA (butyryl-CoA) was not a substrate, and in con-trast the C12 dicarboxylyl-CoA was not a substrate eventhough the corresponding C12 monocarboxylyl-CoAwas a good substrate (data not shown). These data demonstrate that human ACOT4 has not simplyevolved into a nonspeciﬁc acyl-CoA thioesterase, butrather that human ACOT4 has acquired the combinedactivities of mouse ACOT3, ACOT4, and ACOT5.Kinetic characterization of recombinant humanACOT1 and ACOT2 showed similar substrate speciﬁc-ities, with both enzymes being mainly active on longchain saturated acyl-CoAs of 12 to 20 carbon atoms andlong chain unsaturated acyl-CoAs such as C16:1-CoA,C18:1-CoA (Fig. 5A, B). The data thus show thatACOT1 and ACOT2 function as long chain acyl-CoAthioesterases with no detectable activity with acyl-CoAsof eight carbon atoms or shorter. Kinetic characteriza-tion of ACOT1 and ACOT2 show that the Km for longchain acyl-CoAs is in the low micromolar range, dem-onstrating that these are probably the in vivo substratesfor the enzymes (Table 1). Tissue expression of human ACOTsNorthern blot analysis was carried out to examine tissueexpression of the various human ACOTs (Fig. 6). AsACOT1 and ACOT2 in humans show 99% sequenceidentity to each other, it was not possible to make aprobe that would be speciﬁc for the ACOT1. Using acDNA probe to ACOT1/ACOT2, one transcript of 1.8kb was detected with highest levels in heart, liver,muscle, and kidney. However, a cDNA probe corre-sponding to the mitochondrial targeting signal of theACOT2 was constructed that will distinguish betweenthese two mRNAs. Using the ACOT2-speciﬁc probe, themRNA signal was again strongest in heart, liver, muscle,and kidney and weak in placenta and pancreas, suggest-ing that ACOT2 is much more strongly expressed thanACOT1. This is further supported by searches in theEST database, which showed that ESTs corresponding to ACOT2 were much more abundant than ESTs cor-responding to ACOT1. The ACOT4 was detected as twotranscripts of 1.7 and 2.2 kb, with the strongestexpression in liver and kidney and weaker expression inplacenta, heart, and muscle. These two transcripts weredifferentially expressed with the lower transcript ex-pressed mainly in liver and kidney; the upper transcriptwas detectable in heart, liver, muscle, and kidney.

DISCUSSION
We previously identiﬁed and characterized a genecluster on chromosome 12 D3 in mouse (15–17) con-taining six individual genes: Acot1 (cytosolic), Acot2(mitochondrial), and Acot3, 4, 5, and 6 (all peroxiso-mal). Here we have characterized the correspondingcluster in human that consists of four ACOT genes onchromosome 14q24.3. Three of these genes—ACOT1,ACOT2, and ACOT4— encode full-length ACOT pro-teins and one gene, ACOT6, is translated from a methi-onine at the end of exon 2 into a putative open readingframe of only 207 amino acids. Although the catalyticamino acids would be contained in the protein, it is notclear whether the protein will be active. The mouseACOT6 ortholog contains a canonical PTS-1 targetingsignal of –SKL in the C-terminal end that targets mouseACOT6 to peroxisomes (M. A. K. Westin et al., unpub-lished results), whereas human ACOT6 ends with anisoleucine instead of leucine (C-terminal end of –SKI),which results in a cytosolic localization. It is remarkablethat the mouse contains so many peroxisomal ACOTenzymes, whereas human contains only one functionalperoxisomal Type-I ACOT. However, our ﬁnding thathuman ACOT4 hydrolyzes succinyl-CoA, glutaryl-CoA,and long chain acyl-CoAs, provides a plausible explana-tion for the difference in the number of peroxisomalACOTs in humans and mice. In the mouse there arethree Type-I ACOT enzymes characterized to date thathydrolyze straight chain acyl-CoA esters, the ACOT3active on long chain acyl-CoAs and the ACOT5 active on medium chain acyl-CoAs (16), together withACOT4, a newly identiﬁed succinyl-CoA/glutaryl-CoAthioesterase (17). While mouse ACOT4 only hydrolyzessuccinyl-CoA with high activity and glutaryl-CoA withlow activity, human ACOT4 also hydrolyzes saturatedand unsaturated medium to long chain acyl-CoAs. It istherefore reasonable to suggest that human ACOT4catalyzes the combined activities of mouse ACOT3, 4,and 5. Also, human ACOT4 is mainly expressed in liverand kidney, similar to mouse Acot3 and 4, furtherstrengthening a functional redundancy. It would there-fore be interesting to compare this gene cluster invarious species to trace the appearance/disappearanceof genes in this cluster and to follow the acquisition ofthe different activities in ACOT4 in higher vertebrates.A similar convergent evolution from mouse to human isseen among acyl-CoA oxidases, peroxisomal enzymescatalyzing the ﬁrst reaction in the -oxidation of vari-ous acyl-CoAs in peroxisomes. While rat and mousehave three genes encoding straight chain acyl-CoAoxidase, trihydroxycoprostanoyl-CoA oxidase, andbranched chain (pristanoyl-CoA) acyl-CoA oxidase,(25), humans have only two genes encoding thestraight chain oxidase and a combined trihydroxyco-prostanoyl-CoA and pristanoyl-CoA oxidase (26, 27). Inhumans there is also an intron-less ACOT pseudogenelocated on chromosome 19q13.12, which shows a highsimilarity to ACOT4. Although this pseudogene is ex-pressed at mRNA level in several tissues, the function isnot known. However, recently it was shown that apseudogene of the Makorin 1 gene (Makorin 1-p1)could regulate mRNA stability of its homologous cod-ing gene (28). Therefore, the ACOT pseudogene mayhave a regulatory function on the expression of ACOT4.The fourth gene in the ACOT gene cluster, ACOT6,contains the genetic information for all three codingexons common to the ACOT genes described in thiswork; however, translation apparently starts from amethionine present at the end of exon 2. We were ableto amplify a PCR product containing this truncatedopen reading frame of ACOT6, but it is not knownwhether ACOT6 is expressed as an active protein. Thecorresponding mouse ACOT6 gene encodes a 46 kDaprotein that is expressed, but so far the substrate forthis enzyme has not been deﬁned (M. A. K. Westin etal., unpublished results).Cloning and sequence analysis of ACOT1 and ACOT2revealed open reading frames encoding proteins of 421amino acids that aligned to each other, with 98.6%sequence identity. While ACOT2 contains a further 62amino acids in-frame at the N-terminal end that func-tions as a mitochondrial targeting signal, ACOT1 lacksthese amino acids. ACOT2 was previously cloned as ahuman peroxisomal acyl-CoA thioesterase named PTE2(29), but sequence alignment of PTE2 reveals that itrelates to ACOT2 without its mitochondrial targetingsignal. The assignment of the name PTE2 was based onthe ﬁnding that the –SKV tripeptide at the C-terminalend acted as a weak peroxisomal targeting signal,mediating some import of this protein into peroxisomes. Indeed, it has been shown that mutation of theperoxisomal targeting signal from the consensus –SKLto –SKV results in mistargeting to cytosol (30). We nowshow that ACOT2 contains a mitochondrial targetingsignal at its N-terminal end, which targets the protein tomitochondria. In line with the apparent lack of target-ing signals in ACOT1, the protein remained in thecytosol in the GFP experiments.Mouse and human peroxisomes contain a furtheracyl-CoA thioesterase, now renamed ACOT8 (previ-ously called PTE1, hTE, hACTEIII, and PTE-2) in a newacyl-CoA thioesterase nomenclature system (31), whichcan hydrolyze a wide variety of CoA esters, includingbile acid CoAs, branched chain CoAs, and long, me-dium, and short chain acyl-CoAs (20, 32). Therefore itappears that mouse peroxisomes contain ﬁve differentperoxisomal acyl-CoA thioesterases, hydrolyzing abroad spectrum of CoA esters, whereas human containsonly two genes coding for peroxisomal acyl-CoA thio-esterases, whose activity cover the same span of CoAester substrates. The need for several peroxisomalACOT enzymes with different speciﬁcities becomesevident in view of the multiple functions that peroxi-somes play in chain shortening of various carboxylicacids (as peroxisomes do not catalyze complete -oxi-dation of lipids), including long and very long chainfatty acids, dicarboxylic acids, bile acid intermediates,and xenobiotic carboxylic acids (19, 33). Furthermore,fatty acids are apparently transported across the perox-isomal membrane as CoA esters (in contrast to mito-chondria that utilizes a carnitine-acylcarnitine trans-port system), whereas fatty acid degradation productsmay be transported out of the peroxisome as carnitineesters, glycine, or taurine conjugates or as the freeacids. This implies that ACOTs may serve essentialfunctions in peroxisomes to regulate -oxidation(CoASH levels) as well as in the termination of -oxi-dation at various chain lengths for exit out of theorganelle. In view of this, we were surprised to only ﬁndone peroxisomal Type-I ACOT in the human genome.However, the ﬁnding here that ACOT4 in fact catalyzesthe activities of three mouse ACOTs not only explainsthe lower number of human ACOT genes, but under-scores the physiological importance of these ACOTs inperoxisomal lipid metabolism.ACOTs play key roles in maintaining the intracellularratio between the CoA esters of various lipids and thefree acid (e.g., acyl-CoAs and free fatty acids). Putativefunctions for these ACOT enzymes in cytosol, mito-chondria, and peroxisomes have been described indetail in a recent review, based mainly on work carriedout on the mouse enzymes (12). ACOT1 and ACOT2have quite similar substrate speciﬁcities, both active onlong chain acyl-CoAs, which is not surprising based ontheir extremely high level of sequence identity( 98%). However, these enzymes show two distinctcellular localizations in cytosol and mitochondria, andtherefore have speciﬁc functions within these compart-ments in the metabolism of long chain acyl-CoAs. Inmitochondria, ACOT2 has been suggested to be in volved in a coordinate shuttle pathway together withuncoupling protein 3 (UCP3) in muscle and brownadipose tissue (34). This hypothesis suggests that freefatty acids are shuttled out of the mitochondria byUCP3 when fatty acid -oxidation predominates. Thesefree fatty acids would result from the hydrolysis ofacyl-CoAs by ACOT2, thus releasing CoASH for furtherreactions within the mitochondria during -oxidation.The free fatty acids transported out of the mitochon-dria by UCP3 would then be reactivated by acyl-CoAsynthetases to form acyl-CoAs, which could subse-quently be transported back into the mitochondria as acarnitine ester via the sequential action of carnitinepalmitoyl transferase I (CPTI) and the carnitine acyl-carnitine (CAC) transporter. This shuttle mechanismwould prevent overloading of the mitochondria withacyl-CoA and trapping of CoASH, which is vital for-oxidation and the citric acid cycle to proceed. Arole for ACOT1 has been suggested in control ofligand supply for the PPAR family of nuclear recep-tors in the form of acyl-CoAs or free fatty acidsand/or channeling fatty acids toward degradationrather than esteriﬁcation (22).In summary, the identiﬁcation of a family of humanacyl-CoA thioesterases with distinct tissue expressionand substrate speciﬁcities opens up avenues for furtherresearch into these enzymes, which may be importantin regulation of numerous intracellular processes, aswell as for maintaining robustness in response to rapidchanges in availability of energy substrates. Patientswith lowered ACOT activity have recently been de-scribed (35); however, no patients deﬁcient in theType-I family of ACOT enzymes characterized in thisstudy have yet been identiﬁed. The role of ACOTenzymes in lipid metabolism within different intracel-lular compartments suggests that future studies mayreveal their importance in inborn errors of metabolismand lipid metabolism.This study is supported by AFA sjukfo¨rsa¨krings jubileumss-tiftelse, Svenska Sa¨llskapet fo¨r Medicinsk Forskning, TheSwedish Research Council, FP6 European Union Project“Peroxisome” (LSHG-CT-2004 –512018), Åke Wibergs stif-telse, Hja¨rt-Lungfonden, Lars Hiertas Minne, Fredrik ochIngrid Thurings Stiftelse, Ruth och Richard Julins Stiftelse,Stiftelsen Professor Nanna Svartz fond, the National Networkfor Cardiovascular Research (Sweden), The Swedish Heartand Lung Foundation, and Stiftelsen Goljes minne. We thankBengt Frode Kase for Zellweger ﬁbroblasts.
